question: Boethius wrote one of the most influential books of the Middle Ages — Consolation of Philosophy — in a Roman prison cell awaiting execution. Why a consolation?
answer: Lady Philosophy visits his cell and shows that fortune's gifts were never his to lose.
choices: Lady Philosophy visits his cell and shows that fortune's gifts were never his to lose.
Christ appears in a vision and promises a heavenly reward for the suffering endured.
His friends gather outside and remind him of bonds no earthly power can take away.
He recalls a childhood faith and finds peace in the prayers his mother once taught.
context: Around 524 the senator Boethius was imprisoned by the Ostrogothic king Theodoric on a charge of treason. Awaiting execution, he wrote a dialogue in which Lady Philosophy argues that fortune's wheel turns for everyone — what fortune gives, she can take, so the things she gives were never really our possessions. Real happiness must rest on what cannot be taken. The book shaped European thought for a thousand years. Distractors are other consolation traditions: visionary, friendship, devotional.

question: By day Maimonides served as physician to Saladin's court in twelfth-century Cairo. By evening he answered legal and theological questions from Jewish communities everywhere. What work is he most remembered for?
answer: The Guide for the Perplexed — showing Aristotle and the Hebrew Bible can be read together.
choices: The Guide for the Perplexed — showing Aristotle and the Hebrew Bible can be read together.
The Kuzari — a dialogue arguing a king should choose Judaism over rival religious paths.
The Book of Beliefs — defending the Bible from skeptics by reason and observation alone.
The Zohar — a mystical reading arguing each word of Torah holds a hidden divine meaning.
context: Moses ben Maimon (1138-1204), the Rambam, fled Almohad persecution in Spain as a boy, settled in Cairo, became court physician to Saladin's vizier, codified Jewish law in the Mishneh Torah, and wrote the Guide for readers who knew both Aristotelian philosophy and Scripture and could not see how to hold them together. The distractors are real, important medieval Jewish works by other authors: Judah Halevi's Kuzari, Saadia Gaon's Book of Beliefs, and the Zohar.

question: Saadia Gaon, tenth-century head of the academy at Sura, asked a question unusual for his time: if Scripture and reason both come from God, what should you do when they seem to disagree?
answer: Reread the passage non-literally, since revelation cannot contradict what reason establishes.
choices: Reread the passage non-literally, since revelation cannot contradict what reason establishes.
Trust the plain text completely, since human reason is corrupted and revelation always wins.
Suspend judgment on the question, since limited human minds cannot resolve such a high clash.
Reject the philosophical claim, since reason was a Greek borrowing foreign to the prophets.
context: Saadia ben Joseph (882-942), the first major Jewish thinker to write systematic philosophy in Arabic, headed the great Babylonian academy at Sura. His Book of Beliefs and Opinions argued that reason and revelation are two roads to the same truths; apparent contradiction signals a misreading of one or the other — usually the literal text. The distractors are real positions actually held: scriptural literalism (some Karaite readings), skeptical suspension, and reason-rejection (a tradition Saadia was specifically arguing against).

question: Al-Ghazali was one of the most respected philosophers in the Islamic world when he abruptly resigned his Baghdad professorship, gave away his books, and walked into the desert as a wandering Sufi. What had he concluded?
answer: Philosophical proofs could only carry you so far — the rest had to be lived, not argued.
choices: Philosophical proofs could only carry you so far — the rest had to be lived, not argued.
Religious authority had grown so corrupt that only a new order could preserve honest faith.
Political life had grown so risky that his enemies at court would soon arrange a quiet end.
Greek philosophy had been refuted, so Muslims should now drop reasoning and follow prophets.
context: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (1058-1111) left his post at the Nizamiyya in 1095 after a crisis of doubt described in Deliverance from Error. He spent more than a decade traveling and writing, producing the Revival of the Religious Sciences — a synthesis arguing that the deepest knowledge of God comes through experience, not only through demonstration. He did not reject philosophy wholesale; his Incoherence of the Philosophers is a careful philosophical critique. Distractors are real medieval narratives.

question: Kripke argued 'water is H2O' is a discovery, not a definition. Once we found out water's chemistry, the identity became necessary — true in every possible situation. What followed?
answer: Some necessary truths can only be discovered by experiment, not by armchair analysis.
choices: Some necessary truths can only be discovered by experiment, not by armchair analysis.
All necessary truths are analytic, since necessity belongs only to relations among ideas.
Identity statements like 'water is H2O' are contingent — water could have had other chemistry.
Empirical inquiry can never reach necessity; chemistry tells us what is, never what must be.
context: Kripke's Naming and Necessity (1972) broke the long-standing tie between 'necessary' and 'knowable a priori.' Water might have looked different — but whatever it actually is, it could not have been anything else. Hume held the position offered in the second distractor.

question: Lewis took 'possible worlds' talk literally. When we say it was possible Napoleon won at Waterloo, he said, we mean there is a real world where he did. What did he call this view?
answer: Modal realism — every way the world could have been is a complete world that genuinely exists.
choices: Modal realism — every way the world could have been is a complete world that genuinely exists.
Modal fictionalism — possible-world talk is useful pretense; no such worlds are really out there.
Conceptualism — possibilities are mental constructions, real only insofar as some mind holds them.
Linguistic conventionalism — what counts as 'possible' is whatever community usage permits.
context: Lewis's On the Plurality of Worlds (1986) defended modal realism not as metaphor but as the simplest theory of what 'possible' really means. Most philosophers think the price is too high. The distractors are the live rivals — fictionalist, conceptualist, conventionalist accounts.

question: Aristotle laid out a three-line form: 'All men are mortal. Socrates is a man. So Socrates is mortal.' The conclusion is forced by the form alone. What did he call this?
answer: Syllogism — two premises and a conclusion forced by the form.
choices: Syllogism — two premises and a conclusion forced by the form.
Enthymeme — an argument with one premise left unstated.
Sorites — a chain of premises sliding toward a conclusion.
Dialectic — testing rival claims through question and answer.
context: The syllogism is the foundation of Western formal logic. The reasoning works because of its structure — no matter what fills the slots, the conclusion is locked in.

question: Stoics, Epicureans, and Pyrrhonian Skeptics offered students roughly the same prize at the end of philosophy: different routes, one destination. What did all three aim at?
answer: Ataraxia — an unshakable calm that no fortune, no loss, no quarrel could disturb in the wise soul.
choices: Ataraxia — an unshakable calm that no fortune, no loss, no quarrel could disturb in the wise soul.
Eudaimonia — the full flourishing of a complete human life lived well over time in a well-ordered city.
Apocatastasis — the soul's eventual restoration to its divine origin once it has been purified of matter.
Henosis — a final mystical union with the One, in which the philosopher's individual mind is absorbed.
context: The Hellenistic age was an age of empire, exile, and lost cities. The schools competed fiercely on doctrine but converged on the goal: a soul that could not be ruined from outside. Their disagreements were about which road actually got you there.

question: South Africans render the Nguni maxim "a person is a person through other persons." Beyond a kindness slogan, what metaphysical-ethical claim does Ubuntu make?
answer: Selfhood does not arrive first and then get refined by others — it is constituted by the network of recognitions and obligations a person stands inside.
choices: Selfhood does not arrive first and then get refined by others — it is constituted by the network of recognitions and obligations a person stands inside.
Each person holds inviolable natural rights prior to society; community is a voluntary contract entered for the mutual gain of its parties.
The self is an illusion; liberation requires dissolving the ego into an impersonal cosmic order that lies beyond all human attachments.
Moral worth flows from autonomous rational willing; treating others well matters because reason demands it, not because of any social tie.
context: Ubuntu, developed by Tutu and Ramose, makes a constitutive rather than additive claim: there is no pre-social self that community then polishes. Personhood is brought into being through the web of mutual recognition and obligation that the person inhabits. Distractors map onto Locke (rights-bearing self prior to society), Advaita (illusion of the ego), and Kant (autonomous rational will).

question: Stoics and Buddhists each traced suffering to a wrong relation with desire. Where do they converge — and where diverge?
answer: Both name attachment to fleeting goods as the root; Stoics retrain judgment, Buddhists uproot craving by the path.
choices: Both name attachment to fleeting goods as the root; Stoics retrain judgment, Buddhists uproot craving by the path.
Both deny desire any role; the sage extinguishes wanting itself, and each school calls that final state nirvana.
Both treat suffering as illusion; the awakened sees pain as empty and the body's distress as a category error.
Both prescribe withdrawal from the world; apatheia and nibbana converge on a shared ideal of bodily ascesis.
context: Epictetus held suffering comes from judgments about events, not events. The Buddha held suffering arises from tanha within dependent origination — extinguish craving via the path. Both locate the lever inside; the mechanism differs.

question: Aristotle said virtue is a hexis — a settled disposition built by repeated action, the way a carpenter becomes a carpenter by doing carpentry. Mencius spoke of siduan — four sprouts of moral feeling (compassion, shame, deference, judgment) the heart is born with. Where did the two agree?
answer: Virtue is a natural capacity that must be cultivated to mature; the seed is given, the tree requires practice.
choices: Virtue is a natural capacity that must be cultivated to mature; the seed is given, the tree requires practice.
Virtue is wholly innate and complete at birth; education merely uncovers what is already in the soul.
Virtue is imposed from outside; human nature is raw clay shaped only by ritual, law, and discipline.
Virtue is knowledge alone; once a person grasps the good with reason, right action follows without training.
context: Aristotle's hexis is a stable disposition formed by right action — virtue acquired like a craft. Mencius held the heart already contains four sprouts (compassion, shame, deference, judgment) that must be nourished or wither.

question: The Chandogya Upanishad has a father teach his son with the phrase tat tvam asi — that thou art. What was the philosophical claim packed into those three words?
answer: Atman, the innermost self, and Brahman, the ground of reality, are one — what seeks is what is sought.
choices: Atman, the innermost self, and Brahman, the ground of reality, are one — what seeks is what is sought.
Authoritative transmission, not personal reflection, is what secures the knowledge that liberates the soul.
The self is a fragment of the divine that returns to its source slowly across many honest lifetimes.
Each soul is made by a god who stays forever distinct from it; the right relation is reverence, not identity.
context: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8–6.16. Uddalaka Aruni teaches Svetaketu using salt-water and seed analogies and repeats tat tvam asi nine times. The claim is monist: the brahman that is the ground of the cosmos is the atman that is the ground of the person. Distractors are real Hindu rivals — Mimamsa (authority), bhakti-emanationism, and Madhva's Dvaita (no identity).

question: Confucius gave many answers when asked what ren (humaneness) was. To Yan Hui he tied it directly to li. What was the link?
answer: Ren is the inward disposition; li is its outward shape. To subdue self and return to ritual is to be humane.
choices: Ren is the inward disposition; li is its outward shape. To subdue self and return to ritual is to be humane.
Ren is universal impartial care for every person; li is the political device that publishes that care broadly.
Ren is calculation of greatest gain for family and state; li is the rule that posts the calculation clearly.
Ren is spontaneous response to the Way of nature; li a later artifice the humane person learns to drop entirely.
context: Analects 12.1: ke ji fu li wei ren — subdue the self and return to ritual is humaneness. Confucius kept ren plural in expression but firm in shape: without li, ren has no body; without ren, li is empty form. The two require each other.

question: Boethius wrote the Consolation in prison awaiting execution. Lady Philosophy challenges his grief over lost fortune — what does she argue about Fortune's gifts?
answer: They were never his to lose; the gifts stay Fortune's, and her nature is to take them back as her wheel turns.
choices: They were never his to lose; the gifts stay Fortune's, and her nature is to take them back as her wheel turns.
They were sent as a test of virtue; the man who keeps faith earns greater rewards in fullness of time.
They were arranged by fate above her; what looks cruel is part of a wider cosmic order one life cannot see.
They were illusions all along; one who studies philosophy finds her wheel never truly turned in real time.
context: Boethius wrote in a Pavia cell around 524 AD, condemned by Theodoric. Lady Philosophy personifies Fortune as a goddess turning a wheel — riches, fame, power belong to her, not to you. To grieve their loss is to misunderstand the loan. The image shaped medieval philosophy for a thousand years.

question: Aristotle in the Nicomachean Ethics distinguished two intellectual excellences. Episteme is scientific knowledge — math and physics. The other is messier and harder to teach. What is phronesis?
answer: Practical wisdom — the seasoned judgement that knows the right thing in particular cases, where rules underdetermine action.
choices: Practical wisdom — the seasoned judgement that knows the right thing in particular cases, where rules underdetermine action.
Theoretical insight — the contemplative grasp of eternal truths beyond particulars, the highest activity according to Book X.
Productive skill — the technical knowledge of the craftsman who shapes raw materials into useful or beautiful artifacts.
Civic excellence — the political competence weighing the city's competing interests, the chief virtue of lawgivers.
context: Phronesis is why Aristotle's ethics is not a set of rules. The phronimos — the practically wise person — sees the features of a particular situation and judges. There is no algorithm for living well.

question: Heraclitus said the cosmos was governed by a unifying principle he called the logos — but most people, he complained, walked through life deaf to it. What did he mean by logos, and why did he think people missed it?
answer: An ordering rational principle holding opposites in tension — like the bow whose string and frame pull against each other for power.
choices: An ordering rational principle holding opposites in tension — like the bow whose string and frame pull against each other for power.
A divine word spoken at the beginning of the cosmos — that word continues to echo through all things in continuous speech.
A mathematical ratio governing the proportions of visible things — that ratio appears in stars, plants, and shells everywhere.
A spiritual breath flowing through all things — that breath connects each soul to the cosmos as a whole through its movement.
context: Heraclitus's logos was a deep word. Stoics took it up. The Gospel of John opens with it ('in the beginning was the logos'). The Greek term covered both rational order and the speech that expresses it — a unity Heraclitus saw before the concept had a name.

question: Spinoza published his Tractatus Theologico-Politicus anonymously in 1670. The book ended with an argument that startled even tolerant readers of the day. What did he defend?
answer: Every citizen's right to think freely and say what he thinks — the state cannot rule inner judgment, and trying breeds only hypocrisy.
choices: Every citizen's right to think freely and say what he thinks — the state cannot rule inner judgment, and trying breeds only hypocrisy.
Every faith's right to its own ecclesiastical courts — religious communities should govern their members internally without civil interference.
Every guild's right to set its own trade rules — economic life should run through self-governing associations, not centralized state regulation.
Every household's right to choose its faith — fathers should determine the religion of their families, and no state may compel worship.
context: Tractatus, ch. 20. Spinoza had been excommunicated by the Amsterdam Jewish community in 1656. His defense of free expression shaped Locke, Mill, and modern liberalism.

question: Hayek argued that 'social justice' was a category mistake — like asking what color a number is. Why did he say justice could not apply to market outcomes?
answer: Justice describes intentional acts; a market outcome is not intended by any single agent who could answer for it.
choices: Justice describes intentional acts; a market outcome is not intended by any single agent who could answer for it.
Justice requires that wages match merit; a modern economy is too large for anyone to assess merit reliably.
Justice describes relations among equals; in a modern industrial society, citizens stand at very unequal stations.
Justice is a virtue of private character; extending it to public policy debases the word to mere preference.
context: For Hayek the rain that ruins a wedding is unfortunate, not unjust — there is no one whose intent it was. The pattern of incomes from millions of trades, he thought, is like the rain: it can be regretted, but to call it unjust misapplies a word that belongs to actions, not weather.

question: Boethius wrote the Consolation awaiting execution. Lady Philosophy argues the wicked are unhappier than their victims. Why?
answer: Punishment restores some good to the wicked; unpunished wickedness leaves the soul wholly disordered — the worst state.
choices: Punishment restores some good to the wicked; unpunished wickedness leaves the soul wholly disordered — the worst state.
Victims keep their virtue intact and virtue alone is happiness; the wicked spend the very faculty by which any are happy.
Victims know they have done no wrong; a clear conscience outweighs any outward suffering one endures from another.
Fortune favors the wicked only briefly so their pleasures are short; the suffering of the just is rewarded hereafter.
context: Boethius inverts the common picture. Doing evil and getting away with it looks like the best outcome; suffering evil and being avenged looks the worst. He says the opposite. Wickedness is itself the deepest wound, because it deforms the very part of a person that could attain the good. Punishment is medicine; impunity leaves the disease.

question: At third-century Alexandria, Origen taught one scripture passage could be read on three levels at once — not allegory replacing the letter, not Old paired with New, but three readings layered together. What did he map them onto?
answer: Body, soul, and spirit of the text — the literal, the moral, and the spiritual sense, all at once.
choices: Body, soul, and spirit of the text — the literal, the moral, and the spiritual sense, all at once.
Hebrew, Greek, and Latin witnesses — three textual versions cross-checked line by line for fidelity.
Author's intent, church tradition, and reader's faith — three guides triangulating one meaning.
Each Old Testament passage paired with its New Testament fulfillment — meaning fixed by the pair.
context: Origen, at the Alexandrian school, formalized a way of reading that ran from the letter to its moral application to its spiritual sense. The body, the soul, and the spirit of a passage all spoke. Later readers narrowed or expanded the scheme, but the practice of layered reading runs through medieval exegesis straight from him.

question: Proclus's Elements of Theology proves 211 propositions about the divine in Euclid's order. Each follows from the last. What was he showing?
answer: That Neoplatonism's claims hang together as one demonstrative system — metaphysics with the rigor of geometry.
choices: That Neoplatonism's claims hang together as one demonstrative system — metaphysics with the rigor of geometry.
That the gods of Greek religion could be safely abandoned, since reason alone reaches principles they pictured.
That contemplation needs no argument once the soul is purified, since the truth becomes self-evident on arrival.
That every doctrine of pagan philosophy must in time yield to the new Christian theology rising up around it.
context: Born in 412, Proclus wrote when Christianity was ascendant and pagan teaching under pressure. The Elements was a defense by demonstration: here is a system, axiom and theorem, principle and consequence. It would later steer Pseudo-Dionysius, the medieval Liber de Causis, and through them Aquinas.

question: Placide Tempels's 1945 Bantu Philosophy claimed the Baluba held a metaphysics of "vital force." Paulin Hountondji later attacked the book. What was his core objection?
answer: It described a collective worldview, not philosophy; philosophy is critical written argument by named thinkers.
choices: It described a collective worldview, not philosophy; philosophy is critical written argument by named thinkers.
It overstated African rationality; pre-colonial thought was mythic, and only colonial schools taught philosophy.
It ignored Islamic falsafa; real African philosophy ran through Cairo and Timbuktu in the Arabic tradition.
It missed the political stakes; philosophy worthy of the name must serve liberation, not metaphysical speculation.
context: Hountondji's Sur la philosophie africaine (1976) argued 'ethnophilosophy' confuses anthropology with philosophy. Distractors are colonial dismissal, Islamic-centric, and Marxist-functionalist views.

question: Kwame Anthony Appiah, raised between Kumasi and England, defends "rooted cosmopolitanism" against both nationalism and abstract universalism. What does he hold?
answer: We owe particular loyalty to the communities that formed us and real concern to every stranger; both are genuine.
choices: We owe particular loyalty to the communities that formed us and real concern to every stranger; both are genuine.
Local identities are colonial residues moral progress should dissolve; only a planetary citizenship secures real justice.
Cultural identity precedes any moral claim; outsiders cannot judge a tradition, and cross-cultural judgment is imperial.
Moral duty tracks shared blood and territory; concern for distant strangers is sentimental cover for duties at home.
context: Appiah's Cosmopolitanism (2006) holds thick local belonging and universal moral concern as compatible — against globalist erasure and identity-essentialist refusals of cross-cultural judgment.

question: Linda Tuhiwai Smith's Decolonizing Methodologies (1999) noted research on Maori was almost always by outsiders. What was her central claim?
answer: Which questions get asked, and who frames them, is itself political; method is never prior to the politics of inquiry.
choices: Which questions get asked, and who frames them, is itself political; method is never prior to the politics of inquiry.
Empirical methods stay neutral when researchers report data faithfully; bias enters only at the interpretation of results.
Knowledge belongs to its community of origin alone; outsiders studying a culture must distort what they try to describe.
Scientific procedure is universal; cultural differences shape what gets studied but cannot reach how inquiry properly works.
context: Smith argued the research question itself encodes whose categories count. Distractors are positivist neutrality, strong epistemic insularity, and Popperian universalism about method.

question: John Mohawk described the Haudenosaunee Grand Council as deciding by consensus, never by vote. What claim about legitimacy did this embody?
answer: A decision binds only those who can give reasons for it; until each objector is answered, the matter is not yet decided.
choices: A decision binds only those who can give reasons for it; until each objector is answered, the matter is not yet decided.
Legitimacy flows from clear lines of authority; a council with no final voice drifts and stalls when swift action is needed.
Procedure cannot generate legitimacy; only the consent of the governed, freely given through majority voting, can secure it.
Real political authority belongs to inherited title and lineage; deliberation refines but does not produce legitimate rule.
context: Mohawk argued the Great Law of Peace held that unanswered dissent leaves a decision incomplete. Distractors are Hobbesian sovereignty, Lockean majoritarianism, and traditionalist hereditary rule.

question: Arne Naess in 1973 contrasted 'shallow' environmentalism with 'deep ecology.' What was the *philosophical* difference, not the policy difference?
answer: Shallow values nature for human welfare; deep holds non-human life has worth independent of any use to us
choices: Shallow values nature for human welfare; deep holds non-human life has worth independent of any use to us
Shallow relies on national regulation; deep argues only voluntary local stewardship can protect land long-term
Shallow accepts moderate population growth; deep requires reducing human numbers through state-coercive policies
Shallow builds on Christian stewardship; deep returns to pre-Christian animism as the only viable cosmology
context: Naess's eight-point platform (with Sessions, 1984) opens with intrinsic value: the flourishing of non-human life has worth in itself, independent of usefulness. The contrast is not about policy intensity but about whether nature counts morally on its own terms.

question: Hans Jonas's *Imperative of Responsibility* (1979) argued traditional ethics could not handle technology's reach across generations. What new imperative did he propose?
answer: Act so the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life on Earth
choices: Act so the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life on Earth
Discount the welfare of future generations only by their probability of existing, never by pure time preference
Treat future persons as you would treat contemporaries, since temporal location is morally arbitrary in itself
Choose policies whose worst-case outcome leaves no future person worse off than the average human alive now
context: Jonas reframed Kant for an age of biotech and ecological reach: where Kant's imperative governed acts within one generation, Jonas argued technology's scale demands a duty to the *existence* of future humanity itself. His 'heuristics of fear' anticipated the precautionary principle.

question: Hume and Nagarjuna each argued there is no substantial self. Yet their metaphysical conclusions diverged sharply. How?
answer: Hume found only a bundle of perceptions and stopped at skeptical naturalism; Nagarjuna read no-self as universal emptiness.
choices: Hume found only a bundle of perceptions and stopped at skeptical naturalism; Nagarjuna read no-self as universal emptiness.
Hume held the self is a useful social fiction grounded in custom; Nagarjuna held it is a real stream of momentary dharmas.
Hume argued the self is the brain mistaken for a soul; Nagarjuna argued the body is mistaken for a witness above it.
Hume reduced the self to a transcendental unity of apperception; Nagarjuna reduced it to atman beneath the aggregates.
context: Hume in the Treatise: introspection finds only perceptions, never a self that has them. Nagarjuna extended anatman — not just persons but every dharma is sunya, empty of svabhava. Shared starting move; further step differs.

question: Augustine in his Confessions turned inward and found God 'more inward than my inmost being.' Centuries later in India, Sankara inquired into the silent witness behind every thought, searching for Brahman (the single reality underneath all appearances). Where did the two thinkers converge?
answer: Both used a stripping-away approach (apophatic): the deepest self cannot be grasped as object; it is found by saying what it is not.
choices: Both used a stripping-away approach (apophatic): the deepest self cannot be grasped as object; it is found by saying what it is not.
Both identified the soul with the rational intellect; the person is soul plus a temporary tie to one particular body.
Both held the inward self is a private mental theatre; introspection reveals states no outside observer could access.
Both took the self to be a social construction; what feels deepest is community's inherited voice speaking within.
context: Augustine's Confessions found God 'more inward than my inmost being.' Sankara's Advaita said atman is the unobjectifiable witness; neti-neti strips false identifications. Different theologies, shared apophatic structure.

question: Hamilton called the judiciary 'the least dangerous branch' in Federalist 78. What specific institutional weakness did he point to as the reason?
answer: Courts hold no army and no treasury; rulings depend on the other branches to be enforced at all.
choices: Courts hold no army and no treasury; rulings depend on the other branches to be enforced at all.
Tenure during good behavior insulates judges from voters, so partisan passion never reaches the bench.
Federal courts hear only narrow constitutional disputes; everyday questions remain with the states.
Judicial reasoning binds only the parties to a case; the public may freely ignore unconvincing rulings.
context: Hamilton's argument set up his defense of judicial review: precisely because the court is weak in the means of action — no sword, no purse — giving it the duty to read the Constitution against the legislature was no tyranny. The branch with no army and no treasury could not swallow the other two.

question: Loury in Anatomy of Racial Inequality argued that even after anti-discrimination law is enforced, a second mechanism keeps group gaps fixed. What did he name?
answer: Development bias — kids inherit parents' mentors and networks, so unequal starts compound across generations.
choices: Development bias — kids inherit parents' mentors and networks, so unequal starts compound across generations.
Structural racism — formally neutral institutions encode the dominant group's preferences and reproduce them.
Statistical discrimination — employers use group averages as proxies and penalize typical members of stigmatized groups.
Internalized inferiority — stigmatized groups absorb the culture's verdict and lower the demands placed on themselves.
context: Loury distinguished discrimination in contract (hiring, lending — which law can reach) from discrimination in contact (who mentors whom, whose child gets the introduction). The second, he argued, is the harder problem, and the one the civil rights framework was not built to solve.

question: Pluckrose and Lindsay in Cynical Theories traced 1960s French postmodernism into 2010s activist scholarship. What shift defined the later phase?
answer: Skepticism of all grand narratives hardened into one settled narrative: knowledge is structured by power along identity lines.
choices: Skepticism of all grand narratives hardened into one settled narrative: knowledge is structured by power along identity lines.
Playful textual experiment gave way to systematic analysis modeled on the rigor of the natural sciences of those decades.
The early figures broke with Marx; the later activists rebuilt the bridge between class analysis and cultural critique.
Continental thought lost ground in philosophy and migrated into literature and sociology, where it went unchallenged.
context: Pluckrose and Lindsay called the second phase 'applied postmodernism': claims the originals had advanced as suspicions were now asserted as facts. A method built to question every certainty had been turned into one that questioned every certainty except its own.

question: Readers often take Descartes's evil demon as a serious metaphysical proposal. He himself treated it as something narrower. What was its role?
answer: A device of method — a worst-case doubt set up to test which beliefs survive, then dropped once the cogito is found.
choices: A device of method — a worst-case doubt set up to test which beliefs survive, then dropped once the cogito is found.
A theological claim — the demon stands for the fallen angels, whose deceit shapes the world the senses present.
A psychological model — the demon names the mind's own deceptive tendencies before reason has been disciplined.
A serious metaphysical claim — Descartes thought a malevolent power probably governed the sensible world we know.
context: The demon appears in the First Meditation and vanishes by the Third. It is the strongest doubt Descartes can manufacture, designed to scour away every belief that could be false. Once the cogito stands even against the demon, the demon has done its job and the rebuilding can begin.

question: William James in Varieties of Religious Experience (1902) judged religion pragmatically — by its fruits in a believer's life. Rudolf Otto in The Idea of the Holy (1917) named what he thought James missed: a feeling that mixes shrinking dread with magnetic pull toward something wholly other. What was Otto's emphasis?
answer: The numinous — awe-laden dread mixed with drawing fascination; Otto's Latin name was 'mysterium tremendum et fascinans.'
choices: The numinous — awe-laden dread mixed with drawing fascination; Otto's Latin name was 'mysterium tremendum et fascinans.'
The pragmatic — a religious belief is true insofar as it makes a real, livable difference in the believer's life.
The communal — experience matters only as it forms a shared liturgy carried by a tradition across generations.
The perceptual — a sense of contact with a mind beyond one's own, evaluated like any other perceptual claim.
context: James (1902) treated religious experience pragmatically — judged by its fruits in a believer's life. Otto (1917) named what he thought James missed: the wholly-other quality of holiness itself, before any pragmatic test. The two readings still divide work on religious experience today; Alston's perceptual account is a third route.

question: Averroes replied to Al-Ghazali with The Incoherence of the Incoherence. Latins later said he taught a 'double truth' — faith and reason might flatly contradict. What did he hold?
answer: One truth, three modes — demonstration for philosophers, dialectic for theologians, rhetoric for most.
choices: One truth, three modes — demonstration for philosophers, dialectic for theologians, rhetoric for most.
Two truths held apart — what reason proves and what revelation says both bind, even when they clash.
Faith above reason — when philosophy and Quran conflict, the philosopher must submit and silence himself.
Reason above faith — when Quran conflicts with philosophy, the verse must be read as poetry, not claim.
context: Latin Averroists at Paris in the 1270s were charged with the 'double truth' thesis, and Averroes was blamed for it. But in the Decisive Treatise, Ibn Rushd argued the opposite: Quran and demonstration cannot really conflict, and where they seem to, the believer reads the verse allegorically — one truth reaching different audiences in different modes.

question: Sidgwick took ordinary intuitions — promises, gratitude, prudence — as evidence while defending utilitarianism. What role did they play?
answer: Provisional data, refined by reflection — rules survive only where they redescribe as workable utilitarian approximations.
choices: Provisional data, refined by reflection — rules survive only where they redescribe as workable utilitarian approximations.
Final authority by accumulation — the verdict of generations cannot be overturned by one philosopher's argument.
Decorative trappings — folk rules persist in language but contribute nothing once a consequentialist calculus exists.
Independent knowledge — settled intuitions are direct perceptions of moral fact, immune to theoretical revision.
context: Sidgwick's strategy was to take the rules of ordinary morality, show where they roughly tracked utility, keep what survived, and discard or revise the rest. He treated intuitions as data a philosopher tests, neither bedrock nor noise. The method later acquired names like reflective equilibrium; Sidgwick was the Victorian who first practiced it on a long scale.

question: Ockham's razor is often rendered 'the simplest explanation is best.' What did Ockham actually write, and what was he targeting with it?
answer: 'Plurality is not to be posited without necessity' — a strike against multiplying unseen entities like universals.
choices: 'Plurality is not to be posited without necessity' — a strike against multiplying unseen entities like universals.
'The simpler explanation is more probable' — a probabilistic principle later formalized by Bayesian thinkers.
'Nature does nothing in vain' — Aristotle's principle of economy, taken over to limit speculative metaphysics.
'A theory must be falsifiable' — a criterion to separate scientific claims from empty metaphysical speculation.
context: The actual Latin (in various forms across Ockham's *Summa Logicae* and commentaries) is 'pluralitas non est ponenda sine necessitate' — *don't multiply entities beyond need*. The original target was not parsimony for its own sake but specifically the bloated medieval ontology of universals, common natures, and intentional species. The 'simplest explanation' gloss came centuries later. Popper's falsifiability is a different criterion altogether.

question: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad describes brahman as neti neti — not this, not this. Why a negative method rather than positive description?
answer: Every positive predicate adds a finite limit; only by ruling out every limit does the seeker stop confusing a part for the whole.
choices: Every positive predicate adds a finite limit; only by ruling out every limit does the seeker stop confusing a part for the whole.
Brahman is a permanent mystery no sage can ever grasp, so the phrase is a humbling devotion to that ignorance.
Direct description is reserved for priests; the householder gets a negative formula his stage cannot mishandle.
Brahman exists only as the sum of negations, much as zero exists only as the absence of any quantity at all.
context: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.3.6 and 4.5.15. The via negativa strips every predicate — large, small, bright, dark, even existent — because each is a determination that confines. The move parallels Pseudo-Dionysius and Plotinus on the One. Shankara built his epistemology on it. Distractors are a fideist misread, a sociological misread, and the literal-zero error.

question: Shankara taught strict non-dualism: only Brahman (ultimate reality) is real; selves and matter are ultimately illusion. Ramanuja agreed Brahman is one — but refused to call selves and matter illusory. He named his school Vishishtadvaita ('qualified non-dualism'). What is the qualification?
answer: Brahman is one as a body is one: a unity really containing distinct selves and matter as parts, not illusions.
choices: Brahman is one as a body is one: a unity really containing distinct selves and matter as parts, not illusions.
Brahman is fully one but appears as many to finite minds; the qualification is psychological, not metaphysical.
Brahman is one essence shared among three cosmic persons, the qualification preserving devotion within unity.
Brahman is one only at the start and end of each cosmic cycle; in between, its unity is genuinely broken up.
context: Ramanuja (11th-12th c.), Sri-Bhashya on the Brahma Sutras. His sarira-sariri-bhava (body-soul) doctrine holds that selves and matter are real parts of brahman as a hand is part of a person. This rescues bhakti — you can love a beloved who is really other — without losing monism. Distractors: softened Shankara, Christian trinitarian template, Puranic cyclic view.

question: Vedanta is the Indian school that reads the Upanishads. Its first two commentators, Shankara and Ramanuja, both held Brahman (ultimate reality) is in some sense one — strict or qualified monism. Madhva, the third (13th c.), broke with both and taught Dvaita: full, permanent dualism. What defined Madhva's school?
answer: Five differences are eternally real: god from self, god from matter, self from self, self from matter, matter from matter.
choices: Five differences are eternally real: god from self, god from matter, self from self, self from matter, matter from matter.
Two realities are ultimately distinct: awareness and inert world; every other difference reduces to that one line.
All distinctions are conventional appearances within a deeper unity, and his case for monism was simply cleaner.
Soul and god are two while the soul lives; at liberation the soul reabsorbs and the duality finally collapses.
context: Madhva (13th c.) named his system the pancha-bheda, the fivefold difference, in commentaries on the Brahma Sutras and the Anuvyakhyana. The move blocks every avenue by which a clever monist could reabsorb plurality. Distractors: Samkhya's two-line dualism, a flattening Advaita misread, and a Ramanuja-style final reabsorption.

question: Pinker's The Blank Slate identifies three doctrines he says quietly shape modern thinking about human nature. What three did he name?
answer: The blank slate, the noble savage, and the ghost in the machine — Locke, Rousseau, and Cartesian dualism.
choices: The blank slate, the noble savage, and the ghost in the machine — Locke, Rousseau, and Cartesian dualism.
Original sin, free will, and divine grace — the Augustinian triad of fallen but morally accountable nature.
Id, ego, and superego — Freud's division of mind that Pinker calls the most stubborn folk model still.
Reason, passion, and appetite — Plato's tripartite soul, recast by Hume and rejected by behaviorism.
context: Pinker borrowed 'ghost in the machine' from Gilbert Ryle's 1949 jibe at Descartes. His point was not that the three doctrines are simply wrong, but that they are held tacitly — as moral backdrops rather than empirical claims — and so insulate themselves from the behavioral-genetics and cognitive-science evidence that bears on them.

question: Confucius wept when he saw ritual neglected at a sacrifice. Why did he treat li as philosophically central, not merely as etiquette?
answer: Ritual forms the inner person through bodily practice; a community in li shapes characters no rule book legislates.
choices: Ritual forms the inner person through bodily practice; a community in li shapes characters no rule book legislates.
Ritual secures obedience by impressing the people; the ruler who masters ceremony rules without needing force.
Ritual repeats the patterns of Heaven and attunes the human realm to a cosmic order most cannot perceive directly.
Ritual signals piety to spirits and ancestors; the careful sacrifice secures fortune for the family for years to come.
context: For Confucius, li was practice that worked on the practitioner. A society held by punishments breeds shame-avoidance; a society held by ritual breeds character. The bow done a thousand times shapes the bowing self. The point was formation, not decorum.

question: The junzi — the exemplary person — was Confucius's central moral ideal. What chiefly marked one, in contrast to the petty person (xiaoren)?
answer: The junzi seeks what is right; the petty person seeks what is profitable. Each weighs every choice by that test.
choices: The junzi seeks what is right; the petty person seeks what is profitable. Each weighs every choice by that test.
The junzi acts from inner spontaneity; the petty person stays bound to inherited rules and cannot improvise.
The junzi is born of noble lineage; the petty person of low family. The terms preserve an old aristocratic divide.
The junzi calculates the longest-run good for all; the petty person attends only to gains of the present hour.
context: Confucius took aristocratic vocabulary and rewrote it. Junzi had meant 'son of a lord' — birth talk. He made it character talk: whoever chose yi (rightness) over li (here meaning profit) was a junzi. Analects 4.16 sets that contrast as the simplest test.

question: Twelve centuries on, Zhu Xi rebuilt the tradition by adapting two concepts from the Daoist and Buddhist debates of his day. Which pair?
answer: Li (principle, the pattern in each thing) and qi (material force). Every thing is li expressed through some qi.
choices: Li (principle, the pattern in each thing) and qi (material force). Every thing is li expressed through some qi.
Sunyata (emptiness of self-nature) and karma (residue of past acts), used to ground why the moral self needs work.
Dao (the unconditioned way) and de (its inner power), used to anchor ritual in the impersonal order of nature.
Yin and yang (the two complementary forces), used to explain how ritual harmonizes opposites in person and state.
context: Zhu Xi (1130-1200) faced a Confucianism that had lost ground to Chan Buddhist depth and Daoist cosmology. His synthesis kept Mencius's moral seriousness but grounded it in li (here meaning principle, not ritual) and qi — concepts already at work in the rival schools.

question: Filial piety (xiao) — devotion to parents — is the cornerstone Confucian virtue. Why did Confucians treat it as philosophically deep, not custom?
answer: It is where humaneness first learns to grow. Care for parents is the root from which wider concern can spread.
choices: It is where humaneness first learns to grow. Care for parents is the root from which wider concern can spread.
It binds the political order by extending obedience to the ruler from obedience first practiced to a father.
It pays a strict moral debt: each child owes a life back to those who gave it; the accounts must be settled.
It cultivates impartial care by teaching that all are siblings, all alike descended from common ancestors.
context: Analects 1.2: filial and fraternal conduct is the root of humaneness. The argument was developmental. A person who has never learned to love particular near ones will not love distant strangers solidly. Wider concern grows outward from where love begins.

question: Maimonides wrote the *Guide* not for beginners but for one specific reader, and said he built deliberate contradictions into the text. Who was the reader, and why the contradictions?
answer: A Jew torn between Torah and Aristotle: contradictions shield esoteric truths from the unready.
choices: A Jew torn between Torah and Aristotle: contradictions shield esoteric truths from the unready.
A Muslim convert needing Aristotle and Torah reconciled at the level a mutakallim would accept.
A Kabbalist initiate prepared for sefirotic ascent: contradictions mark rungs of contemplative climb.
A talmudic jurist resolving legal contradictions: the *Guide* applies Mishnaic harmonization to theology.
context: The *Guide* opens addressed to Joseph ben Judah, Maimonides' student, and through him to readers fluent in Torah but unsettled by Aristotle. Maimonides' famous Introduction lists seven kinds of contradiction; the seventh, he says, he has used deliberately to conceal doctrines too dangerous for the unprepared. Leo Strauss read this as the founding text of esoteric writing. Whether the hidden doctrine is mortalism, eternity of the world, or something else remains disputed.

question: Bodhidharma met Emperor Wu, who listed his merit: monasteries built, sutras copied, monks fed. Bodhidharma said, "No merit." What did the refusal do philosophically?
answer: Treats merit-counting itself as the bondage Chan cuts — the ledger still posits the self that owns it.
choices: Treats merit-counting itself as the bondage Chan cuts — the ledger still posits the self that owns it.
Denies merit without inner intention — funding without true devotion behind it ripens into nothing at all.
Reserves merit for those who recite Amida's name — works outside that faith do not ripen for the doer.
Assigns merit to the sangha that did the ritual — a lay patron is one step removed from any karma.
context: Blue Cliff Record, Case 1. Bodhidharma is not denying the donations; he is denying the frame. As long as Wu counts a self that owns the merit, he has not seen what Chan points at. The reply is deflation, not insult. Intention-ethics, Pure Land, and sangha-merit distractors are positions Buddhists actually held.

question: Aristotle named two basic valid inferences. The first: 'If P then Q. P. So Q.' Rain implies wet streets; it's raining; so streets are wet. What Latin tag did logicians give this?
answer: Modus ponens — affirming the antecedent of a conditional lets you affirm its consequent, the basic forward step in deduction.
choices: Modus ponens — affirming the antecedent of a conditional lets you affirm its consequent, the basic forward step in deduction.
Modus tollens — denying the consequent of a conditional lets you deny its antecedent, the move behind theory falsification.
Disjunctive syllogism — eliminating one option in an either/or claim lets you affirm the other, used in process-of-elimination.
Hypothetical syllogism — chaining two conditionals so the first antecedent leads through the middle to the final consequent.
context: Modus ponens feels like nothing — yet it is one of two inference rules behind every deductive proof. Lewis Carroll wrote a famous puzzle about whether one needs another rule to use this one.

question: A doctor reports a hundred swans, all white. The next year a black swan turns up in Australia. Her reasoning wasn't invalid — just not the same as proof. What is its name?
answer: Inductive reasoning — generalizing from observed cases to a broader claim, where the conclusion is supported by probability but never guaranteed.
choices: Inductive reasoning — generalizing from observed cases to a broader claim, where the conclusion is supported by probability but never guaranteed.
Deductive reasoning — drawing necessary conclusions from premises whose truth forces the conclusion, where the form alone secures the inference.
Abductive reasoning — inferring the best available explanation of an observation from among rival candidates, used by detectives and physicians.
Analogical reasoning — drawing a tentative conclusion about one case from a structural similarity to another already familiar case.
context: Hume's problem of induction asks what justifies the leap — past swans gave no logical guarantee about future ones. The black swan is the textbook reminder that induction is always defeasible.

question: Mill argued utilitarianism does not require the agent to calculate consequences before every act. What did he say settled the cases of ordinary life?
answer: Inherited rules and habits — the wisdom of past calculations made by the species over centuries of practical experience.
choices: Inherited rules and habits — the wisdom of past calculations made by the species over centuries of practical experience.
Intuition of self-evident duties — a faculty independent of consequence-counting that resolves daily moral questions reliably.
Universalization of maxims — asking whether the act's principle could be willed as a law every rational agent must follow.
Consultation of experts — moral specialists trained in detailed calculation hand down the rules ordinary citizens then apply.
context: Mill answered critics who imagined a utilitarian frozen at every decision, weighing alternatives. Most cases, he said, are settled by 'secondary principles' — be honest, keep your promises, do not steal. These are inherited rules of thumb that condense centuries of consequence-counting. Calculation kicks in only where the rules conflict.

question: Daniel Callahan argued against extending the human lifespan indefinitely. His objection was not biological but conceptual. What did he claim a finite life provides?
answer: The shape that makes a human life intelligible — beginning, growth, work, and conclusion, each phase given weight by its place in a whole.
choices: The shape that makes a human life intelligible — beginning, growth, work, and conclusion, each phase given weight by its place in a whole.
The check on overpopulation that resource constraints would otherwise impose by force, making policy redundant for the question.
The fairness that comes from each generation yielding to the next, without which the young could not find places of their own.
The motivation to live well today, which dissolves once nothing pressing forecloses indefinite postponement of every important task.
context: Callahan's Setting Limits and later The Troubled Dream of Life argued that medicine's drive against death had passed beyond healing into something else. Without a sense that life is a shape and not a stretch, he thought, even successful life-extension would deliver a life harder to live well, not easier.

question: Anscombe wrote a celebrated paper on 'Intention' in 1957 that reshaped philosophy of action. What did she say marked an action as intentional?
answer: The reason for which it was done — an intentional action is one to which a certain kind of 'why?' question makes sense to ask.
choices: The reason for which it was done — an intentional action is one to which a certain kind of 'why?' question makes sense to ask.
The accompanying mental state — an intentional action is one preceded by a conscious episode of forming an intention to do it.
The bodily movement performed — an intentional action is whatever the agent caused their body to do, regardless of underlying reason.
The agent's later endorsement — an intentional action is one the agent would, on reflection, acknowledge as their own.
context: Anscombe's Intention turned philosophy of action away from inner-cause models. Her test was Aristotelian — practical reasoning visible in what the agent could say about why they were doing what they did. The work shaped Davidson, Bratman, and a generation of analytic philosophy of mind.

question: Behavioral geneticists like Plomin found that personality traits are substantially heritable — twin studies show genetic effects on shyness, openness, conscientiousness. What did Plomin say this did *not* show?
answer: That any particular outcome is fixed — heritability is a population statistic; an individual's trajectory still depends on circumstance and choice.
choices: That any particular outcome is fixed — heritability is a population statistic; an individual's trajectory still depends on circumstance and choice.
That environment matters at all — once heritability is established, the remaining variance is statistical noise rather than meaningful effects.
That training has no role — high heritability of a trait means the trait is uneducable in any practical sense for policy or schooling.
That cultural variation is illusory — high heritability of personality implies that cross-cultural personality differences must be artifacts.
context: Plomin's Blueprint (2018) summarized decades of twin and adoption studies. The findings were striking — but heritability tells you what fraction of *variance in a population* is explained by genetic differences. It does not tell you what is fixed for any given person. Confusing the two is the most common error in popular discussion of the field.

question: Hume in 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) faced an awkward fact: people disagree wildly about beauty. Yet some judgments seem clearly better than others. How did he reconcile the two?
answer: Reliable judgments require a 'true judge' — long practice, freedom from prejudice, good sense, fine perception, and broad comparison.
choices: Reliable judgments require a 'true judge' — long practice, freedom from prejudice, good sense, fine perception, and broad comparison.
Reliable judgments require objective rules — once the principles of art are codified, anyone applying them correctly reaches the same verdict.
Reliable judgments are impossible — Hume conceded the skeptic and grounded taste in nothing more than convention of one's social set.
Reliable judgments require religious sensibility — only one trained in spiritual perception can tell true beauty from its merely worldly imitations.
context: Hume's solution was to anchor taste in expert judgment without claiming objective standards. The unanimous verdict of qualified judges, formed under specified conditions, defines the standard. The move parallels his treatment of induction: not deductive certainty, but a defensible practice that survives examination of its own limits.

question: Smart and Williams argued in a famous 1973 book about a tension in act-utilitarianism: it seems to require an agent to do anything that maximizes utility. What case troubled Williams most?
answer: When acting maximally would dissolve the very projects that make the agent a person — the theory would have him erase his own identity to add a small public gain.
choices: When acting maximally would dissolve the very projects that make the agent a person — the theory would have him erase his own identity to add a small public gain.
When acting maximally would require knowing future consequences no one could possibly predict — the theory becomes impossible to apply.
When acting maximally would conflict with promises the agent had already made — the theory cannot accommodate the moral weight of given commitments.
When acting maximally would distribute goods very unequally — the theory cannot distinguish a single rich winner from a million slightly better lives.
context: Williams's chapter pressed the integrity objection: utilitarianism asks the agent to think as anyone might think, and so demands that the agent step out of their own projects whenever calculation calls for it. Smart, the utilitarian, accepted that the theory makes hard demands and held the demands defensible. The book's contrast became a standard text in ethics.

question: Rawls's later work, Political Liberalism, made a move he had not made in A Theory of Justice. What did he say his theory was now about?
answer: Not the true moral foundations of justice, but the public reasons free citizens of differing comprehensive doctrines could share for cooperating.
choices: Not the true moral foundations of justice, but the public reasons free citizens of differing comprehensive doctrines could share for cooperating.
Not the structure of any modern society, but the deeper natural law that obtains across every legitimate political community.
Not the practical implications of liberalism, but the historical conditions under which liberal regimes first arose in early modern Europe.
Not the formal axioms of a moral theory, but the psychological mechanisms by which actual citizens come to accept the principles of justice.
context: Rawls's shift was significant. A Theory of Justice presented its arguments as something close to moral truth. Political Liberalism (1993) re-cast the project as 'political, not metaphysical' — addressed to citizens who hold incompatible religious and philosophical views but who need shared public principles. The move responded to communitarian critics like Sandel.

question: Simone Weil insisted that attention — the kind given to a difficult problem in geometry, say — was itself a moral and even spiritual achievement. What did she claim attention required?
answer: Suspending the self that wants to dominate the problem — waiting empty-handed for what is there, instead of imposing what one expects to find.
choices: Suspending the self that wants to dominate the problem — waiting empty-handed for what is there, instead of imposing what one expects to find.
Concentrating the will firmly — the more forcefully the mind grips the object, the more the object yields its hidden structure to study.
Sustaining a fixed routine of training — repeated drills in concentration build attention as exercise builds physical capacity over time.
Following the natural inclinations of curiosity — attention arises wherever interest does, and cultivation merely follows the path interest opens.
context: Weil's essay 'Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God' described attention as a kind of waiting. She wrote that a wrong solution to a geometry problem can be more spiritually fruitful than the right solution if it required honest attention. Murdoch later credited Weil as a central influence on her own attention-led moral philosophy.

question: Zeno's dichotomy: to reach the door you first cross the halfway point; to reach that, the quarter point; on infinitely. So how can you ever start? Zeno was not denying motion. What was he arguing?
answer: If space divides infinitely, motion needs completing infinite tasks — and that seemed impossible, so the picture of continuous space had to be wrong.
choices: If space divides infinitely, motion needs completing infinite tasks — and that seemed impossible, so the picture of continuous space had to be wrong.
If observers measure motion at different speeds, no objective time exists — Zeno was anticipating relativistic insights about reference frames.
If objects are atoms moving in void, motion among them makes no sense — Zeno was preparing an atomist alternative to continuous Eleatic being.
If motion is rapid succession of static images, the apparent flow is mental — Zeno was making an early case for idealism about the physical world.
context: Aristotle, Physics VI. Zeno's paradoxes defended Parmenides by reductio: grant continuous motion, contradictions follow. Cauchy and Weierstrass on convergent series resolved it mathematically.

question: Marcus Aurelius praised cosmopolitanism — every rational being a citizen of one world-city. The claim was not soft globalism. What did it commit a Roman emperor to specifically?
answer: Recognizing fellow citizens of the cosmos in every barbarian, slave, and prisoner — treating each rational being as having equal moral claims.
choices: Recognizing fellow citizens of the cosmos in every barbarian, slave, and prisoner — treating each rational being as having equal moral claims.
Defending Roman frontiers as the boundary of civilization — beyond which the cosmic city could not extend without losing its working order.
Spreading Greek philosophical culture by force when needed — bringing Stoic rationality to subject peoples not yet able to appreciate it.
Subordinating Roman law to a universal divine code only philosophers grasp — putting the philosopher-emperor over the local magistrates.
context: Meditations II.1, IV.4, VI.44. The cosmopolitan ideal goes back to Diogenes ('I am a citizen of the world') through Zeno's Republic. Nussbaum's Cultivating Humanity (1997) revived the lineage.

question: Diogenes the Cynic lived in a barrel, urinated in public, ate raw meat in the marketplace. The Greek was anaideia — shamelessness. The point was not just to shock onlookers. What was he showing?
answer: That customs treating natural functions as shameful are arbitrary social convention — and seeing this frees a person from much pretense and suffering.
choices: That customs treating natural functions as shameful are arbitrary social convention — and seeing this frees a person from much pretense and suffering.
That virtue demands identification with the lowest classes — Diogenes inverted aristocratic Greek values by living as the poorest lived, in sympathy.
That public spectacle is the most effective form of education — Diogenes pioneered street theater as moral teaching, reaching beyond school walls.
That asceticism mortifies the body and elevates the soul — Diogenes drew on the older Pythagorean tradition of hardship as spiritual training.
context: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI. Cynic anaideia was philosophical theater — making the strangeness of social convention visible by violating it openly. Crates, Hipparchia, and the Stoics drew on the lineage.

question: Plato's divided line splits cognition into four levels. Lowest: conjecture about shadows. Then belief about ordinary objects. Then math reasoning from hypotheses. What did Plato place at the top?
answer: Direct intellectual grasp of the Forms themselves — unhypothetical knowledge reaching the unconditioned principles everything else descends from.
choices: Direct intellectual grasp of the Forms themselves — unhypothetical knowledge reaching the unconditioned principles everything else descends from.
Mystical union with the One that lies beyond all Forms — anticipating the Neoplatonist ascent Plotinus would later cast as cognition's summit.
Practical wisdom in concrete cases — the philosopher-king's capacity to apply abstract principles to specific decisions, above theoretical reason.
Self-knowledge of one's own immortal soul — the highest faculty turns inward to recognize its own divine nature beyond all outer objects.
context: Republic VI, 509d–511e. The line ascends from doxa (opinion) to episteme (knowledge), with the Form of the Good at the summit — illuminating all the Forms as the sun illuminates visible things.

question: Imagine consciousness as a tiny stage inside your head, with a little homunculus seated in the audience watching the show. Daniel Dennett called this the 'Cartesian Theater' and spent decades arguing it is wrong from the start — the homunculus would just need its own inner stage, and so on forever. His method, heterophenomenology, takes what a person SAYS about their experience as data, with no further authority. What does Dennett deny we have any access to?
answer: No privileged inner stage — only the brain's verbal reports about itself; nothing extra hides behind what a subject can say.
choices: No privileged inner stage — only the brain's verbal reports about itself; nothing extra hides behind what a subject can say.
No genuine causal role for mental events — pain, belief, intention — once neural states have been described.
No objective viewpoint on the world independent of the conceptual scheme an observer happens to use.
No sharp line between knowing how to do something and knowing the propositions that describe doing it.
context: Dennett's claim is that all anyone ever has of consciousness — including the conscious person — is the reports they can make. There is no inner viewer with privileged access to the show; the homunculus would just need its own inner stage, and so on forever. He called his method heterophenomenology: take reports as data, grant them no further authority. Chalmers and Block reply that the inner show is exactly what an account of consciousness must explain, not assume away.

question: Kant examined the classical proofs of God. The cosmological proof works from the world (something contingent exists, therefore a necessary cause must exist). The ontological proof works from the concept (a perfect being must, by definition, exist). Kant said the first proof secretly depends on the second. Why?
answer: Its last step moves from 'a necessary being is possible' to 'one actually exists' — and that move is the ontological argument: existence treated as part of a concept.
choices: Its last step moves from 'a necessary being is possible' to 'one actually exists' — and that move is the ontological argument: existence treated as part of a concept.
Its last step borrows from the teleological argument — design in the world is the real premise, dressed up in causal vocabulary rather than the language of purpose.
Its last step assumes the world ought to have a sufficient reason — a moral demand, not a causal one, smuggled in beneath the appearance of strict deductive logic.
Its last step rests on religious experience — the felt conviction that God exists closes the gap, not the logic of causation alone unaided by inner feeling.
context: Kant's surgery on natural theology: any cosmological proof must, at its last step, pass from the concept of an absolutely necessary being to that being's existence. But that move is exactly the ontological argument, which Kant had already attacked separately for treating existence as a property.

question: Kant denied we can prove God exists or that the soul survives death. Yet he said both must be 'postulated' — assumed as a condition — by anyone serious about morality. He starts with the highest good: virtue rewarded by the happiness it deserves. Why did this force the two postulates?
answer: If morality bids us aim at virtue rewarded with happiness, that outcome must be possible — and only an immortal soul (time to be rewarded) plus a just God (to do the rewarding) can secure it.
choices: If morality bids us aim at virtue rewarded with happiness, that outcome must be possible — and only an immortal soul (time to be rewarded) plus a just God (to do the rewarding) can secure it.
The moral law names a divine commander; a duty without a lawgiver behind it would be no real duty but only friendly advice we are at liberty to dismiss whenever inconvenient.
Nearly every culture has affirmed God and immortality, and reason gives weight to that consensus; what most peoples have agreed cannot lightly be set aside on doctrinal grounds.
Without hope of an afterlife, fear of death distorts moral judgment; immortality is conceded as a psychological aid for the moral weakness all finite humans suffer.
context: Kant's postulates of practical reason were not articles of faith but conditions of moral seriousness. If duty commands us to seek the highest good — virtue rewarded with the happiness it merits — then we must be entitled to believe in the conditions that make such an end possible, even where proof escapes us.

question: Most readers, hearing 'noumenon — the thing as it is in itself,' imagine Kant pointing to a deeper reality behind appearances. Kant said the opposite: the term is only a limit. What did he mean?
answer: The concept marks where understanding stops — it says appearances are not the whole, but offers no content.
choices: The concept marks where understanding stops — it says appearances are not the whole, but offers no content.
The concept names a special intellectual intuition that mature philosophers can train themselves to acquire.
The concept refers to divine ideas in which finite things participate — noumenal reality as archetype.
The concept is a confused holdover from pre-critical metaphysics that the mature Kant later abandoned.
context: Kant distinguished the noumenon in the negative sense — a placeholder telling us appearances are not absolute — from a positive sense in which it would name an object of some non-sensory intuition. The first is essential to the critical project. The second, he said, is something no human mind possesses.

question: Take an ordinary judgment: 'the flower is red.' Aristotle's logic treats red as a property belonging to a thing called the flower. The Kyoto-school philosopher Nishida said this gets it backwards. He called his alternative basho — Japanese for 'place' or 'field.' What was his move?
answer: Redness is not owned by a thing; it shows up in a field (vision, then consciousness, then absolute nothingness). The thing is what the field makes visible, not what carries the property.
choices: Redness is not owned by a thing; it shows up in a field (vision, then consciousness, then absolute nothingness). The thing is what the field makes visible, not what carries the property.
Redness still belongs to a substance — basho is just a new Japanese name for the underlying bearer Aristotle already identified, with the logic of subject and predicate left untouched.
Redness has its meaning only inside the public practice of language — basho is the social space where colour-claims get used, with no deeper ground beyond shared practice.
Redness is a moment in absolute spirit unfolding through history — basho is Hegel's developing whole rendered into Japanese vocabulary, with the dialectic running underneath.
context: Basho inverts subject-logic. A red flower is not a substance bearing redness; redness shows in a field of vision, set in consciousness, set in absolute nothingness (zettai mu). Aristotelian substance, Wittgensteinian language-games, and Hegelian spirit are real rivals — basho is none, and the nothingness is not the absolute whole.

question: Nishitani thought Europe had not yet thought nihilism — the loss of meaning — through to the end. He answered from sunyata, the Mahayana idea of emptiness: no thing has a self-contained nature. Look at a pine tree. What does emptiness do to it, and so to nihilism?
answer: It passes through nihilism. The pine loses its look of being self-grounded; on the far side of that loss it returns as itself — just the pine, with nothing propping it up.
choices: It passes through nihilism. The pine loses its look of being self-grounded; on the far side of that loss it returns as itself — just the pine, with nothing propping it up.
It refuses nihilism from the start. Buddhist metaphysics already holds the ground the West lost in modernity, so the European problem simply never arises with real force on Buddhist soil.
It accepts nihilism as final. The noble individual must create meaning where the indifferent world offers none — in the style of the Paris existentialists writing through the cafés.
It treats nihilism as a passing social mood. Modernity disenchanted ritual life; the cure is renewed communal practice and shared liturgy, not a metaphysical move into emptiness.
context: Religion and Nothingness (1961). Nishitani read Nietzsche, Heidegger, and the Mahayana sunyata literature together. Not refutation but transit: at the standpoint of emptiness, the pine is no self-grounded thing, and just so the pine is wholly the pine. The apologetic, Sartrean, and sociological distractors are real responses — none Nishitani's.

question: Two schools, separated by language and centuries: the Greek Pyrrhonist skeptics aimed at ataraxia — untroubled calm — by suspending all metaphysical judgment. The Indian Madhyamaka Buddhists aimed at peace through emptiness — the view that no thing has a fixed self-nature. Different worlds, same therapeutic shape. What did the two methods share?
answer: Suspension itself was the cure. The mind quiets when it stops insisting on essences. Peace follows from letting metaphysical claims go — not from finding the right one.
choices: Suspension itself was the cure. The mind quiets when it stops insisting on essences. Peace follows from letting metaphysical claims go — not from finding the right one.
Both reached the certainty that nothing exists at all; it is the radical denial of being itself that brings the practitioner peace at last.
Both held that ordinary perception is wholly reliable; the disputes that disturb the mind are caused only by careless use of philosophical jargon.
Both grounded their peace in a positive metaphysics of the One; tranquility comes from contact with the single substance behind appearances.
context: Sextus Empiricus described epoche — suspension of assent — producing ataraxia. Nagarjuna's catuskoti refused all four positions on inherent existence; emptiness is not a thesis but release from theses. Philosophy as therapy.

question: Hegel's dialectic — development through contradiction, where opposing tendencies generate a new form — was his account of how ideas and history move. Engels in Dialectics of Nature (1870s, pub. 1925) extended it into the physical world. What central claim did he defend?
answer: Nature itself develops through contradiction: heat water enough and a quantitative change (rising temperature) yields a qualitative one (becoming steam) — dialectic at work in matter.
choices: Nature itself develops through contradiction: heat water enough and a quantitative change (rising temperature) yields a qualitative one (becoming steam) — dialectic at work in matter.
Nature is fundamentally mechanical: every change at every scale reduces to the motion of matter under fixed Newtonian laws, with no deeper pattern at work in chemistry or biology.
Nature is teleological: each species, mineral, and force aims at an end set for it in the rational order of beings, and the task of natural science is patiently to trace that order.
Nature is layered: each level of organization (atomic, chemical, biological) adds powers not derivable from the level beneath, but no contradiction is at work in any upward step.
context: Engels wrote Dialectics of Nature in the 1870s but left it unpublished; it appeared only in 1925. He drew examples from chemistry, biology, and physics — water heated through a threshold becomes steam, a seed negates itself in the plant, the plant in the seed — and argued the dialectical pattern Hegel had seen in thought was at work in matter. Later philosophers of science have contested the move sharply.

question: The fourth-century Yogacara school summed up its position as cittamatra — mind-only. Rivals heard solipsism. What were Vasubandhu and Asanga actually claiming?
answer: What we take as outer objects is built by mental processes; the analysis is about appearance, not other minds.
choices: What we take as outer objects is built by mental processes; the analysis is about appearance, not other minds.
Only one mind exists, and every other apparent mind is a projection that mind has generated within itself.
Matter exists but cannot be known directly; the mind copies what is out there, and the copy is what we meet.
Mind and matter are two aspects of one neutral substance; the appearance of difference is itself a mental effect.
context: Yogacara — also called Cittamatra or Vijnanavada — emerges with Asanga and his half-brother Vasubandhu in the fourth century. Their claim concerns the structure of experience: every object we encounter has already been processed by perception, conception, and karmic predisposition. They were not denying other minds (that was the Madhyamaka-leaning critique of them) and not denying matter outright (that was Berkeley's later position, structurally distinct). The dual-aspect distractor is Spinoza's view, a real rival from a much later tradition.

question: Wittgenstein closed his Tractatus with a strange instruction: the reader who has understood his sentences must finally recognize them as nonsensical and throw them away — "kick the ladder down" after climbing it. What did he mean about his own book?
answer: Its sentences violate its own theory of meaningful language, so they work only as a ladder to a view that cannot itself be stated
