choices: It is a draft that he intended to revise once symbolic logic had matured enough to express its claims rigorously and properly
Its sentences violate its own theory of meaningful language, so they work only as a ladder to a view that cannot itself be stated
It is meant as deliberate parody of metaphysics, showing every philosophical sentence ever written collapses into pure technical nonsense
Its propositions are true only for the author and become false the moment any other reader tries to make philosophical use of them
context: Tractatus 6.54 — the famous "ladder" passage. Wittgenstein's picture theory says only sentences depicting possible facts are meaningful; but his own sentences are about the logical form of meaning itself, not facts. So by his own lights they are nonsense — yet useful nonsense, like a ladder you discard after climbing. This self-undermining structure is what distinguishes the Tractatus from ordinary metaphysics.

question: "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent" — the closing line of the Tractatus. The Vienna Circle read it as dismissing metaphysics. Wittgenstein was furious. What did he say the silence actually honors?
answer: Ethics, aesthetics, and the meaning of life — the most important things, which show themselves but cannot be stated as propositions
choices: Empirical science, since only scientific claims meet the strict logical requirements that propositional language must satisfy to count as sensible
Ethics, aesthetics, and the meaning of life — the most important things, which show themselves but cannot be stated as propositions
Religion specifically, which he regarded as refined superstition that polite philosophical conversation ought to pass over and leave without comment
Personal experience, because subjective states are private and so any attempt to put them into shared public language must necessarily distort them
context: Tractatus 7. Wittgenstein wrote to his publisher that the unwritten half of the book was the important half — "that which I have not written." The Vienna Circle read him as a fellow positivist saying metaphysics is nonsense and good riddance. He insisted they had it backward: silence about the highest things is reverence for them, not dismissal of them.

question: A census taker counting bodies, a vaccination program rolling through a province, a sewer plan drawn over a city map — Foucault dated a shift in the late 18th century when power began acting on populations like this rather than commanding individuals one by one. He called it biopolitics. What was its object and aim?
answer: The life of the population as a whole — its birth rates, health, longevity — managed by statistics and public hygiene.
choices: The life of the population as a whole — its birth rates, health, longevity — managed by statistics and public hygiene.
The conscience of the individual subject — examined, confessed, and corrected by the parish priest or his secular heir.
The political authority of the monarch — gradually shared with parliaments answerable to a propertied middle class.
The legal definition of the citizen — codified in constitutions and bills of rights guaranteeing inalienable liberties.
context: Foucault dated the shift to roughly the late 18th century, when states started counting bodies and tracking causes of death. A census, a vaccination program, a sewer plan: these manage a population rather than command an individual. The right to kill receded; the duty to administer life advanced.

question: The Quebec government commissioned Lyotard in 1979 to report on knowledge in computerized societies. His phrase 'incredulity toward metanarratives' — the grand stories of Enlightenment progress and Marxist emancipation — got read as moral verdict. He insisted it was something else. What was his claim?
answer: A descriptive report that, in computerized societies, those grand legitimating stories no longer command working belief.
choices: A descriptive report that, in computerized societies, those grand legitimating stories no longer command working belief.
A normative argument that those grand stories of universal progress had been morally falsified by the wars of the century.
A theological wager that any narrative beyond the parable of the individual soul exceeds what reason can warrant.
A psychological diagnosis that modern subjects, exhausted by ideology, can no longer summon the energy such stories ask.
context: Lyotard's commissioned study was a sociology of knowledge: in technical, information-rich societies, knowledge is justified locally by 'small narratives' tied to performance rather than by appeal to a single universal story. He was not declaring metanarratives wicked. He was reporting that, as a matter of fact, they had stopped doing the legitimating work they once did.

question: Picture a sincere seeker — open to God, looking, finding no belief. Schellenberg's 1993 hiddenness argument: a perfectly loving God would not let such a person stay in the dark. Such people exist. What follows, and how do theists reply?
answer: No such all-loving God exists. Theist replies fall in three families: free will (God lets people resist grace), epistemic distance (faith needs the room hiddenness gives), final reconciliation.
choices: No such all-loving God exists. Theist replies fall in three families: free will (God lets people resist grace), epistemic distance (faith needs the room hiddenness gives), final reconciliation.
The argument suspends itself: 'open to relationship' cannot be defined without circular appeal to the very belief at issue, so the central premise turns out unstable on close inspection.
Hiddenness reveals divine pedagogy at work in formation; theist replies converge on free-will theodicy combined with Hick's soul-making framework as a single unified position, not three.
Hiddenness tells against deism but leaves classical theism untouched; theist replies turn on the difference between a personal and a merely cosmic divinity — only the latter in the dock.
context: Schellenberg's argument is the major hiddenness move in current philosophy of religion. The 1993 version concludes that an all-loving God of the relevant kind does not exist. The three live theistic replies are free-will (resistible grace), epistemic-distance (faith requires hiddenness — John Hick), and universalist (final reconciliation). The distractors scramble those positions in instructive ways.

question: Kuhn said normal science is "puzzle-solving" within a framework no one questions. Anomalies accumulate, crisis arrives, revolution happens. What specifically changes when the new paradigm wins?
answer: Standards for what counts as a legitimate problem, a good explanation, and a relevant observation shift together; the old questions stop seeming pressing
choices: A single false prediction is decisively refuted by a crucial experiment, prompting the community to abandon the old theory for its successor
Standards for what counts as a legitimate problem, a good explanation, and a relevant observation shift together; the old questions stop seeming pressing
A more comprehensive theory absorbs the older one as a limiting case, so the previous framework is preserved as an approximation, not overturned
A younger generation of researchers introduces new mathematical tools that finally allow the existing puzzles to be solved with the methods at hand
context: Structure of Scientific Revolutions, chs. 4–9. Newtonian mechanics did not just get replaced; the questions Newtonians cared about (force at a distance) and the ones Einsteinians cared about (frame-relative measurement) are not the same questions. This is not Popper's falsification model — Kuhn argued no single experiment ever forces a paradigm out.

question: Aristotle's 'motion' meant any change toward a thing's natural place — a falling rock, a growing plant. Galileo's 'motion' meant displacement in time. Same word, different worlds. Kuhn called this incommensurability. What did Kuhn claim?
answer: Terms get their meaning from their place in a web of surrounding concepts; change the web and the terms shift with it, leaving no neutral vocabulary above paradigms to translate sentence by sentence.
choices: Terms get their meaning from their place in a web of surrounding concepts; change the web and the terms shift with it, leaving no neutral vocabulary above paradigms to translate sentence by sentence.
Rival paradigms cannot be rationally compared at all; choice between them is settled by preference or social conformity — Feyerabend's stronger move, sometimes miscredited to Kuhn.
Rival paradigms cannot both be true, so a scientific community must collectively decide which to accept by majority vote of working researchers in good methodological standing.
Rival paradigms describe distinct domains of nature that do not really overlap, letting each remain authoritative within its own bounded territory of scientific inquiry.
context: Structure, postscript (1969). Kuhn's point is semantic-holist: scientific terms get their content from their place in the surrounding conceptual web, so changing the paradigm silently changes what the words mean. There is no paradigm-neutral vocabulary to do clean sentence-by-sentence translation. Kuhn denied this meant 'no rational comparison' — that was Feyerabend's stronger move, often miscredited to Kuhn.

question: Feyerabend's 1975 Against Method ended in 'anything goes.' Critics read it as 'science is no better than astrology.' He resisted that — called himself a 'flippant Dadaist' — and pointed to the historical record. What was his argument?
answer: Every methodological rule philosophers proposed has been violated by some successful real science; the rules are bad descriptions, not bad practice.
choices: Every methodological rule philosophers proposed has been violated by some successful real science; the rules are bad descriptions, not bad practice.
Science has no special claim to truth; it stands on the same epistemic footing as astrology or any traditional knowledge a culture happens to produce.
Science is a purely social construction in which truth is decided by powerful institutions; methodological talk just disguises academic politics.
Scientists should deliberately drop all methodological constraints in their daily work, since following any rules systematically prevents breakthroughs.
context: Against Method, ch. 1. Feyerabend's argument was historical: Galileo violated the empirical-evidence rule (the tower argument), Bohr violated consistency (electron orbits vs. Maxwell), Einstein violated falsificationism. 'Anything goes' was a sarcastic gloss on the only methodology compatible with the actual record. The strong-relativist reading came later — Feyerabend himself resisted it.

question: Williams pictured Jim: a captain has lined up twenty villagers; shoot one and nineteen go free, refuse and all twenty die. Utilitarianism says shoot. Williams's objection was not about cruelty, rules, or virtue. What was it?
answer: Utilitarianism treats Jim as a neutral conduit for impersonal calculation, dissolving the projects and commitments that make him this agent.
choices: Utilitarianism treats Jim as a neutral conduit for impersonal calculation, dissolving the projects and commitments that make him this agent.
Utilitarianism wrongly counts the captain's cruelty as one more disutility, missing that killing innocents is a distinct wrong (Murdoch/Anscombe).
The arithmetic is correct, but the precedent erodes society's general inhibition against killing innocents — a rule-consequentialist worry.
Refusing expresses a compassion the captain lacks; virtue ethics judges by character rather than consequences, and commends refusal here.
context: Williams used the Jim case in 'A Critique of Utilitarianism' (1973) to show that utilitarian calculation cannot recognize the personal shape of moral life. Jim is not a neutral calculator; he is a particular person with projects and commitments that constitute who he is. Asking him to shoot — even when the arithmetic says shoot — alienates him from his own moral agency. The three rival objections (cruelty, rule-erosion, virtue-ethics reframing) are presented alongside as the standard contenders.

question: MacIntyre's After Virtue (1981): emotivism — 'X is good' means 'I approve, do as I do' — is wrong as theory of how moral language should work, yet accurate of how it now functions. How can both halves be true?
answer: Aristotle's framework — humans aimed at a telos at which virtues let us flourish — once gave 'good' real content. We lost it; the words remain, and now function emotively, as emotivism describes.
choices: Aristotle's framework — humans aimed at a telos at which virtues let us flourish — once gave 'good' real content. We lost it; the words remain, and now function emotively, as emotivism describes.
Moral language never had genuine cognitive content from the start; emotivists notice aloud what other ethical schools had long obscured behind layers of metaphysical apparatus and pretended depth.
Modern science showed there are no moral facts to refer to, so whatever teleology the older Aristotelian tradition imagined was false from the start (Mackie's error theory, no loss involved).
The institutions that trained moral judgment — church, guild, village — have collapsed; private morality necessarily becomes emotive once communal practice no longer anchors its day-to-day use.
context: In After Virtue (1981), MacIntyre argued that modern moral debates feel interminable because we use moral language detached from the Aristotelian framework — virtues directed at a human telos — that once made the language tractable. Emotivism is false as a theory of how moral language must work, but a correct description of how it works now. Distractor B is the strong emotivism MacIntyre rejects; C is a Mackie-flavored error-theory reading; D is a sociological gloss that misses MacIntyre's specifically Aristotelian point.

question: Suhrawardi, executed at 36 in Aleppo, founded Illuminationism. Aristotle's recipe for definition — broader kind (animal) plus distinguishing trait (rational) — works for ordinary things but fails on the deepest realities: light, pain, self. What did he offer?
answer: Direct presence. Light shines, pain hurts, the self is self-aware — known by their own appearance, not by placement under a wider genus. He called it luminous self-disclosure.
choices: Direct presence. Light shines, pain hurts, the self is self-aware — known by their own appearance, not by placement under a wider genus. He called it luminous self-disclosure.
Negation alone — for these realities we can only say what each is not (not finite, not dark, not divided); every positive statement we attempt falsifies the thing it tries to describe.
Mystical silence — the highest objects of thought are reached only when the philosopher gives up speech and reasoning; they cannot be theorized, only encountered in inward wordless attention.
Demonstration from cause — to know what light truly is, we must show what physical or metaphysical agency produces it; the philosopher's task is the patient business of causal explanation.
context: Shihab al-Din al-Suhrawardi's Hikmat al-Ishraq recast the Platonic Forms as degrees of light and grounded knowledge in unmediated self-presence rather than in Aristotelian syllogism. The tradition shaped Persian philosophy for centuries through Mulla Sadra. Suhrawardi was executed in Aleppo in 1191 on the orders of Saladin's son.

question: Two voices speak in practical reason. Egoism: pursue your own good. Utilitarianism: pursue the general good. Sidgwick spent The Methods of Ethics trying to show that on reflection these collapse into one principle. He could not. What did he call the gap?
answer: The 'dualism of practical reason' — both voices look self-evident on honest reflection, neither yields to the other, and reason alone cannot say which to obey when they pull apart.
choices: The 'dualism of practical reason' — both voices look self-evident on honest reflection, neither yields to the other, and reason alone cannot say which to obey when they pull apart.
The 'is-ought gap' — no description of what nature is can ever ground a prescription about how one ought to act, so ethics floats free of empirical fact and natural science alike.
The 'naturalistic fallacy' — 'good' cannot be defined by any natural property such as pleasure (Moore, 1903), so utilitarianism's identification of good with pleasure fails at the first step.
The 'fact-value distinction' — values are projected onto a neutral natural world, so two rational agents may genuinely disagree about values without either being in error about the world.
context: Sidgwick admitted at the close of his great book that without an appeal to theism — a moral order in which doing right and doing well coincide — practical reason fractured. Either pursue your own happiness or the general happiness; each looked self-evident, and reason alone could not arbitrate. He called this the most discouraging conclusion of his life's work.

question: Husserl took from Brentano the claim that every mental act reaches out toward an object — fear is fear of, hope is hope of. What did Husserl add to this picture of intentionality?
answer: Each act has a paired noesis (the meaning-act) and noema (object-as-meant) — the object's mode of givenness is itself part of the act.
choices: A real external cause behind each act, since without a worldly cause the apparent directedness of the mind would have no content to fix on at all.
A hidden drive expressed by each act, making the conscious object a mere screen onto which deeper unconscious aims project themselves systematically.
Each act has a paired noesis (the meaning-act) and noema (object-as-meant) — the object's mode of givenness is itself part of the act.
A neural process realizing each act, so 'aboutness' is finally a relation between brain states and the causal environment they have evolved to track.
context: Brentano in 1874 revived intentionality from the Scholastics. Husserl's Logical Investigations and Ideas I added the noesis/noema pair: the same tree can be perceived, doubted, remembered, or hoped-for; the aspect under which the object is given belongs to the act itself, not merely to a private inner image of the thing.

question: Heidegger refused to call us 'rational animals' or 'subjects.' He used Dasein — 'being-there' — to mark what older labels missed. What structural feature sets Dasein apart, on his account?
answer: Dasein is the being for whom its own being is an issue — it cares what it is, projects possibilities, and must take a stance on its existence.
choices: Dasein is the being equipped with reason and language, able to grasp universal essences that other animals can only respond to as bare biological stimuli.
Dasein is the being made in the image of God, bearing a rational soul whose dignity grounds the rights that distinguish persons from mere things in nature.
Dasein is the being for whom its own being is an issue — it cares what it is, projects possibilities, and must take a stance on its existence.
Dasein is the being shaped by social structures — kinship, language, economy — that no animal inherits and that determine what each individual can come to be.
context: Being and Time (1927). Heidegger chose Dasein to avoid every loaded inheritance: not soul, not mind, not subject, not consciousness. The hyphen in being-there marks what he wanted in view: a being whose being is in question for it. The rock does not care whether it is a rock; Dasein cares whether it is itself.

question: Heidegger said every Dasein finds itself underway — born into a body, language, century, mood — none chosen. He called this thrownness (Geworfenheit). What did the term add?
answer: Facticity is not contingent backdrop but the structure of existence — Dasein never starts from a neutral zero; it is always already partway through a situation.
choices: Circumstance determines character — choices are products of environment, and the appearance of freedom reduces to ignorance about the real causes at work.
Facticity is not contingent backdrop but the structure of existence — Dasein never starts from a neutral zero; it is always already partway through a situation.
Suffering is universal and instructive — the unchosen conditions teach humility and form a moral education that an easier life would have spared us from having.
Society shapes the self at every level — any account of personal freedom that ignores class, race, and gender is naive about the conditions that make agency possible.
context: Being and Time §29. Geworfenheit names a structural feature, not a sad fact. Sartre would later say existence precedes essence; for Heidegger no Dasein ever stands at a Sartrean zero point. The situation is already begun, the mood is already set, the possibilities are already narrowed. Projection always rides on thrownness.

question: Medieval thinkers fought over whether universals like 'redness' or 'humanity' exist. Abelard rejected both pure realism and pure nominalism. What was his middle path?
answer: Universals are not things but mental concepts (sermones) abstracted from real similarities among particulars.
choices: Universals are not things but mental concepts (sermones) abstracted from real similarities among particulars.
Universals are real things existing apart from particulars, accessed by intellect as Plato's Forms taught.
Universals are real things in particulars themselves, the shared form embedded in each member of a kind.
Universals are merely names (flatus vocis) — breath in the air with no foundation in things at all.
context: Abelard's *Logica Ingredientibus* threads between Roscelin's pure nominalism (universals are just sounds) and William of Champeaux's pure realism (universals are things). His conceptualism: the mind abstracts a common concept from real resemblances — neither inventing the likeness nor finding a Platonic Form. The position resurfaces in Locke, Hume, and contemporary 'trope theory' debates.

question: Does 'exists' mean the same in 'God exists' and 'this oak exists'? Aquinas said no — it applies analogically (by likeness, not same sense). Scotus: it applies univocally — same sense — to both. What was his argument?
answer: If 'being' meant something different of God than of creatures, we could not form the thought 'God exists' — minds would lack a shared concept to extend. One minimum concept must apply the same way.
choices: If 'being' meant something different of God than of creatures, we could not form the thought 'God exists' — minds would lack a shared concept to extend. One minimum concept must apply the same way.
Being is predicated of God and creatures equivocally — they share only the bare noise of 'exists,' with no real concept the human mind can hold in common between the two cases at all.
Being is predicated of God only negatively — we can say what God is not (not finite, not temporal, not material), never anything positive, since finite minds cannot grasp the infinite directly.
Being is grasped only by direct mystical vision — what 'exists' means when said of God is encountered, never conceived; theology only records the vision rather than reasoning to it from premises.
context: Scotus's argument: if 'being' shifted meaning between God and creatures, we could not even *form* the thought 'God exists' — our minds would have no shared concept to extend. So one minimum-content concept of being must apply univocally; analogy enters only at the level of *how* a being is, not *that* it is. The dispute shaped Christian philosophy for centuries; Heidegger blamed univocity for inaugurating the 'forgetting of being.'

question: In 1902 Russell sent Frege a letter that destroyed his life work. Consider the set of all sets not members of themselves. Is it a member of itself? Either answer contradicts the other. What did the paradox show?
answer: Frege's axiom that every concept defines a set was inconsistent — you cannot let any well-formed condition carve out a set without breeding contradictions
choices: Frege's axiom that every concept defines a set was inconsistent — you cannot let any well-formed condition carve out a set without breeding contradictions
Mathematics could not be founded on set theory at all, since collections of abstract objects turned out to be a fundamentally incoherent notion
Self-reference is illegitimate in any formal system, so axioms must explicitly forbid any sentence that mentions the system it belongs to
Infinite collections cannot be treated as completed totalities, leaving only finite sets as legitimate mathematical objects for foundations
context: Russell's paradox, 1902. Frege had just sent volume 2 of the Grundgesetze to press; in the appendix he wrote that "a scientist can hardly meet with anything more undesirable than to have the foundation give way as the work is finished." His fix didn't hold. Russell's eventual escape was type theory — stratifying objects into levels so the paradoxical set couldn't even be formed. Zermelo's separation axiom became the standard repair instead.

question: G.E. Moore raised his hand at a 1939 lecture: "Here is one hand." Then the other: "And here is another." He claimed this refuted skepticism about the external world. Why did this work?
answer: He was more certain his hands existed than of any premise leading to skepticism — so the skeptical argument must contain a less certain premise to reject
choices: He was more certain his hands existed than of any premise leading to skepticism — so the skeptical argument must contain a less certain premise to reject
Direct sense perception is logically prior to philosophical reasoning, so any conclusion conflicting with what we see is refuted by the perceptual evidence
Skeptics depend on language shared with non-skeptics, so denying that hands exist already presupposes the common-sense framework they wished to deny
Holding up a hand is a public act witnesses can verify, so the existence of the hand is confirmed independently by everyone present at the demonstration
context: Moore's 1939 "Proof of an External World." The move looks naive but is sophisticated: Moore wasn't claiming to refute the skeptic on the skeptic's own terms. He was running the argument backward — if a chain of reasoning leads to "no hands exist," but I am more sure hands exist than of any link in the chain, I am rationally entitled to reject the chain. Wittgenstein took the move seriously enough to spend his last notebook (On Certainty) wrestling with it.

question: Frege made a sentence that looks like a joke: "the concept horse is not a concept." His point: in "Bessie is a horse," the words "is a horse" don't name a thing — they say something of Bessie. He called that role predicative. What goes wrong if you try to refer to a concept by saying "the concept horse"?
answer: The phrase puts the concept into a name-slot, but concepts live in the predicate-slot ("…is a horse"). Naming one converts it into an object — the kind of thing concepts apply to.
choices: The phrase puts the concept into a name-slot, but concepts live in the predicate-slot ("…is a horse"). Naming one converts it into an object — the kind of thing concepts apply to.
Concepts are private mental items, so language can only point at them indirectly, through the public objects different thinkers happen to share between them.
Universals like horseness lack independent existence, so phrases that look like they name a universal must really be naming some class of similar individuals.
Names refer through descriptions, and concepts lack descriptions, so "the concept horse" must denote whichever description fits the predicative role.
context: Frege's 1892 "On Concept and Object." In "the horse is brown," "the horse" is the object slot, "is brown" is the concept slot. The two roles cannot exchange. The paradox: no theory of the distinction can be stated without violating it. Wittgenstein turned this into the Tractarian doctrine of what can be shown but not said.

question: The Vienna Circle's verification principle held that a sentence is meaningful only if it can be empirically verified or is true by definition. Critics noticed the principle wrecks itself. Why?
answer: It is itself neither empirically verifiable nor true by its own definitions — so by its own standard the principle is literally meaningless
choices: It is itself neither empirically verifiable nor true by its own definitions — so by its own standard the principle is literally meaningless
Empirical verification requires inductive inference, which rests on metaphysical assumptions about nature the principle was designed to expressly forbid
Definitions can never be wholly stipulative, so the analytic escape clause secretly imports synthetic content the framers wished to keep out
Universal scientific generalizations cannot be conclusively verified by finite observation, leaving most laws of science on the meaningless side
context: Critics like Popper and (eventually) Ayer himself raised the self-refutation objection. Ayer tried weakening verifiability to confirmability, but each loosening either let metaphysics back in or still excluded the principle itself. Proponents replied that the principle was a proposal or convention — but stating positivism in positivist terms haunted the program.

question: In *Der logische Aufbau der Welt* (1928), Carnap tried to build the world — physics, minds, objects — from one primitive relation between experiences. What was the radical aim?
answer: To show every scientific concept could be logically built from one observer's stream of experience, so all knowledge rests on a transparent base
choices: To show every scientific concept could be logically built from one observer's stream of experience, so all knowledge rests on a transparent base
To replace metaphysical disputes with a sociological survey of how scientific communities settle questions, turning philosophy into empirical study of inquiry
To derive necessary truths of physics from updated Kantian categories, so the synthetic a priori survives in modern science as a structural constraint
To found mathematics on a primitive ordering relation among formal symbols, finishing the logicist program Russell and Whitehead left incomplete in Principia
context: Carnap's *Aufbau*. The primitive was "remembered similarity" between cross-sections of experience. He attempted constitution-definitions for the autopsychological, physical, heteropsychological, and cultural realms in turn. Goodman's *Structure of Appearance* (1951) showed the basic similarity construction wouldn't carry the load — but the ambition shaped later epistemology, including Quine's naturalism.

question: By the late 1950s logical positivism had collapsed. Blows came from Popper, the later Wittgenstein, and Quine. Quine's "Two Dogmas" (1951) struck which load-bearing pillar?
answer: The analytic-synthetic distinction — no clean line separates truths-by-meaning from truths-about-the-world, so the positivist sorting of sentences cannot be drawn
choices: The analytic-synthetic distinction — no clean line separates truths-by-meaning from truths-about-the-world, so the positivist sorting of sentences cannot be drawn
The principle's demarcation of science from metaphysics, since falsifiability rather than verifiability is the criterion that tracks real scientific practice
The doctrine that ordinary-language usage exhausts meaning, since technical scientific concepts go beyond what competent speakers ordinarily do with words
The behaviorist account of mental states, since first-person reports of inner experience cannot be reduced to dispositions to give verbal or bodily replies
context: Quine's "Two Dogmas" (1951) attacked two pillars: the analytic-synthetic distinction, and reductionism (each meaningful sentence reduces to a construction from immediate experience). His alternative was confirmational holism — only whole theories face the tribunal of experience. Popper had attacked with falsifiability; Wittgenstein's *Investigations* (1953) dissolved the picture of language the *Tractatus* had given the Circle.

question: Adorno and Horkheimer wrote Dialectic of Enlightenment in exile from the Nazis. They argued something disturbing: the Nazism they fled was not Enlightenment's failure but its consequence. What was their central claim?
answer: Enlightenment reason, by reducing all things to what can be calculated and controlled, turned on itself and produced new myths and new barbarism.
choices: Enlightenment reason, by reducing all things to what can be calculated and controlled, turned on itself and produced new myths and new barbarism.
Enlightenment ideals were sound but betrayed by irrationalists who hijacked them; the right response is to recover the original Kantian project.
Enlightenment failed because it never fully escaped religion; only a more complete secularization of reason can deliver on its original promise.
Enlightenment is a Western parochialism mistaken for universal truth; only stepping outside its frame can show what its categories had occluded.
context: The book opens with the line that the Enlightenment aimed to disenchant the world and ended by enchanting it differently. Adorno and Horkheimer saw instrumental reason — reason as pure calculation of means — as containing the seed of its own reversal.

question: Habermas worried that Adorno and Horkheimer had left reason itself in ruins, with no resources to criticize anything. His Theory of Communicative Action proposed a different kind of rationality. What did he argue?
answer: Reason oriented to reaching understanding through argument, not to controlling outcomes, has its own standards built into ordinary speech itself.
choices: Reason oriented to reaching understanding through argument, not to controlling outcomes, has its own standards built into ordinary speech itself.
Reason is fully exhausted by instrumental calculation; the older critical theorists were right, and the only remaining stance is aesthetic refusal.
Reason is a Western construct masking power relations; the task of theory is to unmask each claim to reason as a disguised demand for domination.
Reason is best modeled on natural science and engineering; political and ethical disputes reduce to technical questions of efficient policy design.
context: Habermas thought everyday acts of arguing already commit speakers to standards — that what one says be true, sincere, and right. These standards are not external to discourse; they are what makes discourse possible at all.

question: Reliabilism: knowledge is belief from a reliable process. But every belief comes from many processes at once — "vision," "vision in good light," "vision of a barn at noon." This is the generality problem. Why does the choice bite?
answer: Pick narrow process types and everything looks reliable; pick broad ones and nothing does
choices: Pick narrow process types and everything looks reliable; pick broad ones and nothing does
Reliability runs across possible worlds, and world-rankings depend on prior similarity judgments
Process types are mental categories, so reliability rests on psychology externalism denies matters
Reliable processes still yield occasional falsehoods, so any threshold for "enough" is arbitrary
context: Conee and Feldman, 1998. Reliabilism gives no answer until "the" process type is fixed, and nothing internal to the theory picks one. Goldman tried anchoring it in cognitive science (the type the system actually employs); critics replied that the relevant grain is itself a normative choice.

question: Sosa thought reliabilism still missed something. A working thermometer is reliable — but we credit it with accurate readings, not knowledge. What did virtue epistemology add to lift true belief into knowledge?
answer: The belief must be true because of the believer's competence — an achievement, not just an output
choices: The belief must be true because of the believer's competence — an achievement, not just an output
The belief must be the conclusion of an argument the believer could lay out on demand
The belief must survive in nearby worlds where details of the situation are varied a bit
The belief must serve the believer's practical ends rather than meeting an idealized standard
context: Sosa's archery image: an arrow hits the target accurately (luck), adroitly (skill), or aptly (because of skill). Knowledge is apt belief. Greco and Zagzebski added thicker virtues — open-mindedness, intellectual courage, humility. Distractors: access-internalism, safety, pragmatism, social corrective.

question: Every reason you give for a belief rests on another reason; that one on another. The skeptic Agrippa noted only three things this chain can do — stop, loop back, or run forever. That's his trilemma. Foundationalism — call it the stop-view — picks the first. What is it betting on?
answer: Basic beliefs warranted without further evidence — direct experience or rational insight stop the regress not by escaping it but by being a kind of warrant the regress argument never threatened.
choices: Basic beliefs warranted without further evidence — direct experience or rational insight stop the regress not by escaping it but by being a kind of warrant the regress argument never threatened.
That the chain loops back, with beliefs mutually supporting one another across a single coherent whole — a web of mutual support rather than a tower with a ground floor.
That the chain runs through infinitely many distinct reasons, and the very demand to make it stop somewhere is itself the central philosophical mistake driving the problem.
That the chain dissolves once justification is reframed as a public practice — a social game of giving reasons to each other rather than a private mental ladder of certainty.
context: Foundationalism (Descartes, Russell, classical empiricists) takes the stop-horn but earns its keep with a structural move — the basics aren't beliefs that win the regress race by being so obvious they outrun further questioning; they are warranted by something other than another belief (acquaintance, rational insight), so the regress argument, which demands belief-for-belief support, never targeted them. Coherentism (Neurath, Quine, early BonJour) accepts the loop; infinitism (Klein) accepts the infinite chain.

question: BonJour, 1980. Norman has reliable but unrecognized clairvoyance; he comes to believe truly that the President is in New York, with no idea why he believes it. Why does the case sting externalist accounts of knowledge?
answer: His belief is reliable and true, yet he has no inkling why — leaving the believer's perspective out
choices: His belief is reliable and true, yet he has no inkling why — leaving the believer's perspective out
His reliability rests on a faculty no one verifies, collapsing externalism into private conviction
His belief tracks the truth across nearby worlds, forcing externalists to drop modal conditions
His case demands clairvoyance is possible, importing metaphysics externalism wanted to avoid
context: "Externalist Theories of Empirical Knowledge." The intuition: a believer who has done no epistemic work — who cannot tell why his belief might be reliable — does not really know, however well-tuned the underlying mechanism. Externalists reply the intuition just re-imports internalism; reliabilists concede a meta-reliability demand; virtue theorists deny the cognitive achievement.

question: Gadamer rehabilitated 'prejudice' (Vorurteil) — fore-judgment. He said the Enlightenment was wrong to demand prejudice-free reasoning. What was his charge?
answer: The demand was itself a prejudice — the prejudice against prejudice — disguised as neutrality; no one reads from nowhere, and pretending so hides the tradition.
choices: The demand rested on an obsolete faculty psychology, since cognitive science shows the mind never reasons by pure inference but by associative leaps bypassing reflection.
The demand was itself a prejudice — the prejudice against prejudice — disguised as neutrality; no one reads from nowhere, and pretending so hides the tradition.
The demand led directly to political reaction, since denying inherited prejudice deprives reformers of the cultural memory required to rebuild what critique has torn down.
The demand confused logical inference with rhetoric, since Enlightenment reason silently borrows the trust-relations of the very tradition it claims to overcome in turn.
context: Truth and Method (1960). Vorurteil is literally pre-judgment. The Enlightenment cast all such judgments as bias to clear away; Gadamer asks where the clearing stands. We come with fore-meanings the tradition handed us; the task is to test which the text confirms.

question: Ricoeur set a 'hermeneutics of suspicion' (Marx, Nietzsche, Freud) against a 'hermeneutics of recovery.' Suspicion reads beneath the symbol for hidden interest; what does recovery do?
answer: It listens to the symbol as also disclosing truth — after unmasking false consciousness, recovery hears in it a fuller meaning suspicion would silence.
choices: It listens to the symbol as also disclosing truth — after unmasking false consciousness, recovery hears in it a fuller meaning suspicion would silence.
It treats the symbol as the surface of an underlying binary code — recovery makes plain what suspicion only gestured at, reading culture as a closed system of signs.
It defers the symbol's meaning down a chain of further signs — recovery refuses any final reading, since every interpretation rests on another interpretation behind it.
It reduces the symbol to the neuro-cognitive process producing it — recovery completes suspicion by replacing folk vocabularies of meaning with a mature scientific image.
context: Freud and Philosophy (1965). Ricoeur honored Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud as the great masters of suspicion: each treats the manifest as a screen over hidden forces. But the symbol of evil, a dream, or a parable can also give rise to thought. Suspicion clears; recovery still must listen.

question: Foot's 1967 trolley case rested on double effect: a foreseen bad side-effect (one death) is permissible if not aimed at — not used as means. Diverting kills as side-effect. Thomson's twist: the trolley loops back. Only the heavy man stops it. Same numbers. But his body stops it. Why does the loop matter?
answer: It breaks double-effect: the man's body is now a means, not a side-effect. Yet most still call diverting permissible — so the intend/foresee line is not the moral work.
choices: It breaks double-effect: the man's body is now a means, not a side-effect. Yet most still call diverting permissible — so the intend/foresee line is not the moral work.
Trolley intuitions have no stable shape once numbers shift from the original five-to-one ratio that Foot deliberately built her 1967 case around in the first place.
Consequentialism — judging only by outcomes — is the only ethical framework that handles each loop variant cleanly without producing verdicts that contradict across nearby cases.
Trolley intuitions track only physical proximity to the eventual victim, not any deeper distinction between what an agent intends by an act and what the agent merely foresees.
context: Foot's 1967 case turned on double effect: redirecting foresees the one death but does not intend it. Thomson's 1985 loop variant breaks that defense — the heavy man on the loop is needed to stop the trolley, so his death is the means, not a side effect. Yet many still call diverting permissible. Thomson concluded the doing/allowing line, not the intend/foresee line, is what does the moral work.

question: Tolstoy and Collingwood, decades apart, both argued art is not about beautiful objects but about something the artist does inwardly. What did the 'expression theory' say a work of art actually is?
answer: The completion of an emotion the artist clarifies by working it out in a medium — the work is the finished form of a feeling the artist did not fully know before
choices: The deliberate communication of a moral lesson in vivid form, meant to persuade audiences toward virtue by the techniques an orator uses in a hostile assembly
The completion of an emotion the artist clarifies by working it out in a medium — the work is the finished form of a feeling the artist did not fully know before
The skilled imitation of nature, judged by how closely the finished representation matches the appearance of the thing it represents, in the tradition of mimesis
The technical solving of a formal problem within a tradition, judged by how elegantly the rules of the medium and genre are met by the artist's own invention
context: Tolstoy's What Is Art? (1898) argued art transmits feeling from one person to another by signs — a sincere artist 'infects' the viewer. Collingwood's Principles of Art (1938) refined this: bad art is craft (knowing the feeling in advance and producing it on demand); real art is the discovery of an emotion by expressing it. Both views make sincerity and clarification of feeling primary; beauty and skill secondary. Formalists (Bell) and institutionalists (Danto) later pushed back hard.

question: Plato in the Timaeus describes the cosmos as fashioned by a divine craftsman working with two materials: the eternal Forms as patterns, and a strange receiving medium he calls the chora. What role does the receptacle play?
answer: It is the formless 'space' or 'matrix' that takes the imprint of every Form without being any of them, providing the somewhere divine copies of Forms appear as physical things.
choices: It is the formless 'space' or 'matrix' that takes the imprint of every Form without being any of them, providing the somewhere divine copies of Forms appear as physical things.
It is the active soul animating the world, the one living principle moving the cosmos and producing the orderly motions of the heavens the craftsman first set in motion eternally.
It is the rational principle limiting the chaos of becoming, the structuring logos holding the four elements in their proportions and keeping the cosmos from permanent disorder.
It is the mathematical structure underlying every appearance, the field of numbers and ratios informing each physical thing and giving the cosmos its harmonious proportions.
context: The Timaeus is Plato's most difficult dialogue. The chora has been read as proto-space, proto-matter, even (by Derrida) as a place outside the Form/copy dichotomy entirely. It haunted philosophy for two millennia.

question: The Stoics held strict determinism — every event flows from prior causes — yet insisted on full moral responsibility. Chrysippus offered an analogy: a cylinder pushed downhill rolls because of the shove AND its own shape. What did the analogy show?
answer: External causes give the impulse, but a thing's reaction follows from its own inner nature; the wise person is responsible for character though every action arises from both joint causes.
choices: External causes give the impulse, but a thing's reaction follows from its own inner nature; the wise person is responsible for character though every action arises from both joint causes.
External causes are the only real causes; inner nature is a passive substrate that gets shaped by them, so responsibility ultimately falls on social and cosmic forces that mold character.
Inner nature is the only real cause; external causes are illusory occasions the soul uses to express what it would have done anyway, so responsibility is reserved for the inner agent.
External and internal causes are aspects of one divine logos; responsibility is a useful fiction the wise see through, while still acting as if it were real for practical living.
context: Chrysippus's cylinder is one of the earliest serious compatibilist moves in philosophy: determinism and responsibility live together because not every cause is the same kind of cause. The argument runs through Hobbes and Hume into modern compatibilism.

question: Leibniz argued this world must be the best of all possible worlds because a perfect God would create only the best. Voltaire mocked this with Candide. But Leibniz had a careful sense of 'best' the joke missed. What did 'best' actually mean for him?
answer: The world maximizing variety and richness of phenomena while preserving the greatest possible simplicity of natural laws — not the world with least suffering or most pleasure for humans.
choices: The world maximizing variety and richness of phenomena while preserving the greatest possible simplicity of natural laws — not the world with least suffering or most pleasure for humans.
The world in which the moral balance between happiness and merit is most precisely arranged — so the virtuous flourish and the wicked suffer in exact proportion to their deserved share.
The world in which divine attributes are most fully expressed in created things — so creatures resemble God in wisdom, power, and goodness more nearly than they would in any rival.
The world in which finite minds have the greatest scope for free choice — so the largest space of moral and intellectual development is opened to the rational creatures within.
context: Voltaire's Candide rolls the Lisbon earthquake into Leibniz's optimism with cruel efficiency. But Leibniz was not denying suffering — he was arguing it is the price of a world rich enough to contain free rational creatures at all.

question: Engels in the 1880s tried to extend dialectic beyond human history into nature itself. Stones, plants, chemistry, evolution — all of it, he argued, moved by the same three Hegelian 'laws.' Later Western Marxists split sharply on this move. What was the worry?
answer: Dialectical laws were drawn from how human history seems to work; bolting them onto rocks and animals risked mistaking metaphor for physics.
choices: Dialectical laws were drawn from how human history seems to work; bolting them onto rocks and animals risked mistaking metaphor for physics.
Engels was unfaithful to Marx by reintroducing Hegel; Marx had wanted dialectic kept only inside the study of religion under capitalism.
Engels conceded too much to Darwin; reducing human society to natural selection would erase class struggle's role in shaping history.
Engels relied on chemistry he did not really understand; later editors found his examples of qualitative transitions drawn from outdated texts.
context: Engels's Dialectics of Nature was unpublished at his 1895 death. Lukacs and the Frankfurt School thought it was a wrong turn.

question: Twentieth-century regimes — Nazi propagandists especially — seized the word Übermensch and gave it a racial reading: the master race over the subhuman. Kaufmann's postwar translations worked hard to undo the mistake. What did Nietzsche himself mean by Übermensch in Zarathustra?
answer: A future kind of self-overcoming individual who creates values rather than inheriting them — a personal, not racial, ideal of becoming.
choices: A future kind of self-overcoming individual who creates values rather than inheriting them — a personal, not racial, ideal of becoming.
A biologically purified ruling caste that would emerge through state-managed breeding and the removal of weaker hereditary lines.
A returning hero in the Greek epic mode who would re-found European civilization on the war-virtues of the Homeric age.
A perfected technological humanity that would finally master the natural world through science and engineering instead of religion.
context: Zarathustra Prologue. Nietzsche's sister Elisabeth, who controlled his archive, pushed the racial misreading; the texts themselves do not support it.

question: Kierkegaard published most of his early books under invented names — Johannes Climacus, Johannes de Silentio, Constantin Constantius. He called this 'indirect communication.' Why did he think a treatise signed with his own name would have been the wrong vehicle?
answer: Authentic religious choice is each person's own; a signed treatise would let the reader take the conclusion without making the choice for himself.
choices: Authentic religious choice is each person's own; a signed treatise would let the reader take the conclusion without making the choice for himself.
Danish censorship in the 1840s forbade theology under one's own name, so Kierkegaard's pen names were a practical workaround imposed by law.
Kierkegaard wanted to test public reception without his social class influencing the verdict, much as he had earlier published anonymous poetry.
His teacher Hans Lassen Martensen had registered the family name with the university, so a former student could not write theology under it.
context: The Point of View for My Work as an Author (posthumous). He signed his religious 'discourses' but kept the philosophical works pseudonymous.

question: Dostoevsky's Underground Man delivers a long monologue against the 'crystal palace' — the reformers' picture of a perfectly rational society where every desire is met by enlightened planning. Why, on his argument, would humans smash the crystal palace from inside?
answer: To prove they are not piano keys — human will would assert itself against any system, however good, that left no room to choose against it.
choices: To prove they are not piano keys — human will would assert itself against any system, however good, that left no room to choose against it.
To return to traditional religious authority — material satisfaction would not fill the spiritual hole left when the older faith had been displaced.
To start fresh through revolution — the reformers' designs would always benefit a new ruling class, and ordinary people would tear them down.
To restore aristocratic privilege — the underground man speaks for displaced nobles preferring old hierarchy to bourgeois rational order.
context: Notes from Underground (1864). Dostoevsky was attacking Chernyshevsky's What Is to Be Done?, which envisioned a rationally engineered socialist society.

question: Schelling broke with Fichte around 1800. Fichte built everything on the I — nature, for Fichte, was a stage set the I posits to have something to overcome. Schelling refused this asymmetry. What did his Naturphilosophie claim instead?
answer: Nature is not dead matter posited by mind but a living, productive activity — mind and nature are one absolute seen from two sides.
choices: Nature is not dead matter posited by mind but a living, productive activity — mind and nature are one absolute seen from two sides.
Nature is a mechanical clockwork created by God at the start, with mind being a thinking substance entirely independent of its workings.
Nature is a system of forces explained completely by Newtonian physics, and philosophy should restrict itself to the mental side of reality.
Nature is an illusion projected by the transcendental ego, and the goal of philosophy is to dissolve it into a finally clear self-knowledge.
context: Ideas for a Philosophy of Nature (1797). His identity philosophy followed: the absolute is the indifference point of mind and nature.

question: Hegel's word Geist gets translated as Spirit, Mind, sometimes Ghost. None is quite right. Kojève and the French read it one way; the British idealists another. What is closer to what Geist actually names across the Phenomenology?
answer: The shared life of a people — customs, language, law, art, religion — a collective subject that thinks through its individual members.
choices: The shared life of a people — customs, language, law, art, religion — a collective subject that thinks through its individual members.
An individual immortal soul that survives the death of the body and reunites with God in a personal afterlife awaiting it after history.
A nonmaterial substance pervading the universe that explains apparent supernatural phenomena like apparitions and inspired prophecy.
A psychological faculty distinguishing humans from animals, located by Hegel in the cerebral cortex and studied through introspection.
context: Hegel speaks of objective Geist (institutions, customs) and absolute Geist (art, religion, philosophy) as stages of one developing reality.

question: Husserl's epoché — bracketing — asks the philosopher to suspend the natural attitude, the unexamined assumption that the world is independently there. He insisted this was not skepticism. He was not doubting the world. What was he doing?
answer: Setting aside the question of the world's independent existence in order to describe carefully how it shows up in consciousness in the first place.
choices: Setting aside the question of the world's independent existence in order to describe carefully how it shows up in consciousness in the first place.
Arguing that the world does not exist outside the mind, and that all objects of perception are mental constructs without external reference.
Denying that science can know anything about the world, and recommending a return to ordinary commonsense reports of perception.
Replacing logic with intuition as the criterion of truth, on the grounds that careful introspection reveals certainties that proof cannot.
context: Ideas I (1913). Bracketing lets phenomenology study how experience is structured (intentional acts and their objects) without metaphysical claims.

question: The early Wittgenstein in the 1921 Tractatus ended with a famous instruction: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.' The Vienna Circle read this as a clean ban on metaphysics. Wittgenstein wrote to a friend that the real point was the opposite. What did he mean?
answer: Everything important — ethics, value, the meaning of life — falls outside what language can say; it shows itself, and silence honors it.
choices: Everything important — ethics, value, the meaning of life — falls outside what language can say; it shows itself, and silence honors it.
Religion and ethics should be replaced by a public conversation of citizens about shared interests, with private faith confined to private life.
Mathematics and logic are nonsense in disguise; the apparent power of these subjects comes from their being unstated background assumptions.
Philosophy is dispensable once the natural sciences mature, and the silence is a long quiet that science will eventually deliver to thought.
context: Wittgenstein to Ludwig von Ficker, 1919. The Vienna Circle thought him dismissing the unsayable as nonsense; for him it was the important nonsense.

question: Adorno and Horkheimer wrote Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944) in Los Angeles, refugees from the Nazis. The book's central claim is darker than any earlier Marxist line. The Enlightenment had promised emancipation through reason. What did they argue had instead happened?
answer: Instrumental reason had become a new form of domination — reducing humans and nature alike to means, and clearing the way for the camps.
choices: Instrumental reason had become a new form of domination — reducing humans and nature alike to means, and clearing the way for the camps.
Capitalist owners had captured the press and propagandized workers out of class consciousness, so revolution had become structurally impossible.
Religion's collapse left no moral framework, and so totalitarianism filled the vacuum left by churches that earlier centuries had relied on.
Mass democracy unleashed irrational majorities, and the educated elite had failed to defend constitutional limits when the test came.
context: Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944). The pessimism marked a break with classical Marxism, which had still seen rational progress as on the workers' side.

question: James in 'The Will to Believe' (1896) defended believing on incomplete evidence in a narrow class of cases. Critics — Russell sharpest — accused him of licensing wishful thinking. James's reply: the doctrine applies only when three conditions hold. A bet on Mars colonies fails. Why?
answer: The option is not 'forced' — you can suspend judgment and lose nothing, so the urgency that justifies belief without proof is absent.
choices: The option is not 'forced' — you can suspend judgment and lose nothing, so the urgency that justifies belief without proof is absent.
The hypothesis is too remote from ordinary experience — James restricted the doctrine to ideas drawn from everyday human social life.
The evidence is one-sided in favor of skepticism — James limited his rule to cases where the data weighed strongly toward the belief.
The hypothesis would not be testable in the believer's lifetime — James required practical verification before any belief was permitted.
context: Three conditions: the option must be living (a real possibility for you), forced (no easy abstention), and momentous (substantial stakes).

question: Diderot spent twenty-five years editing the Encyclopédie — the great Enlightenment project to gather all reliable knowledge between two covers. Twenty-eight volumes, four thousand subscribers despite royal suppression. What was the editorial wager beneath the enterprise?
answer: If practical-arts and scientific knowledge were widely available, citizens could think for themselves and old authorities would weaken.
choices: If practical-arts and scientific knowledge were widely available, citizens could think for themselves and old authorities would weaken.
If learning could be made entertaining, popular literacy would rise sharply across France within two generations of the work's completion.
If a single comprehensive reference replaced scattered older books, the Catholic Church would lose its monopoly on the publishing trade.
If trade secrets were exposed publicly, French manufacturers could close the technological gap with their longer-established English rivals.
context: Encyclopédie, ou Dictionnaire raisonné des sciences, des arts et des métiers (1751–72). Diderot defended the project when partners abandoned him.

question: Newton's Principia (1687) gave a law of universal gravitation but offered no mechanism for how bodies pulled across empty space. Continental rivals — Leibniz especially — attacked this. Action at a distance, they said, was an occult quality dressed in mathematics. Newton's reply was terse. What did he say?
answer: 'Hypotheses non fingo' — I do not feign hypotheses. The mathematics describes the regularity; speculating about hidden mechanism is no part of his task.
choices: 'Hypotheses non fingo' — I do not feign hypotheses. The mathematics describes the regularity; speculating about hidden mechanism is no part of his task.
'Natura non facit saltus' — Nature does not make leaps. The continuity of motion ruled out any unbridgeable gap between distant gravitating bodies.
'Cogito ergo sum' — I think, therefore I am. The certainty of inner reflection alone justifies the conclusions arrived at in mathematical physics.
'Plus ultra' — further beyond. The unknown mechanism would be discovered by later generations, and current rejection of his law was simply premature.
context: General Scholium to the Principia, second edition (1713). Newton's stance shaped one strand of philosophy of science: describe; hold off on mechanism.

question: Wittgenstein in the later Investigations asked a deceptively simple question: what do all games share? Chess, solitaire, ring-around-the-rosie, the Olympics. He listed candidate criteria — competition, rules, winning — and each failed for some game. What did he conclude?
answer: Words like 'game' do not name a shared essence — they pick out a 'family resemblance' of overlapping features with no single thread running through all.
choices: Words like 'game' do not name a shared essence — they pick out a 'family resemblance' of overlapping features with no single thread running through all.
Words like 'game' point to a Platonic Form in a separate realm, and the variety of cases shows how imperfectly any one game realizes its archetype.
Words like 'game' fail outright in any precise philosophical use, and ordinary speech should be replaced with stipulated technical vocabulary.
Words like 'game' name biological functions — playing has an evolutionary purpose, and every case shares whatever that purpose finally turns out to be.
context: Philosophical Investigations §§65–67. The image: features overlapping like resemblances in a family — eyes, nose, chin — with no feature shared by all.

question: Foucault opened the first volume of History of Sexuality (1976) by mocking what he called 'the repressive hypothesis' — the popular story that the Victorians silenced sex and the 20th century has been a long liberation since. He thought the story was historically backward. What did he find?
answer: Talk about sex exploded under the Victorians — medicine, law, religion, psychiatry generated endless classifications and confessions, not silence.
choices: Talk about sex exploded under the Victorians — medicine, law, religion, psychiatry generated endless classifications and confessions, not silence.
Sexual liberation has been an illusion — actual behavior has not changed much, and the language has only been adjusted to give the appearance of change.
Sex was discussed openly in 18th-century salons and then again from the 1960s, with the 19th century being a brief and atypical interruption.
Sexual mores follow climate and geography, not historical change — the Mediterranean has been steady for two thousand years while northern Europe has not.
context: History of Sexuality v.1 (1976). The opening reframed the field: not 'how was sex repressed?' but 'why have we built so many discourses around it?'

question: Hegel ended the Phenomenology of Spirit with 'absolute knowing' — Geist finally recognizing itself across the whole of its development. Critics from Schelling onward complained the picture had a strange feature. What did they object to?
answer: Hegel's system seemed to close history — once Geist has recognized itself, no genuinely new shape of spirit can appear, and human creativity is finished.
choices: Hegel's system seemed to close history — once Geist has recognized itself, no genuinely new shape of spirit can appear, and human creativity is finished.
Hegel's system reduced human persons to passive vehicles for Geist, with individual choice doing no real work in the unfolding of the dialectic.
Hegel's system depended on premises borrowed silently from theology, making it religious dogma dressed up in the costume of secular philosophy.
Hegel's system could not account for natural science, which had grown explosively since Kant and now ran on principles his dialectic could not capture.
context: The 'end of history' worry runs through Schelling, Kierkegaard, and Marx. Each took the diagnosis as a starting point for breaking with Hegel.

question: Marx in The German Ideology (1846, unpublished) advanced a thesis about the relationship between dominant ideas and dominant material conditions. The slogan version is famous. What does the slogan claim?
answer: The ruling ideas of any epoch are the ideas of its ruling class — those who own material production also control intellectual production.
choices: The ruling ideas of any epoch are the ideas of its ruling class — those who own material production also control intellectual production.
The ruling ideas of any epoch arise spontaneously from the people — folk culture remains underneath every elite ideology, waiting to surface again.
The ruling ideas of any epoch come from religious authority — control of dogma is what allows a class to hold power across the generations.
The ruling ideas of any epoch follow technology — each new productive technique forces a new worldview on rulers and workers together alike.
context: The German Ideology, 'Feuerbach.' The book was published posthumously in 1932. The thesis is the kernel of what later Marxists called the theory of ideology.

question: The Yogacara school argued that what we take for an outside world is structured by consciousness all the way down — vijnaptimatra, 'cognition-only.' Critics read this as Berkeleyan idealism. How does Vasubandhu's view differ?
answer: Berkeley's minds were stable individual substances that received ideas from God; Vasubandhu denied any standing substantial mind — only a stream of mental events conditioning further mental events.
choices: Berkeley's minds were stable individual substances that received ideas from God; Vasubandhu denied any standing substantial mind — only a stream of mental events conditioning further mental events.
Berkeley denied matter while keeping spirits real; Vasubandhu denied both matter and spirits, leaving only the formal patterns of Buddhist scripture as truly existing realities.
Berkeley argued ideas exist only when perceived by some mind; Vasubandhu argued ideas can exist unperceived in a storehouse, contradicting the very meaning of cognition-only.
Berkeley believed God grounds the regularity of experience; Vasubandhu replaced God with karma, but otherwise his metaphysics is the same Christian-style idealism in Buddhist clothing.
context: Vasubandhu's Vimsatika argued against external objects without thereby positing any abiding subject. The alaya-vijnana (storehouse consciousness) is itself a stream conditioned by karmic seeds — not a Cartesian or Berkeleyan substance. The comparison to Berkeley is one of the standard student errors that careful readers like Lusthaus and Garfield are at pains to correct.

question: The Buddha was asked by a disciple whether the world is eternal, whether the soul is the same as the body, what happens to a buddha after death — fourteen metaphysical questions in all. He refused to answer any of them. Why?
answer: A man shot with a poisoned arrow does not refuse treatment until he knows the archer's name — speculative questions delay the practical work of ending suffering.
choices: A man shot with a poisoned arrow does not refuse treatment until he knows the archer's name — speculative questions delay the practical work of ending suffering.
The questions presupposed metaphysical commitments that pious followers should accept on the Buddha's authority without troubling themselves about the underlying reasons.
The questions had been answered by earlier Vedic seers and the Buddha respected the Brahmanical settlement enough not to revisit ground already covered by older sages.
The questions concerned topics on which the Buddha simply lacked knowledge, since his enlightenment was about ethical conduct rather than cosmological matters of fact.
context: The Cula-Malunkyovada Sutta. The poisoned-arrow parable was the Buddha's reply: speculation about the cosmos is fine for those with leisure, but it does not pull the arrow out. The avyakata (undeclared) questions mark a methodological commitment — Buddhism is therapy first, metaphysics only insofar as it serves the therapy. The position contrasts sharply with Brahmanical philosophy of the same period.

question: Theravada Buddhists hold the arhat — one who has ended craving and will not be reborn — as the goal. Mahayana Buddhists reject this and hold the bodhisattva as higher. What is the bodhisattva's defining vow?
answer: To delay full nirvana until every sentient being has been carried across — liberation is not personal exit but universal commitment that takes lifetimes of work.
choices: To delay full nirvana until every sentient being has been carried across — liberation is not personal exit but universal commitment that takes lifetimes of work.
To master every sutra in the canon before claiming any spiritual attainment — knowledge of the texts is the precondition for any genuine release from the cycle of rebirth.
To remain in monastic discipline for at least one thousand lives — Theravada permits householders to attain arhatship, but Mahayana requires the monk's path for everyone.
To worship the buddhas of the ten directions through ritual offerings — bodhisattvas earn merit through devotion that arhats refuse to engage in out of austere pride.
context: The bodhisattva vow appears in many Mahayana texts including the Bodhicaryavatara of Santideva. The contrast with the Theravada arhat is doctrinal and structural — Mahayana texts often present arhats as having stopped short. The deeper philosophical point is that on Madhyamaka grounds (nothing has self-nature) a private liberation makes no sense; ones own freedom and others' are not finally separable.

question: Dignaga and Dharmakirti built a Buddhist epistemology around two and only two valid means of knowing — pratyaksa (perception) and anumana (inference). They rejected the Brahmanical sabda — scriptural testimony — as a third source. What was their reason?
answer: Testimony reduces to perception or inference once unpacked — either the speaker perceived something or inferred it, so the apparent third source dissolves under analysis.
choices: Testimony reduces to perception or inference once unpacked — either the speaker perceived something or inferred it, so the apparent third source dissolves under analysis.
Testimony presupposes a stable conventional language and Buddhism's doctrine of momentariness made any stable linguistic meaning a metaphysical impossibility to defend.
Testimony was reliable in the era of the Buddha but the gradual decline of dharma had so corrupted later teachers that the source could no longer be epistemically trusted.
Testimony as a source assumes a community of speakers stable enough to transmit it, and the doctrine of no-self made the existence of such a community internally incoherent.
context: Dignaga's Pramanasamuccaya and Dharmakirti's Pramanavarttika set out the two-pramana view that became the standard Buddhist epistemology in India and Tibet. The Brahmanical schools — especially Nyaya and Mimamsa — held testimony as an independent pramana, in Mimamsa's case to underwrite Vedic authority. The Buddhist reduction of testimony to perception-plus-inference is a careful logical move, not a dismissal of scripture.

question: Asanga's Yogacara school posited an alaya-vijnana, often translated 'storehouse consciousness' — a stream where karmic seeds wait to ripen. Critics from Madhyamaka charged that this had reinvented the self the Buddha had denied. How did Yogacara reply?
answer: The storehouse is itself a stream of momentary events with no abiding owner — what looks like a soul is just karmic continuity, no more substantial than a river named twice.
choices: The storehouse is itself a stream of momentary events with no abiding owner — what looks like a soul is just karmic continuity, no more substantial than a river named twice.
The storehouse is a real persisting substance and the Buddha's anatman doctrine was a teaching expedient appropriate only to listeners not yet ready for the deeper view.
The storehouse exists only at the conventional level and Madhyamaka critics had missed that Yogacara texts always meant the term as a metaphor for the body and brain.
The storehouse is identical with the dharmakaya (the buddha's body of truth) and so transcends the categories of self and not-self entirely from the start of the analysis.
context: Asanga's Mahayanasamgraha and Vasubandhu's Trimsika lay out the alaya-vijnana doctrine. Whether this constitutes a sneaky reintroduction of atman is a perennial Buddhist debate — Madhyamikas like Candrakirti pressed the charge; Yogacarins answered that the storehouse is a process, not a thing. Tibetan doxography preserved both readings as live positions.

question: Dogen wrote that practice and enlightenment are not two — zazen is not a technique that produces awakening later, but is itself the awakening. What classical Buddhist picture was he rejecting?
answer: The means-end picture where meditation is a vehicle that delivers the practitioner to a separate destination called enlightenment somewhere down the road.
choices: The means-end picture where meditation is a vehicle that delivers the practitioner to a separate destination called enlightenment somewhere down the road.
The Pure Land picture where rebirth in Amida's paradise is the goal — Dogen held that paradise should be sought in this life rather than the next one as Pure Land taught.
The koan picture where intellectual breakthrough on a question is the milestone — Dogen rejected this in favor of devotional chanting drawn from earlier Tendai practice.
The bodhisattva picture where compassion for others is the orientation — Dogen redirected practitioners toward private self-cultivation in solitude apart from the wider community.
context: Dogen's Bendowa and the opening of Shobogenzo make the practice-realization (shusho-itto) point: zazen is not preparation for enlightenment, it is the activity of an already-buddha. This collapses the Mahayana picture inherited from India where bodhisattvas progress through stages. Soto Zen took this principle as central; Rinzai under Hakuin kept the koan-as-vehicle picture and the two schools have argued the point for eight centuries.

question: Confucius placed ren — usually rendered humaneness or benevolence — at the center of his ethics. Yet when asked directly what ren is, he answered different students differently each time. What does this teaching pattern suggest about how he treated the virtue?
answer: Ren is not a definition to memorize but a way of responding to specific persons and situations — what counts as humane action varies with the particular case at hand.
choices: Ren is not a definition to memorize but a way of responding to specific persons and situations — what counts as humane action varies with the particular case at hand.
Ren has a single technical meaning but Confucius hid it deliberately from his lesser students, reserving the genuine teaching for an inner circle who would prove themselves worthy.
Ren is a vague placeholder that Confucius used to signal moral seriousness without committing to any concrete content — the variation reflects an absence of substantive theory.
Ren divides into ranked subtypes corresponding to social station, and Confucius assigned each student the version appropriate to the family rank into which they had been born.
context: Analects 6.30, 12.1, 12.2, 12.22, 13.19 and others all present ren differently — sometimes as restraining the self by ritual, sometimes as loving others, sometimes as a daily discipline. The variation is the teaching: ren is a virtue practiced in particulars, and what counts as humane treatment of a parent differs from humane treatment of a stranger. Aristotle's practical wisdom (phronesis) is structurally similar — and the comparison is genuinely illuminating.

question: Confucius held that the cultivated person treats parents with reverence at a higher pitch than the merely correct treatment of strangers. Critics from the rival Mohist school called this favoritism. What did Confucians answer?
answer: Graded love is realistic and trainable — moral concern that does not begin near home and extend outward is sentimental abstraction that cannot actually be lived out by humans.
choices: Graded love is realistic and trainable — moral concern that does not begin near home and extend outward is sentimental abstraction that cannot actually be lived out by humans.
Strangers are owed equal concern in principle but each station of life has its own preferred ritual practices that should not be applied indiscriminately across personal contexts.
Family preference is granted only as a transitional teaching for those not yet capable of impartial concern — the sage finally treats all persons identically in feeling and act.
