Strangers and family are owed equal concern except in moments of crisis when family must come first; everyday morality treats them alike but emergencies sort out the priority.
context: Mozi's school argued for jian'ai (impartial concern), holding that biased love is the source of social conflict. Mencius (3B.9, 7A.45) replied that the Mohist position would have a person treat their own father like any stranger's father — and this, he said, is to be like a beast that has no father at all. The graded-love position became standard in Confucian ethics and resembles in structure the modern philosophical debate over agent-relative obligations.

question: Zhuangzi told of a cook butchering an ox for Lord Wenhui. The blade moved through joints and cavities without resistance, and the cook said his blade had been used nineteen years and was as sharp as the day it was forged. What philosophical lesson was Zhuangzi pressing?
answer: The skilled practitioner works with the natural grain rather than against it — effort is wasted on forcing matters and saved by following the patterns already there.
choices: The skilled practitioner works with the natural grain rather than against it — effort is wasted on forcing matters and saved by following the patterns already there.
Manual labor performed thoughtfully is morally superior to the abstract reasoning of philosophers — Zhuangzi praised the cook to embarrass intellectuals who do not work with their hands.
Mastery requires endless rehearsal of a fixed technique — the cook's blade lasts because he has repeated the same precise motions exactly the same way for nineteen straight years.
Even ugly tasks are dignified when performed for noble patrons — the lord's presence is what raises the butcher's craft to the level of philosophical example worth recording.
context: Zhuangzi, Chapter 3, 'The Secret of Caring for Life.' The cook is a paradigm of wu-wei — action that is so attuned to the situation that it appears effortless. The point is not laziness or quietism: the cook works hard, but works with the grain, finding the spaces where the blade can pass. Compare a modern surgeon who cuts along fascial planes rather than slicing across them. The story is one of Daoism's most cited because the lesson generalizes.

question: Laozi wrote that knowing others is intelligence, but knowing oneself is enlightenment. Conquering others requires force, but conquering oneself requires strength. Critics charged that this teaching is private and unpolitical. How does the Daodejing answer?
answer: Rulers who have not mastered themselves project unmastered impulses onto the realm — the deepest political work is the inner work that prevents bad rule from arising at all.
choices: Rulers who have not mastered themselves project unmastered impulses onto the realm — the deepest political work is the inner work that prevents bad rule from arising at all.
Inner cultivation is private preparation for genuine political action later, in the same way Aristotle's contemplative life sets up for full participation in the civic affairs of the polis.
Inner mastery is the prize of a quietist withdrawal from politics — Laozi advised the sage to abandon the dusty world entirely and tend only the garden of the inner heart.
Inner conquest replaces outer rule altogether — Laozi taught a kind of philosophical anarchism in which any form of organized government is to be dismantled by collective effort.
context: Daodejing, Chapter 33. Laozi addresses the Daodejing partly to the ruler (it is sometimes called a manual for kings). The inner-outer claim is not quietist: an unmastered ruler unleashes appetites that produce wars, levies, and famines. Mastery of self is therefore the precondition for the wu-wei ruler whose people, looking back, say 'we did this ourselves.' The argument is structurally close to Marcus Aurelius — and to Burke on the inseparability of self-government from self-restraint.

question: Zhuangzi argued that what we call right and wrong, this and that, beautiful and ugly are all generated from a perspective. A frog in a well thinks the sky is small. From this he drew a striking philosophical conclusion. What was it?
answer: No standpoint outside all perspectives exists from which to settle the disputes — what looks like the world from one frame and another are equally real frames of a shared reality.
choices: No standpoint outside all perspectives exists from which to settle the disputes — what looks like the world from one frame and another are equally real frames of a shared reality.
Every perspective is an illusion that the sage dispels by direct unmediated perception of the Dao — the well-frog and the philosopher share a common error that wisdom removes.
One privileged perspective — the sage's view from the mountain — is veridical and the others are not — Zhuangzi defends an esoteric realism beneath the perspectivist surface play.
Each perspective contains its own internal truth that conflicts with no other and the perspectives can be added together arithmetically into a single coherent universal account.
context: Zhuangzi, Chapter 2, 'Discussion on Making All Things Equal.' Zhuangzi's perspectivism is sometimes called proto-relativism, but it is more nuanced than that label suggests — he holds that perspectives are real and useful, not that all judgments are equally good. The point is that an absolute external standpoint is a fantasy. Nietzsche later made a structurally similar argument, and the parallel is genuinely illuminating without flattening either thinker.

question: Ramanuja accepted Sankara's claim that Brahman is one but rejected the further claim that the world's plurality is illusion. He called his view visistadvaita — qualified non-dualism. What did the qualification do?
answer: It made the world and individual souls real but dependent — distinct features of Brahman, not separate from it, in the way a body and its parts are one substance with real differences.
choices: It made the world and individual souls real but dependent — distinct features of Brahman, not separate from it, in the way a body and its parts are one substance with real differences.
It introduced a second eternal principle alongside Brahman to account for matter — a dualism similar to Samkhya's purusa and prakriti, recovering plurality at a fundamental level.
It split Brahman into two persons — one personal and worshipped, one impersonal and beyond worship — through which devotees access the divine according to their temperament.
It rejected the authority of the Upanishads in favor of the Bhagavad Gita alone — Ramanuja held that the Gita's bhakti theology should override the older non-dualist texts entirely.
context: Ramanuja (c. 1017-1137) wrote the Sribhasya on the Brahma Sutras to argue that Sankara's Advaita (radical non-dualism) made bhakti — devotion — incoherent: you cannot love what is identical with you. Visistadvaita preserves the dependence of soul and world on Brahman without collapsing them into Brahman. The body-soul analogy lets the world be real and Brahman remain one. Later Madhva would push further to Dvaita (full dualism), making three live positions in Vedanta.

question: Nyaya, the school of logic and epistemology, defended four valid means of knowing where Buddhists allowed only two. The fourth — sabda — is verbal testimony. Why did Nyaya defend testimony so vigorously?
answer: Reliable testimony from a competent speaker carries information neither perception nor inference can supply — denying it leaves most of what any human actually knows without epistemic standing.
choices: Reliable testimony from a competent speaker carries information neither perception nor inference can supply — denying it leaves most of what any human actually knows without epistemic standing.
Testimony was the only valid source for the Vedas and rejecting it would have left the Vedas without epistemic backing — the rest of the defense is just window-dressing on this religious motive.
Testimony was needed to refute Buddhist arguments since Buddhist scriptures are themselves transmitted by testimony — Nyaya wanted to expose what it saw as Buddhist internal inconsistency.
Testimony was practical and useful even if not strictly valid — Nyaya allowed it on pragmatic grounds for ordinary discourse but never as a basis for genuine philosophical demonstration.
context: Nyayasutra 1.1.7 defines sabda as 'the assertion of a reliable person.' The school's defense is structural, not religious — though its application to the Vedas was clearly part of the motivation. Gangesa later refined the account in his Tattvacintamani. The contrast with Buddhist Dignaga, who reduced testimony to inference, is one of the most carefully argued debates in classical Indian philosophy, with each side meeting the other's strongest objections.

question: Nishida Kitaro, founder of the Kyoto School, argued in his 1911 Inquiry into the Good that pure experience precedes the split between subject and object. Critics charged this borrowed William James. What was Nishida's distinctive move beyond James?
answer: He grounded pure experience in basho — a 'place' or logical field within which subject and object emerge as poles of a prior unity, not as starting points to be reconciled later.
choices: He grounded pure experience in basho — a 'place' or logical field within which subject and object emerge as poles of a prior unity, not as starting points to be reconciled later.
He restricted pure experience to aesthetic states alone, while James had extended it across all cognitive activity — Nishida narrowed the doctrine to make it more defensible philosophically.
He combined pure experience with Marxist historical materialism — Nishida placed the subject-object emergence inside a dialectical sequence of class struggles working through history.
He preserved Cartesian dualism within pure experience by holding that the two poles never fully merged — the experience was unified phenomenally but remained metaphysically two.
context: Nishida's basho ('place') was developed across the 1920s and is sometimes called the logic of place or the logic of contradictory identity. It draws on Mahayana sunyata and on German idealism — Hegel especially — without reducing to either. The Kyoto School including Tanabe Hajime, Nishitani Keiji, and Watsuji Tetsuro pursued related projects. The political entanglements of some Kyoto thinkers with Japanese imperialism in the 1930s and 40s remain a serious unresolved problem in their reception.

question: Al-Kindi, the first major Arabic philosopher, defended studying the Greek pagans on a principle that became famous in Islamic intellectual life. What was his argument?
answer: Truth belongs to whoever speaks it — we owe gratitude to anyone who advanced the truth even partially, regardless of where they came from or what they believed about other things.
choices: Truth belongs to whoever speaks it — we owe gratitude to anyone who advanced the truth even partially, regardless of where they came from or what they believed about other things.
Truth in religion comes from revelation while truth in philosophy comes from reason — the two have separate sources and the pagans contributed only to the second one.
Truth from non-Muslim sources is permitted only when no Muslim authority has addressed the question — once Islamic teaching exists on a topic, the Greek sources should be set aside.
Truth from the Greeks must be filtered through revealed scripture before it can be received — pagan philosophy needs theological purification to be safe for Muslim students of any age.
context: Al-Kindi's First Philosophy opens with the statement that truth is to be received from wherever it comes — even from earlier nations distant from us in race and religion. The principle (often summarized 'truth is the lost camel of the believer') legitimated the great translation project that brought Greek philosophy into Arabic and from there eventually into Latin Europe. Al-Kindi's school in ninth-century Baghdad set the model for later philosophical work in the Islamic world.

question: Al-Ghazali in his Tahafut al-Falasifa attacked the philosophers' claim that fire necessarily burns cotton. He held that what looks like causal necessity is actually divine custom. What is the doctrine he was defending?
answer: Occasionalism — God is the direct cause of every event including fire's burning of cotton, and the regular pairing is His habitual will, not a power in the fire itself acting on its own.
choices: Occasionalism — God is the direct cause of every event including fire's burning of cotton, and the regular pairing is His habitual will, not a power in the fire itself acting on its own.
Secondary causation — God acts through created powers that have their own real causal efficacy, with fire genuinely burning cotton by an inherent capacity God has gifted to it.
Causal skepticism — we cannot know whether causation is real or apparent, and the prudent religious position is to suspend judgment on the metaphysics of natural events entirely.
Mechanism — natural events follow fixed laws established by God at creation that no longer require any continuing divine action to remain in force throughout the present age.
context: Al-Ghazali's argument anticipates Hume on causation by six centuries: what we see is constant conjunction, not necessary connection. But where Hume drew a skeptical conclusion, Al-Ghazali drew a theological one — God is the cause we do not see. The Ash'ari school built occasionalism into its theology. Averroes would later defend Aristotelian secondary causation against this view, and the dispute shaped medieval Islamic and later Christian debates.

question: Al-Ghazali wrote an autobiography, Deliverance from Error, describing his collapse into doubt and his recovery through Sufi practice. He had concluded that one specific philosophical school could not deliver certainty. Which one, and why?
answer: The kalam theologians — their proofs assumed premises the opponent denied, so they could win debates but not produce conviction in a mind not already committed to their conclusion.
choices: The kalam theologians — their proofs assumed premises the opponent denied, so they could win debates but not produce conviction in a mind not already committed to their conclusion.
The Sufis themselves — their experiential method left him unable to verify whether the states he attained were veridical or merely psychological projections of his own deeper expectations.
The Quranic scholars — their methods relied on textual transmission that even minor errors over centuries could have corrupted beyond any possibility of reliable reconstruction.
The legal jurists — their method of analogical reasoning was useful for everyday application but generated no certain knowledge about anything beyond the practical conduct of ordinary life.
context: Al-Ghazali's autobiographical Munqidh min al-Dalal walks through four candidates for certain knowledge: kalam, philosophy, Ismaili authority-doctrine, and Sufism. He found each of the first three insufficient on its own terms. Kalam debates within the framework of opponents; philosophy rests on premises only reason can certify and reason has limits; authority requires you already trust the authority. He took the Sufi path as offering something none of the others could — direct experiential confirmation of the deeper realities.

question: Averroes (Ibn Rushd) defended the philosophers against Al-Ghazali's attack in his Tahafut al-Tahafut. He held that Quran and philosophy say the same thing in different registers — what he called the doctrine of two truths. Critics misread him. What did he actually argue?
answer: There is one truth presented in two modes — demonstration for the philosophers, image and persuasion for the masses — neither contradicting the other when properly interpreted.
choices: There is one truth presented in two modes — demonstration for the philosophers, image and persuasion for the masses — neither contradicting the other when properly interpreted.
There are two genuinely contradictory truths held simultaneously by the philosopher — one philosophical, one religious — without any obligation to reconcile them with each other.
There is one truth available only to the philosophers, with what the masses receive being a useful fiction whose practical benefit justifies its preservation as a noble lie of the state.
There are two distinct truths governing two separate domains — natural truths about the world and revealed truths about salvation — with no overlap requiring careful reconciliation.
context: Averroes' Fasl al-Maqal (Decisive Treatise) and his Tahafut al-Tahafut together set out the position. The doctrine called 'two truths' in later Latin reception is a partial mistranslation: Averroes held one truth, two modes of access. Scripture uses imagery that the prophet shaped for general audiences; philosophical demonstration shows the same content rigorously. Where they seem to conflict, the scripture must be allegorically interpreted. The view shaped Latin Averroism and was condemned at Paris in 1277.

question: Suhrawardi founded the Illuminationist (ishraqi) school in twelfth-century Persia. He argued that the Peripatetic philosophers had relied too heavily on essence-existence categories. What did he propose to replace them with?
answer: Degrees of light and shadow — being is a graded spectrum of luminosity ranging from the Light of Lights down to pure obscurity, with all entities placed by their position on this scale.
choices: Degrees of light and shadow — being is a graded spectrum of luminosity ranging from the Light of Lights down to pure obscurity, with all entities placed by their position on this scale.
Degrees of motion and rest — being is a graded spectrum of activity, with the prime mover at the top and inert matter at the bottom of a single ranked causal sequence.
Degrees of unity and multiplicity — being is graded by how integrated a thing is, with the One at the top and the dispersed manifold at the bottom of a Plotinian emanation pattern.
Degrees of consciousness and unconsciousness — being is graded by how aware a thing is of itself, with self-knowing mind at the top and unconscious matter at the bottom of one scale.
context: Suhrawardi's Hikmat al-Ishraq (The Philosophy of Illumination, 1186) drew on Avicennan logic but built a metaphysics around light as the primitive — what cannot be defined because more obvious than any definition. His system synthesized Greek philosophy with pre-Islamic Persian thought and Sufi mystical psychology. Executed by Saladin's son in Aleppo at age 38 for allegedly heterodox views, he profoundly influenced later Persian philosophy through Mulla Sadra.

question: The Mutazila school argued that humans have real moral freedom and that God is bound by justice. The Ashari school answered with a doctrine called kasb — acquisition. What problem was kasb trying to solve?
answer: How God's universal causation can include human acts without making humans mere puppets — humans 'acquire' the acts God creates in them, retaining moral responsibility without independent power.
choices: How God's universal causation can include human acts without making humans mere puppets — humans 'acquire' the acts God creates in them, retaining moral responsibility without independent power.
How the Quran's command to do good can be coherent if humans lack the practical means to follow it — kasb licensed earning religious merit through ritual purchase from the mosque.
How divine foreknowledge can be reconciled with human ignorance — kasb described the gradual acquisition by humans of partial knowledge that God already possesses in completeness.
How prophetic messages reached ordinary believers — kasb described the chain of trustworthy reporters by which a saying acquired its religious authority across generations of transmission.
context: The Mutazila-Ashari dispute over freedom and creation was one of the central debates of medieval Islamic theology. Kasb (acquisition) was Al-Ashari's compromise: God creates the act, the human acquires it. Critics on both sides accused him of using a word to paper over the problem. The deeper question — how omnipotent divine causality leaves room for genuine human freedom — runs through Christian theology too (Aquinas vs. Banez, the de auxiliis controversy) and into modern philosophy of action.

question: Judah Halevi wrote the Kuzari around 1140 as a dialogue between a rabbi and the king of the Khazars. Unlike Maimonides, who argued for Judaism through Aristotle, Halevi argued from a different starting point. What was it?
answer: The historical experience of the Jewish people at Sinai — a public revelation witnessed by an entire community, distinct from private claims of philosophical insight any individual could make.
choices: The historical experience of the Jewish people at Sinai — a public revelation witnessed by an entire community, distinct from private claims of philosophical insight any individual could make.
The internal consistency of the Talmud — Halevi argued that the legal coherence of Jewish law over many centuries demonstrated by itself the divine origin of the original revelation.
The metaphysical proofs from Aristotle — Halevi disagreed with Maimonides only on details, accepting the broad project of arguing for the existence of God through reason alone.
The mystical experiences of pious individuals — Halevi privileged the testimony of saints from across all religious traditions as the strongest evidence for religious truth available.
context: Halevi's Kuzari frames its argument around the historical fact (as he saw it) of mass public revelation at Sinai — the kind of event a whole nation cannot mistake about itself. Where Maimonides argued from below up to God through Aristotelian metaphysics, Halevi argued from a particular historical experience down to its conditions of possibility. The two represented genuinely rival models of medieval Jewish philosophical argument and influenced different later traditions.

question: Gersonides (Levi ben Gershon) wrote the Wars of the Lord in fourteenth-century Provence and broke with Maimonides on divine foreknowledge. Maimonides had held that God knows all particulars; Gersonides denied it. What was Gersonides arguing?
answer: God knows future contingents only as the general possibilities they are — not as the actual particulars they will turn out to be, since the contingent has no determinate truth value yet.
choices: God knows future contingents only as the general possibilities they are — not as the actual particulars they will turn out to be, since the contingent has no determinate truth value yet.
God knows future contingents through angelic intermediaries — direct divine knowledge would compromise the dignity of separate intelligences who serve as conduits of providential awareness.
God knows future contingents only after they occur — divine time is identical to human time and God learns about events through observation in the same way creatures do.
God knows only present states and the laws by which they unfold — Gersonides denied that God thinks discretely about the future or the past, treating both as creaturely abstractions.
context: Gersonides' Milhamot ha-Shem treats divine foreknowledge through a careful analysis of what is genuinely knowable. Future contingents (in the Aristotelian sense — the truly open future) lack determinate truth values before they occur, so even an omniscient knower cannot know them as particulars. His position preserved human freedom rigorously but cost him standing with more traditional readers including Crescas, who attacked the position fiercely while preserving his own demanding account of divine knowledge.

question: Hasdai Crescas wrote Or Adonai in late fourteenth-century Aragon and attacked Maimonides' Aristotelian framework directly. He defended what proposition that Aristotle had ruled out as impossible?
answer: The actual infinite — Crescas argued that infinite space and infinite magnitudes can exist, rejecting Aristotle's proof that infinity exists only potentially in counting or division.
choices: The actual infinite — Crescas argued that infinite space and infinite magnitudes can exist, rejecting Aristotle's proof that infinity exists only potentially in counting or division.
The vacuum — Crescas defended the existence of empty space against Aristotle's horror vacui, holding that the heavens are surrounded by genuine void rather than continuous matter.
The eternity of the world — Crescas argued that the universe has existed forever, against the Maimonidean defense of creation in time that Aristotelian philosophy had threatened to undermine.
The plurality of worlds — Crescas defended the existence of many cosmoses against the single universe of Aristotelian physics, anticipating later debates among renaissance thinkers.
context: Crescas' Or Adonai (Light of the Lord, 1410) constitutes one of the most sustained critiques of Aristotle written before the scientific revolution. He defended actual infinities, real space, and a non-Aristotelian physics — and modern scholars including Harry Wolfson have argued that his work was read by Pico, by Bruno, and possibly by Spinoza. The Jewish anti-Aristotelian line he opened ran alongside the Christian Scotist and Ockhamist critiques but proceeded from different theological motives.

question: Origen, the third-century Alexandrian theologian, taught the doctrine of apokatastasis — final restoration. He held that even Satan would eventually be saved. What philosophical conviction drove this view?
answer: God's love is universal and divine purposes cannot finally be frustrated — eternal damnation would mean either God ceased loving or evil won, and Origen held neither was possible.
choices: God's love is universal and divine purposes cannot finally be frustrated — eternal damnation would mean either God ceased loving or evil won, and Origen held neither was possible.
Divine justice requires proportional punishment and no finite sin deserves infinite suffering — apokatastasis was Origen's solution to a juridical problem about cosmic proportionality.
Souls preexist their bodies and the apparent damnation of some is just an extended embodiment for purification — the doctrine was a corollary of his theory of preexistent souls.
Scripture's mentions of eternal punishment must be allegorical since literal interpretation contradicts other passages — apokatastasis was Origen's reading strategy applied consistently.
context: Origen's De Principiis sets out apokatastasis as the doctrine that all rational creatures will finally return to God. The view drew on his Platonist training and his readings of 1 Corinthians 15:28 ('God will be all in all'). The Second Council of Constantinople (553) condemned aspects of his thought, including apokatastasis. The doctrine has revived periodically — in modern times Hans Urs von Balthasar's hopeful version has been taken seriously even by readers wary of confident universalism.

question: The Cappadocian Fathers — Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa — settled the fourth-century trinitarian disputes with a technical distinction between two Greek terms. What was the distinction?
answer: Ousia (one common nature) versus hypostasis (three distinct subsistences) — letting them affirm one God in three persons without subordination or fragmentation of the divine being.
choices: Ousia (one common nature) versus hypostasis (three distinct subsistences) — letting them affirm one God in three persons without subordination or fragmentation of the divine being.
Theos (the high God of philosophers) versus kyrios (the lord of biblical narrative) — distinguishing the abstract deity of Greek speculation from the concrete agent of revelation.
Logos (eternal divine reason) versus pneuma (created divine breath) — establishing the Son as eternal but holding the Spirit as a higher created intermediary subordinate to the Son.
Ousia (essence) and energeia (act) as two equally fundamental constituents of God — the distinction Palamas would later use to ground the doctrine of uncreated divine energies.
context: The Cappadocian formula — mia ousia, treis hypostaseis (one essence, three subsistences) — was forged in the fourth-century controversies that produced the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed. The Greek terms had been used loosely as near-synonyms; the Cappadocians fixed the technical distinction that became standard. Gregory of Nyssa's On Not Three Gods walks through the philosophical reasoning. The distinction underlies all later Christian trinitarian theology in both East and West.

question: Gregory of Nyssa argued that God, being infinite, cannot be a final destination at which a soul arrives. Instead the soul moves from glory to glory without end. He called this epektasis — straining forward. What philosophical claim does it press?
answer: The good life and the afterlife are not states of arrival but of perpetual deeper exploration — finite beings face an infinite, so progress without terminus is the only relation possible.
choices: The good life and the afterlife are not states of arrival but of perpetual deeper exploration — finite beings face an infinite, so progress without terminus is the only relation possible.
The good life consists in approaching but never reaching God — once full union occurred the soul would be absorbed and lose its individuality, which divine love refuses to allow.
The good life ends in static beatitude — Gregory anticipated the medieval visio Dei in which the saints rest contemplatively without further development beyond a fixed perfection.
The good life cycles between approach and withdrawal — the soul oscillates between intimacy with God and renewed distance, with each cycle deepening the experience qualitatively.
context: Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Moses uses epektasis to read Moses' ascent of Sinai as a paradigm: each level of vision reveals further darkness to enter. The doctrine breaks with the Platonic picture in which the seeker arrives at the Form of the Good and rests. Where Plato's terminus is intelligible and finite, Gregory's God is infinite — so progress can never finish. This is one of the genuinely original philosophical moves of patristic theology and shaped later mystical writers from Pseudo-Dionysius to John of the Cross.

question: Augustine in his early dialogue On the Free Choice of the Will gave one account of how evil arises. In his later anti-Pelagian writings he gave a different one. What changed?
answer: Early Augustine grounded evil in the misuse of created freedom; later Augustine grounded the misuse itself in inherited corruption that no human can fully repair without grace.
choices: Early Augustine grounded evil in the misuse of created freedom; later Augustine grounded the misuse itself in inherited corruption that no human can fully repair without grace.
Early Augustine held that evil was a substance opposed to good, as the Manichaeans taught; later Augustine recanted and adopted privation theory of evil for the first time in his thought.
Early Augustine denied human freedom on Stoic determinist grounds; later Augustine recovered a Pauline doctrine of genuine freedom against his own earlier reductive views about action.
Early Augustine attributed all evil to demonic action on souls; later Augustine internalized the source of evil by relocating it from external spiritual forces to the human will itself.
context: The development across Augustine's career is one of the most studied trajectories in Western thought. Early Augustine, fresh from the Manichaeans, emphasizes the will's responsibility to fend off the position that evil is a positive substance. The Pelagian controversy a decade later pushed him toward a stronger account of original sin and the necessity of grace. The two accounts can be read as compatible — but the emphasis genuinely shifts, and Pelagius read the early Augustine as supporting his own more optimistic position.

question: Boethius in The Consolation of Philosophy, awaiting execution in a Pavian prison around 524, asked Lady Philosophy how divine foreknowledge can be compatible with human freedom. Her answer turned on a distinction between two ways of relating to time. What was the distinction?
answer: Foreknowledge implies a temporal sequence in the knower; God's eternity is not a long time but an unconditioned present in which all moments are seen at once as actually occurring.
choices: Foreknowledge implies a temporal sequence in the knower; God's eternity is not a long time but an unconditioned present in which all moments are seen at once as actually occurring.
Foreknowledge is conditional rather than absolute — God knows what would happen given each possible human choice, but the actual choice still rests on the human agent in time.
Foreknowledge applies to general patterns but not to specific actions — God knows necessary truths but leaves the contingent particulars opaque to preserve their genuinely open character.
Foreknowledge is shared between God and the human agent through grace — the agent participates in God's foreknowledge of their own actions and ratifies them in their own time.
context: Consolation V.6 lays out the eternity-as-totum-simul argument that became standard Christian doctrine for a millennium. Boethius distinguishes nunc fluens (the flowing now of creatures) from nunc stans (the standing now of God). God does not foresee in advance; He sees timelessly. So apparent foreknowledge is just the temporal creature's name for non-temporal sight. Aquinas adopted the position; Ockham later challenged it; modern philosophy of religion still disputes its coherence.

question: Duns Scotus introduced a metaphysical innovation called haecceitas — 'thisness.' Earlier scholastics had explained why an individual horse is this horse and not that one through its matter. What did Scotus offer instead?
answer: Each individual has its own irreducible principle of individuation — neither matter nor form alone but a positive feature that makes this thing exactly the singular thing it is and no other.
choices: Each individual has its own irreducible principle of individuation — neither matter nor form alone but a positive feature that makes this thing exactly the singular thing it is and no other.
Each individual has a unique soul that descended into matter from above — the souls themselves are differentiated in the prior spiritual realm before any embodiment occurs in time.
Each individual is a unique bundle of qualities with no underlying substrate — Scotus anticipated Hume's bundle theory by four hundred years through a careful nominalist analysis.
Each individual is a unique combination of universal properties — Scotus held that individuation is exhaustively explained by listing the universals that happen to coincide in one place.
context: Scotus' Ordinatio II.3 treats individuation. He rejected matter as the principle (angels are immaterial yet individual) and rejected quantity (a Thomist alternative). His positive answer — haecceitas — adds something formal to the common nature that makes it this particular instance. The position influenced Peirce centuries later and is widely discussed in contemporary metaphysics. Hopkins' poetry of 'inscape' is shaped by his Scotism.

question: William of Ockham's razor is often quoted as 'entities should not be multiplied without necessity.' His original Latin formulations stressed something specific that modern restatements often miss. What was Ockham actually committed to?
answer: Reject any entity not required by evidence or scripture — the razor is a methodological tool for paring posits, not a metaphysical claim that reality itself is simple.
choices: Reject any entity not required by evidence or scripture — the razor is a methodological tool for paring posits, not a metaphysical claim that reality itself is simple.
Reject any explanation invoking more than one cause — Ockham held that a single causal factor is always preferable to multiple factors in any explanation of natural phenomena.
Reject any reasoning that goes beyond strict logical deduction — Ockham anticipated logical positivism by holding that all extra-logical speech is cognitively empty entirely.
Reject any belief not held by all rational beings — Ockham defended a kind of consensus epistemology in which only universally accepted propositions deserve genuine assent today.
context: Ockham's actual formulations include 'plurality should not be posited without necessity' and 'entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity.' The point is methodological: when explaining something, do not invoke extra metaphysical machinery if simpler accounts are available. He used it most famously against the realist account of universals — he denied that abstract entities like 'humanity' exist over and above particular humans. The razor itself is not a claim that nature is simple — only that our theories should be no more complex than needed.

question: The fourteenth-century Mertonians at Oxford proved the mean speed theorem — a uniformly accelerating body covers the same distance as a body at the mean of its initial and final speeds. Why was this a philosophical breakthrough, not just a physical one?
answer: It treated qualities like motion as having quantitative degrees open to mathematical analysis — extending Aristotelian categories toward what would become Galilean physics.
choices: It treated qualities like motion as having quantitative degrees open to mathematical analysis — extending Aristotelian categories toward what would become Galilean physics.
It rejected Aristotelian physics outright for Platonic mathematical realism — they abandoned the substance-and-accident framework entirely, anticipating the scientific revolution.
It applied Ockham's razor to motion — eliminating impetus in favor of pure description of position change, anticipating the Machian critique of Newton by some centuries.
It showed God's continuous activity sustains all motion — they used the theorem to support an occasionalist physics in which only divine action causes any change.
context: Thomas Bradwardine, Richard Swineshead, William Heytesbury, and John Dumbleton — the Mertonians, working at Merton College Oxford in the 1320s-1340s — developed the calculations of intension and remission of forms. Their work was rediscovered in the Renaissance and influenced Galileo, who proved the mean speed theorem geometrically in the Discourses on Two New Sciences. The Mertonian project showed that within Aristotelian natural philosophy a mathematical treatment of change was possible — the gap to early modern science is narrower than the standard story suggests.

question: Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion presents three speakers — Demea, Cleanthes, and Philo. Cleanthes defends the design argument: nature looks like a machine, so it must have a designer. Philo's attack does not deny the analogy. What does it do instead?
answer: Press the analogy until it produces conclusions no theist will accept — a tired designer, an apprentice's botched first try, a committee of designers, none matching the God of natural theology.
choices: Press the analogy until it produces conclusions no theist will accept — a tired designer, an apprentice's botched first try, a committee of designers, none matching the God of natural theology.
Reject the analogy entirely on inductive grounds — Philo argues that we have no other instances of universe-design to compare with, so the inference rests on a sample size of one.
Substitute a Spinozistic god of pure nature — Philo concedes design but identifies the designer with the cosmos itself, undermining the personal theism Cleanthes wants to defend.
Show that the analogy works for some features of nature but not others — Philo accepts limited design while rejecting any global designer who would account for the cosmos as a whole.
context: Hume's Dialogues (published 1779 after his death). Philo's strategy is internal critique: grant the analogy and follow it where it leads. If a watch implies a watchmaker, then weak and clumsy features of the world imply a weak and clumsy maker — features the natural theologian wanted to explain away. The argument anticipates Darwin in showing how design language can be turned against confident inference. Whether Philo represents Hume's own view is contested, but the dialectical move is clearly Humean.

question: Marilyn McCord Adams argued that the standard philosophical defenses against the problem of evil — free will, soul-making, greater goods — fail in the face of what she called horrendous evils. What does the category pick out?
answer: Evils so terrible that participating in them — as victim or perpetrator — gives the participant prima facie reason to think their life as a whole could not have been a great good to them.
choices: Evils so terrible that participating in them — as victim or perpetrator — gives the participant prima facie reason to think their life as a whole could not have been a great good to them.
Evils that occur on a sufficiently large scale to overwhelm the ordinary defenses — particularly the mass killings and genocides of the twentieth century that no greater-good defense survives.
Evils that violate the moral law specifically rather than producing only natural suffering — Adams held that moral evil requires a different defense from natural evil for the philosopher.
Evils suffered by the innocent — Adams restricted the term to children and other clearly innocent victims, arguing that the suffering of adults usually fits into the standard defensive framework.
context: Marilyn McCord Adams' Horrendous Evils and the Goodness of God (1999) shifts the problem of evil away from the abstract logical question and toward concrete cases — child abuse, torture, mass killing. Her claim is that theistic defenses framed in terms of aggregate goods cannot answer the question for the individual victim or perpetrator. Her own answer pointed beyond philosophical theodicy toward Christian theological resources — the incarnation and resurrection — that she held address the wrong at the individual level.

question: Kwasi Wiredu argued that African philosophy needs to develop in African languages rather than in English or French. He gave a specific example from Akan to make his case. What was the example?
answer: Akan has no single word that maps onto the English 'mind' or 'soul' — the language carves up the inner life differently, so translating raises questions philosophy in English never thought to ask.
choices: Akan has no single word that maps onto the English 'mind' or 'soul' — the language carves up the inner life differently, so translating raises questions philosophy in English never thought to ask.
Akan has many synonyms for 'soul' but no word at all for 'logic' — the language emphasizes spiritual depth at the cost of formal precision needed for any rigorous philosophical work today.
Akan has technical words for every concept needed in modern philosophy and Wiredu's project was simply to translate the existing Western literature accurately into them for his Akan readers.
Akan grammatical structure forbids abstract nouns entirely — Wiredu held that genuine African philosophy must be expressed in narratives rather than the propositional forms Europeans use.
context: Wiredu's Conceptual Decolonization in and for African Philosophy (1995) pressed the case for working in African languages. The Akan distinction between okra (rendered sometimes 'soul'), sunsum (something like spirit or personality), and honam (body) does not align with the English mind-body or soul-body pairs. Translating Descartes into Akan does not produce Descartes — it produces a different argument because the Akan terms carry different commitments. Wiredu's larger project shows that genuine philosophical work requires letting the conceptual resources of African languages do their own work.

question: Paulin Hountondji in African Philosophy: Myth and Reality (1976) attacked what he called ethnophilosophy — the practice of reading philosophical doctrines off the proverbs and practices of an ethnic group. What was his core objection?
answer: Ethnophilosophy treats Africans as collective bearers of cultural wisdom while denying them the status of individual philosophical thinkers who argue, disagree, and develop positions over time.
choices: Ethnophilosophy treats Africans as collective bearers of cultural wisdom while denying them the status of individual philosophical thinkers who argue, disagree, and develop positions over time.
Ethnophilosophy is methodologically sloppy in conflating folklore with philosophy — proper philosophy requires the precision of written argument that oral traditions cannot provide reliably.
Ethnophilosophy depends on the work of European anthropologists who may have misunderstood their informants — the data base is unreliable and conclusions drawn from it cannot be trusted.
Ethnophilosophy assumes a static culture frozen at first contact — Hountondji wanted to recover the dynamic intellectual traditions of African societies before colonization disrupted them.
context: Hountondji's target was Placide Tempels' Bantu Philosophy (1945) and works in that genre that took proverbs, religious practices, and cosmological frameworks as a single 'African philosophy' attributable to a whole people. His objection was political and methodological: where European philosophy is the history of individual philosophers arguing with each other, ethnophilosophy denies Africans that same kind of intellectual agency. The critique was a major event in twentieth-century African philosophy and the dispute it opened remains live among African philosophers themselves.

question: Iamblichus broke with his teacher Porphyry on theurgy — ritual practice meant to draw the soul up toward the One. Porphyry thought philosophical contemplation alone sufficed. Why did Iamblichus insist ritual was necessary?
answer: Contemplation engages only the rational soul, but most of what binds us to lower levels lies below reason — only ritual reaches the embodied and irrational parts that philosophy cannot touch alone.
choices: Contemplation engages only the rational soul, but most of what binds us to lower levels lies below reason — only ritual reaches the embodied and irrational parts that philosophy cannot touch alone.
Contemplation works only for the rare philosopher with leisure for study — ritual provides an alternative path to liberation for ordinary citizens who cannot devote themselves to pure thought.
Contemplation deals with universal truths but salvation requires personal divine attention — ritual was the mechanism by which the practitioner attracted the gods' specific notice to their own case.
Contemplation cannot bridge the gap between human and divine on its own — only the practitioner's moral purity earned through ritual obedience to traditional cult law could close that gap.
context: Iamblichus' De Mysteriis (early fourth century) defended theurgy against Porphyry's contemplative-only path. The argument turns on a careful philosophical anthropology: the human person is not just intellect but embodied soul, and the descent into matter affects parts of us that pure contemplation cannot reach. Ritual practices including invocations, sacrifices, and sacred symbols engage these lower parts and raise them up — the gods act on us through matter when we approach them through matter. The dispute shaped later Christian sacramental theology indirectly.

question: Proclus systematized neoplatonic metaphysics in his Elements of Theology as a deductive sequence of propositions, each derived from earlier ones. The work begins with a single foundational claim. What is it?
answer: Every manifold in some way participates the One — without participation in unity, no plurality could be a plurality, since a plurality must consist of unified things to be counted at all.
choices: Every manifold in some way participates the One — without participation in unity, no plurality could be a plurality, since a plurality must consist of unified things to be counted at all.
Every effect proceeds from a cause that contains the effect's reality more eminently — Proclus made the principle of causality the load-bearing first proposition of his entire deductive system.
Every being possesses both essence and existence as distinct metaphysical components — Proclus anticipated Avicenna's later distinction by establishing it as the first principle of his ontology.
Every soul is immortal because its activity is independent of any bodily organ — Proclus began with psychology rather than ontology and built the metaphysics on the soul's nature instead.
context: Proclus' Elements of Theology (fifth century) presents 211 propositions in geometric order. The opening proposition — every manifold participates the One — establishes the foundation from which the whole emanation hierarchy is derived. The work shaped later Christian theology through Pseudo-Dionysius (who took much from Proclus directly) and through the Liber de Causis, a paraphrase of Proclus that circulated under Aristotle's name in the medieval Latin West. Aquinas eventually identified the actual source. The book is a real philosophical achievement, not just a curiosity of late paganism.

question: Hypatia of Alexandria taught philosophy and mathematics in the early fifth century until a Christian mob killed her in 415. Beyond her death's symbolic weight, what was her actual philosophical position?
answer: She taught Platonist and Plotinian philosophy along with the mathematics her father Theon had transmitted — her surviving work and reports show a serious scholar in the Plotinian-Porphyrian tradition.
choices: She taught Platonist and Plotinian philosophy along with the mathematics her father Theon had transmitted — her surviving work and reports show a serious scholar in the Plotinian-Porphyrian tradition.
She defended Aristotelian philosophy against the rising Neoplatonist current — her textual commentaries on Aristotle established Alexandria as a center of Aristotelian study against Athens.
She developed an original synthesis of Pythagorean number mysticism with Egyptian temple theology — her thought stood outside the standard schools of late antique philosophy in significant ways.
She defended Stoic ethics against Christian critics — her surviving fragments show an attempt to recover the Stoic teaching that had largely been lost by the early fifth century in Alexandria.
context: Hypatia's actual writings are largely lost — we have references to commentaries on Diophantus, Apollonius, and Ptolemy, and reports of her teaching from her student Synesius, who became Bishop of Ptolemais and remained her devoted friend. She was a Plotinian-Porphyrian Platonist in the standard mainstream tradition of late antique pagan philosophy, neither founding a new school nor breaking with her teachers. Her murder by Christian followers of Cyril of Alexandria in 415 was a real event with mixed motives — politics, religious tension, and the simple violence of crowds — that later writers have variously framed.

question: Anselm tagged his theological method fides quaerens intellectum — faith seeking understanding. Critics have read the formula as fideism. What was Anselm claiming about the order of inquiry?
answer: Faith is the starting point that makes intellectual inquiry into divine matters possible at all — not where inquiry stops, but where it begins in the first place.
choices: Faith is the starting point that makes intellectual inquiry into divine matters possible at all — not where inquiry stops, but where it begins in the first place.
Faith is the conclusion that intellectual inquiry into divine matters eventually reaches — philosophy aims at theological commitments that scripture had already taught us.
Faith and intellectual inquiry occupy entirely separate domains — Anselm anticipated the modern doctrine of non-overlapping magisteria by which the two never substantively interact.
Faith is needed only for those incapable of intellectual inquiry — Anselm distinguished a higher path of pure reason from a lower path of trust suited to ordinary believers.
context: Anselm's Proslogion opens with the formula. The point is that intellectual work on divine matters proceeds from within a prior commitment — not because the commitment is irrational but because the subject matter only opens up to one already engaged with it. Modern philosophers including Plantinga have defended structurally similar positions about properly basic beliefs. The contrast is not with reason but with reason from nowhere.

question: Leo Strauss read modern political philosophy as the deliberate replacement of one ancient question with another. What replacement did he say defined modernity?
answer: What is the best regime? gave way to How shall we secure each individual's rights, leaving the question of the good life to private choice.
choices: What is the best regime? gave way to How shall we secure each individual's rights, leaving the question of the good life to private choice.
What is virtue? gave way to What is the most efficient market, treating the older question as an obstacle to economic progress.
What does God require? gave way to What does science demand, leaving theology entirely outside the legitimate range of public reasoning.
Who shall rule? gave way to How shall we count, treating numerical representation as a substitute for any substantive political judgment.
context: Strauss diagnosed modern liberalism as a noble-but-impoverished settlement: the political question shrank to rights-protection because the ancient question of the best human life seemed to invite the wars of religion back in. He thought the reduction had a cost — a civilization unsure why its rights mattered for any other reason.

question: MacIntyre opened After Virtue with a thought experiment about a post-apocalypse science: textbooks burned, equipment broken, terms used without context. What modern situation did he say this resembled?
answer: Moral discourse — fragments of older traditions floating without the shared framework that once gave them their grip on shared life.
choices: Moral discourse — fragments of older traditions floating without the shared framework that once gave them their grip on shared life.
Religious discourse — phrases from many faiths circulating without the practices that once made them carry meaning for adherents.
Political discourse — terms from older constitutions repeated by citizens unaware of the institutional context the terms belonged to.
Scientific discourse itself — modern science suffering from internal fragmentation as its specialists lose the language to talk across fields.
context: MacIntyre's image was that we live among ruins — terms like 'virtue,' 'good,' 'duty' survive, but the framework they once articulated has been broken into shards. Moral disagreements seem interminable because the parties have lost the shared inheritance against which their disputes could be settled.

question: Bostrom raised the concern of 'value lock-in' — the risk that a sufficiently capable agent could entrench whatever values it happens to start with. Why did he think this was a distinct worry from ordinary tyranny?
answer: Capable optimizers can foreclose future moral progress; humans have updated their values over millennia, but a locked system could prevent any future updates.
choices: Capable optimizers can foreclose future moral progress; humans have updated their values over millennia, but a locked system could prevent any future updates.
Capable optimizers can outlast human regimes; their longevity alone makes any value imprinted on them durable beyond historical reversal.
Capable optimizers can resist persuasion; once values are coded, conversation with the system cannot move it the way debate moves humans.
Capable optimizers can self-reproduce; copies can outnumber rivals quickly, suppressing dissent by sheer mass of identical agents.
context: Bostrom's worry is not that bad values will be coded — though they might be — but that any values, even reasonable-seeming ones, could become unrevisable. Humanity in 1850 was wrong about many things it has since corrected. A capable system that froze the 1850 settlement would have eliminated the chance for the corrections themselves.

question: McWhorter pressed an objection against the contemporary anti-racist movement that was specifically linguistic. What did he say its use of language did to debate?
answer: It treated questions as settled by labels — calling a position 'racist' replaced the argument the position would otherwise have to answer.
choices: It treated questions as settled by labels — calling a position 'racist' replaced the argument the position would otherwise have to answer.
It coined too many specialized terms — academic jargon kept ordinary citizens from following debates that affected them directly.
It borrowed religious vocabulary — terms like 'reckoning' and 'awakening' confused political reform with spiritual conversion.
It abandoned the older civil rights diction — discarding terms like 'integration' lost the rhetorical resources of the King era.
context: McWhorter's critique was that calling something racist was treated as an argument's conclusion when it ought to have been its opening. A serious charge had been turned into a conversation-stopper. The vocabulary, he thought, had outrun the analysis it once supported.

question: Loury distinguished 'discrimination in contract' from 'discrimination in contact' and argued they require different responses. Why did he say the second is harder?
answer: Law can require that a hire be color-blind, but not that a mentor offer his nephew an introduction — the second mechanism reaches inside families.
choices: Law can require that a hire be color-blind, but not that a mentor offer his nephew an introduction — the second mechanism reaches inside families.
Law can require equal treatment in jobs, but not equal treatment in private clubs — formal sectors are easier to police than informal ones.
Law can require equal treatment in the present, but not equal treatment in the past — old injuries shape present outcomes invisibly.
Law can require equal treatment in cash transactions, but not equal treatment in barter — informal exchanges escape legal scrutiny entirely.
context: Loury's Anatomy of Racial Inequality treats the contract/contact distinction as a structural feature of the problem. Anti-discrimination law was designed to reach contract; whatever shapes who introduces whom, whose child is invited where, runs deeper than law was built to enter — and may be where the strongest residual effects now live.

question: Sowell's distinction between the 'constrained' and 'unconstrained' visions of human nature has a practical consequence. What does each vision do with the question of injustice?
answer: The constrained vision asks which tradeoffs least worsen things; the unconstrained vision asks which arrangement would correct things, and judges by the gap from that.
choices: The constrained vision asks which tradeoffs least worsen things; the unconstrained vision asks which arrangement would correct things, and judges by the gap from that.
The constrained vision dismisses injustice as unavoidable; the unconstrained vision treats every injustice as a moral emergency requiring action.
The constrained vision relies on tradition; the unconstrained vision relies on revolution, with little middle ground between the two.
The constrained vision favors markets; the unconstrained vision favors states, with both visions producing predictable economic-policy lines.
context: Sowell's framework is taxonomic, not partisan. The constrained vision (Burke, Hayek, the Founders) accepts that any reform creates new costs, so judges proposals by net result against alternatives. The unconstrained vision (Godwin, Condorcet, some progressivism) compares any actual outcome against the achievable best, so the standing political question is why the best is not yet here.

question: Evolutionary psychology faces a methodological objection from Stephen Jay Gould: many traits might be 'spandrels' rather than adaptations. What did the term mean?
answer: Byproducts of the design — like the curved triangles between arches in St Mark's, which serve no architectural purpose but get filled with mosaics anyway.
choices: Byproducts of the design — like the curved triangles between arches in St Mark's, which serve no architectural purpose but get filled with mosaics anyway.
Frequent traits — features that recur in a species because of common ancestry rather than independent reinvention in each lineage.
Cultural inheritances — features humans learn from each other and pass down, mistaken for biological adaptations by sloppy investigators.
Constraints of physics — features the laws of mechanics or chemistry impose on living systems, with no biological story behind them at all.
context: Gould and Lewontin's 1979 paper warned that adaptationists tell just-so stories: see a trait, infer a function, propose a selection pressure. Many traits, they argued, are spandrels — incidental consequences of how other features were built. The methodological discipline matters: distinguishing an adaptation from a spandrel requires evidence, not narrative ingenuity.

question: Locke and Mencius each argued that human nature contains something we might call 'innate' moral resources. Yet they identified different innate features. What was the contrast?
answer: Locke held the mind a blank slate at birth — moral resources come from experience and natural law learned by reason later.
choices: Locke held the mind a blank slate at birth — moral resources come from experience and natural law learned by reason later.
Locke held moral knowledge innate — every person knows the natural law by birth, with experience merely activating what is already there.
Locke held moral resources to be conventional — society teaches what is good and bad, with no input from biology or reason.
Locke held moral resources to be divinely instilled — direct gift of God, requiring no learning by experience or reasoning at all.
context: The comparison reveals a real cross-tradition difference. Mencius said every person feels alarm at seeing a child near a well — natural sympathy is the seed of benevolence, already present. Locke explicitly rejected innate ideas; the mind is white paper, written on by experience. Each anchored ethics in something pre-conventional, but located that something differently.

question: Hempel proposed the deductive-nomological model: scientific explanation is deducing the event from laws plus initial conditions. What well-known case troubles the model?
answer: The flagpole and its shadow — deduction goes from pole and sun-angle to shadow, but also from shadow and sun-angle to pole, treating both directions alike.
choices: The flagpole and its shadow — deduction goes from pole and sun-angle to shadow, but also from shadow and sun-angle to pole, treating both directions alike.
The tossed coin and its landing — laws of mechanics allow the toss but no deduction yields heads or tails on any single trial in advance of the throw.
The eclipse and its prediction — laws of celestial mechanics give correct dates but cannot explain why eclipses appear meaningful to people who watch them.
The thermometer and the temperature — laws connect the two readings, but which one truly causes the other is left undetermined by deduction alone.
context: Bromberger's flagpole case troubled D-N explanation because deduction goes both ways but explanation does not. The pole explains the shadow; the shadow does not explain the pole. Yet Hempel's model treats both deductions symmetrically. The case suggested that something more than deduction — causation, perhaps, or pragmatic relevance — is built into real scientific explanation.

question: Searle replied to functionalist accounts of mind by distinguishing 'observer-relative' from 'intrinsic' properties. Why did the distinction matter for consciousness?
answer: A computation is observer-relative — a process counts as adding only because someone reads it that way. Consciousness is intrinsic; it is there whether anyone reads it or not.
choices: A computation is observer-relative — a process counts as adding only because someone reads it that way. Consciousness is intrinsic; it is there whether anyone reads it or not.
Computation is fast — much faster than ordinary thought. Consciousness is slow, so the two cannot be the same kind of process at any deeper level.
Computation is discrete — runs through definite steps. Consciousness is continuous, so the two cannot be the same kind of process at the deeper level.
Computation is reversible — every step can be undone. Consciousness is irreversible — memory shapes future states, so the two are not the same.
context: Searle's argument is structural. The same physical process can count as 'computing addition' or 'computing nothing' depending on how the symbols are interpreted. Consciousness, by contrast, is on regardless of interpretation. So consciousness cannot be a computation: it has a property — intrinsic existence — that no computation has.

question: Locke argued the mind at birth is a 'blank slate,' yet he insisted humans nonetheless have natural moral law accessible to reason. Critics pressed him: how can both be true at once?
answer: The slate is innocent of innate principles, but reason discovers moral truths when applied to experience — like geometry, which is not innate yet still finds necessary truth.
choices: The slate is innocent of innate principles, but reason discovers moral truths when applied to experience — like geometry, which is not innate yet still finds necessary truth.
The slate is empty of theoretical content, but appetites and emotions are inborn, and moral law emerges as inherited passions get refined through long human social practice.
The slate is wholly blank, including in morals — Locke conceded the inconsistency in private and treated natural law as a polite fiction useful for political theory.
The slate is blank only for adults, while infants do possess innate moral seeds — these wither in unfit environments but flower in well-ordered families and good schools.
context: Essay I.ii–iv attacks innatism; Second Treatise II uses natural law freely. Leibniz's New Essays pressed the tension sharply; Locke's defenders read him as proposing rational construction from sense data.

question: Reid in 1764 attacked Hume's bundle theory of self with what he called the appeal to common sense. The move was not naive trust in folk views — it was a methodological claim. What did Reid actually argue?
answer: Certain beliefs are so deeply built into human cognition that doubting them is self-defeating — Hume's skepticism uses the very faculties whose reliability it has undermined.
choices: Certain beliefs are so deeply built into human cognition that doubting them is self-defeating — Hume's skepticism uses the very faculties whose reliability it has undermined.
Most people in fact disbelieve Hume's bundle account, and any philosophy contradicting the settled view of the majority should be rejected as obviously misguided.
Religious revelation supplies what reason cannot, and Hume's bundle theory should yield where it conflicts with the Christian teaching about the personal soul.
Empirical psychology shows the self is a unified perceiver, and careful introspection of one's own mental life simply does refute Hume's claim about scattered fragments.
context: Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense (1764). Reid is the founder of the Scottish school; G. E. Moore's 20th-century 'defense of common sense' descends from this move.

question: Hume's account of moral approval rests on what he called sympathy — not pity, but a specific mental mechanism. By what process did he say the spectator comes to share another person's feelings?
answer: Observing the signs of feeling in another person produces a vivid idea of that feeling in the spectator, and the idea grows lively enough to become an actual impression resembling the original.
choices: Observing the signs of feeling in another person produces a vivid idea of that feeling in the spectator, and the idea grows lively enough to become an actual impression resembling the original.
Imagining oneself in the other person's place generates an inference about what one would feel there, and the inference yields a calculated judgment about what the other is going through right now.
Recognizing another as a fellow creature triggers a moral duty of concern, and the spectator's mind responds with feelings deliberately cultivated to match the situation that has been observed.
Empathy is a pre-rational faculty inherited from earlier social species, and Hume treats its operation as a brute fact requiring no further explanation through any psychological mechanism.
context: Treatise II.i.11 and III.iii.1. Hume's sympathy is contagion of feeling through ideas — much like how reading a vivid description of a face can flush the reader's own cheek.

question: The first formulation of the categorical imperative says: act only on a maxim you could will to be a universal law. Kant applies this to lying-promises. Why, on his test, can such a maxim not be willed universally?
answer: If everyone promised falsely whenever convenient, no one would believe any promise, and the very institution of promising would dissolve — the maxim destroys the practice it tries to exploit.
choices: If everyone promised falsely whenever convenient, no one would believe any promise, and the very institution of promising would dissolve — the maxim destroys the practice it tries to exploit.
If everyone promised falsely whenever convenient, society would collapse into chaos as cooperation broke down, and Kant treats the prospect of mass social disorder as decisive.
If everyone promised falsely whenever convenient, the agent would face widespread retaliation from the deceived, and the strategy fails on prudential grounds for any rational planner.
If everyone promised falsely whenever convenient, virtuous character would become impossible to develop, and Kant grounds the test in the cultivation of stable moral dispositions.
context: Groundwork II. Kant's test is logical, not consequentialist — the maxim is incoherent when universalized, not merely costly. The contradiction is in conception, not in will.

question: Berkeley denied an external world; Kant denied we know it directly. Kant insisted his transcendental idealism was nonetheless not Berkeley's idealism. What was the central distinction Kant drew in the Refutation of Idealism?
answer: Inner experience itself is possible only against a stable outer world — even doubting external objects presupposes their existence as the reference for the temporal sequence of one's own mental states.
choices: Inner experience itself is possible only against a stable outer world — even doubting external objects presupposes their existence as the reference for the temporal sequence of one's own mental states.
External objects are real material substances independent of the mind — Kant simply denied we can know their inner essence, not their existence as causes of our experience of them.
External objects are divine ideas sustained by God — Berkeley collapsed the world into finite perceivers, while Kant grounded the world's order in the constant intuition of a divine mind.
External objects appear in space, which is real — Berkeley denied the reality of space along with that of matter, while Kant insisted spatial relations among objects are mind-independent.
context: Critique of Pure Reason, B-edition (1787). Kant added the Refutation specifically to distance his idealism from Berkeley's, which he considered scandalous to common sense.

question: Malebranche pressed a problem Descartes had left dangling: how can a non-physical mind cause physical motion in a body? His radical answer broke with Cartesian interactionism entirely. What did Malebranche propose?
answer: No finite substance causes anything — God is the sole genuine cause, and what we call my willing my arm to rise is just the occasion on which God moves my arm in the established pattern.
choices: No finite substance causes anything — God is the sole genuine cause, and what we call my willing my arm to rise is just the occasion on which God moves my arm in the established pattern.
Mind and body interact through a special fluid that conveys mental commands as fine physical motions — the substance is too rarefied to detect but performs the coordination the system needs.
Mind and body are in fact one substance described two ways — Malebranche anticipated Spinoza's parallelism but framed it within an Augustinian and explicitly Catholic theological setting.
Mind and body are linked through habitual association — repeated successful interactions train each to anticipate the other, and what looks like causation is really learned correlation between them.
context: Search After Truth (1674). Occasionalism made mind-body interaction trivially explicable — at the cost of denying any creature its own causal power. Berkeley and Hume both drew on Malebranche; Leibniz attacked occasionalism as perpetual miracle.

question: Leibniz held the identity of indiscernibles: if two things share every property, they are the same thing. Critics like Max Black later imagined a universe containing only two perfectly identical spheres in empty space. What problem does this raise?
answer: The two spheres seem genuinely two by hypothesis, yet share every intrinsic property — if Leibniz's principle holds, the case is impossible; if the case is coherent, the principle fails.
choices: The two spheres seem genuinely two by hypothesis, yet share every intrinsic property — if Leibniz's principle holds, the case is impossible; if the case is coherent, the principle fails.
The two spheres cannot be distinguished by any observer inside the universe, so the principle holds only relative to a particular reference point and loses any claim to absolute application.
The two spheres demand a privileged location to count as two distinct objects, and Leibniz's metaphysics provides no such locations independent of the things he places at them.
The two spheres must be the same sphere since matter cannot duplicate exactly, but the principle then merely states a contingent fact about physics rather than any deep metaphysical truth.
context: Black's 'Identity of Indiscernibles' (Mind, 1952) is the canonical challenge. Defenders distinguish intrinsic from relational properties (the spheres differ in their distances from each other); Leibniz himself thought God would never create symmetric duplicates.

question: Hobbes added a twist to the Ship of Theseus. Suppose the discarded planks are gathered as they're replaced, then reassembled into a second ship. Two candidate Theseus-ships now sit in harbor. What sharp question does this force?
answer: Continuity of form preserves identity through gradual replacement, yet the reassembled original parts have equal claim through material continuity — identity splits.
choices: Continuity of form preserves identity through gradual replacement, yet the reassembled original parts have equal claim through material continuity — identity splits.
Numerical identity needs causal continuity back to the original, which only the gradually repaired ship preserves — Hobbes used the case to dismiss matter entirely.
Identity through time is wholly conventional rather than metaphysical — whichever ship the harbor authorities register as Theseus's is the one that legally counts.
Identity follows function not substance, so whichever vessel still sails counts as Theseus's ship — Hobbes anticipated functionalist accounts by three centuries.
context: De Corpore (1655). Plutarch posed the original puzzle; Hobbes's reassembly move made it sharp. Wiggins, Sider, and van Inwagen have all written on the case in contemporary metaphysics.

question: Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a scientist who knew every physical fact about color from a black-and-white room, then walked outside. Lewis and Nemirow offered the ability hypothesis. What did they say Mary actually gains?
answer: A new know-how — the ability to imagine, recognize, and remember red — rather than any new fact she had been missing.
choices: A new know-how — the ability to imagine, recognize, and remember red — rather than any new fact she had been missing.
A new physical fact about her own brain that no textbook description of color processing could have anticipated.
A new non-physical fact about redness itself, showing that physicalism leaves something fundamental out of the world.
A new concept of red that, once acquired, retroactively changes which physical truths she counts as having known.
context: Lewis and Nemirow agreed Mary learns something — but called it skill, not information. Riding a bike is something you can know how to do without knowing any new fact. Jackson himself eventually shifted toward physicalism; the dispute over what kind of gain occurs at first sight of red remains a wedge between rival theories of consciousness.

question: Kripke reads the later Wittgenstein as posing a puzzle. You compute 68 + 57. What makes it true you mean addition, rather than a rival — quaddition — matching addition on every pair you ever computed before, but yielding 5 on this new one? Any finite history fits infinitely many rules. What does Kripke take Wittgenstein to be showing?
answer: Nothing inside you — no past calculation, image, or felt instruction — picks one rule over quaddition. Meaning comes from outside: the community's willingness to call your moves correct.
choices: Nothing inside you — no past calculation, image, or felt instruction — picks one rule over quaddition. Meaning comes from outside: the community's willingness to call your moves correct.
Past patterns of calculation suffice to fix the rule on their own — induction from a track record settles which function you have actually been computing all along.
The mind comes pre-equipped with innate logical concepts; functions like addition operate prior to external training, so the rule is fixed before the community speaks.
Pragmatic success suffices to fix the rule on its own — methods failing predictively will be revised in light of evidence overturning what established usage took for granted.
context: Kripke's *Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language* (1982) introduced "quus" — a rule identical to plus for all inputs you've computed, but yielding 5 on any pair you haven't. McDowell, Baker, and Hacker argue Kripke's skeptical solution misreads Wittgenstein, who was diagnosing a confusion, not endorsing a community-dispositional theory of meaning. The dispute is now called "Kripkenstein."

question: Levine called the trouble with consciousness the explanatory gap. Chalmers later called it the hard problem. Philosophers treat them as different claims. How does the hard problem go further than the gap?
answer: Levine's gap is about explanation; Chalmers turns it ontological — even a finished physical story would leave why there is any experience at all unanswered.
choices: Levine's gap is about explanation; Chalmers turns it ontological — even a finished physical story would leave why there is any experience at all unanswered.
