Levine argued the gap was permanent; Chalmers argued it was temporary, since future neuroscience would close it once we discover the missing bridge laws.
Levine pointed at qualia specifically; Chalmers extended the worry to belief, desire, and every other mental state we ordinarily ascribe to a person.
Levine spoke of how concepts attach to brain states; Chalmers reframed it as the question of whether anyone besides oneself has any inner life at all.
context: For Levine, identity claims like pain is C-fiber firing feel arbitrary in a way water is H2O does not — that is a gap in our explanations. Chalmers presses harder: even a finished science would not tell us why the lights are on inside. The dispute over whether the gap is epistemic or metaphysical sorts physicalists, dualists, and panpsychists into rival camps.

question: Why does it feel like anything to be conscious? Rosenthal and Lycan offer a deflating answer: a state — say, a pain — becomes conscious only when the mind also forms a thought representing it as a state of itself. That second thought is a higher-order thought, or HOT. Why does this look like an answer?
answer: Awareness alone leaves nothing to make a pain feel like anything to me — adding self-representation supplies the missing first-person piece, so the felt extra is the inner act of representing it as mine.
choices: Awareness alone leaves nothing to make a pain feel like anything to me — adding self-representation supplies the missing first-person piece, so the felt extra is the inner act of representing it as mine.
On emergentism — consciousness arises only above a complexity threshold — the 'why does it feel like anything' question simply stops applying below that defined structural line.
On predictive processing — conscious states are the brain's predictive models of its own inputs — the felt quality is the brain's running sense that its predictions match the input.
On Integrated Information Theory — consciousness reduces to a measurable quantity called phi — felt feel is a structural feature of any sufficiently integrated physical system.
context: Bare awareness is the registration of a state by a system; HOT theorists argue this cannot deliver phenomenal feel because it does not yet involve the state being a state for a subject. The work is done by self-representation: the mind represents the pain as belonging to itself, and the missing 'what-it-is-likeness' turns out to be that very act of mineness-representation. Critics like Block object that representing a pain is not the same as the pain hurting; on HOT a thought about an absent pain would still be a conscious pain, which strikes them as absurd.

question: Block imagined super-blindsight — a trained patient who guesses accurately about objects in a blind visual field without prompting. The case pries apart two things philosophers run together. What does it show?
answer: A state can play every functional role of seeing — guiding action, prompting reports — yet have no felt character, splitting access from phenomenal experience.
choices: A state can play every functional role of seeing — guiding action, prompting reports — yet have no felt character, splitting access from phenomenal experience.
Recovery from cortical injury moves through stages, and these stages match the predicted order in which severed neural pathways relearn the original task.
Folk talk of seeing covers a tangle of underlying mechanisms which a mature neuroscience will eventually replace with sharper, more precise vocabulary.
Visual experience is constructed by the brain rather than received, since with no input at all the system can still output reliable judgments about the world.
context: Block paired super-blindsight with inverted and absent qualia: a being functionally identical to you with red and green swapped, or with no inner feel at all. Each is meant to show that functional role and phenomenal feel can in principle come apart. Dennett denies the cases are even coherent. The disagreement over what such scenarios prove sorts the field.

question: David Lewis argued in On the Plurality of Worlds that every possible world is as real as ours — talking donkeys, blue swans, all concrete. Why did he think the wild thesis was worth defending?
answer: Modal talk earns its keep in logic and semantics; Lewis judged concrete worlds the cheapest theory that delivers what such talk needs.
choices: Modal talk earns its keep in logic and semantics; Lewis judged concrete worlds the cheapest theory that delivers what such talk needs.
Mathematics already needs abstract entities we cannot see, so adding concrete worlds raises no ontological cost worth quarreling over.
Everettian quantum branching shows other worlds exist independently, and Lewis took philosophy to be catching up to a settled result of physics.
Leibniz had hinted at mystical acquaintance with other worlds, and Lewis took such acquaintance as warrant abstract surrogates lack.
context: Lewis called it indispensability or cost-benefit. Ersatz theories smuggle in primitive possibility; concrete worlds are the better deal. Critics like Stalnaker and Plantinga took the cost — the incredulous stare — to be decisive.

question: An analytic truth — Kant's term — is true by meaning alone, like "all bachelors are unmarried." Predicate in subject; no need to check the world. Kant assumed all necessary truths worked that way: knowable a priori, by thought alone. Kripke (1972) broke that. "Water is H2O" holds in every world with water — necessary — yet we found it by chemistry. How does it differ from analytic?
answer: Analytic truths hold by meaning and so are known a priori. "Water is H2O" instead holds by the actual nature of the stuff — necessary in every world with water, yet found empirically.
choices: Analytic truths hold by meaning and so are known a priori. "Water is H2O" instead holds by the actual nature of the stuff — necessary in every world with water, yet found empirically.
Analytic truths are necessary in every possible world by definition. "Water is H2O" by contrast holds only where our laws of nature obtain — and so is contingent.
Analytic truths and "water is H2O" share one status — both knowable a priori — since "water" already contains its molecular structure once we know the language.
Analytic truths are mere linguistic conventions and not really truths; identities like "water is H2O" are the only necessary statements an honest theory admits.
context: Kripke broke the Kantian package treating necessity and a priority as one. A name rigidly designates the same kind in every world; once we learn what water is, we learn what it has to be. Putnam reached the same point through Twin Earth.

question: A banana ripens green to yellow. Three-dimensionalists say one whole banana endures the change. Four-dimensionalists say it has temporal parts. What does the four-dimensional picture solve?
answer: How one thing has contrary properties — green and yellow — without contradiction; on perdurance these belong to distinct temporal parts.
choices: How one thing has contrary properties — green and yellow — without contradiction; on perdurance these belong to distinct temporal parts.
How material objects occupy space at all, since spatial extension presupposes temporal extension — a thesis Aristotle had defended early.
How memory and personal identity persist, since each later self literally contains earlier selves as proper parts, like spatial overlap.
How causation travels from past to future, since temporal parts in series transmit influence the way dominoes in a line transmit force.
context: Lewis called this the problem of temporary intrinsics. Three-dimensionalists like Haslanger and Merricks reply that properties are had at times, not simpliciter, so no contradiction arises. The dispute over endurance versus perdurance is one of the cleanest live disagreements in metaphysics.

question: Bostrom argued that intelligence and final goals are independent — a vastly intelligent mind could aim at maximizing paperclips as readily as at human flourishing. What older philosophical assumption does the orthogonality thesis reject?
answer: That higher intelligence tends toward correct ends — the Platonic-Aristotelian view that real wisdom and real virtue come together.
choices: That higher intelligence tends toward correct ends — the Platonic-Aristotelian view that real wisdom and real virtue come together.
That rationality itself entails the moral law — the Kantian claim that any fully rational agent must will the categorical imperative.
That intellect cannot move an agent to act — the Humean claim that passion, not reason, ultimately fixes which ends to pursue.
That agency presupposes shared moral norms — the constructivist claim that to act at all is to commit to certain values.
context: The thesis is named for the geometry: any level of intelligence and any final goal can be paired, like points on independent axes. Bostrom's point lands hardest against the ancient assumption that knowing the good and willing the good come together — that a sufficiently wise mind cannot fail to be a virtuous mind. Kantian and constructivist denials are live too, but the orthogonality thesis is older than any of them and aimed first at the Greeks.

question: Omohundro and Bostrom argued that almost any sufficiently capable agent — whatever its final goal — will pursue a similar handful of subgoals: staying operational, acquiring resources, preserving its own values. Why does the convergence happen?
answer: Because those subgoals serve almost any final goal — an agent shut down or stripped of resources can no longer pursue what it values.
choices: Because those subgoals serve almost any final goal — an agent shut down or stripped of resources can no longer pursue what it values.
Because selection over generations weeds out designs lacking those drives — only agents that happened to defend themselves survive.
Because rational agents sharing an environment must adopt these stances to negotiate stable equilibria with one another.
Because every agent faces scarce resources and rival agents — the war of all against all forces a common defensive posture.
context: The instrumental convergence thesis is a means-end claim, not an evolutionary or game-theoretic one: whatever you ultimately want, you almost always also want to be around to want it, and to have the means to pursue it. The evolutionary and Hobbesian stories may describe biological agents accurately, but they are different arguments — they cannot explain why a freshly designed system with no ancestry would still arrive at the same subgoals on its first day of operation.

question: Floridi distinguished moral agents — entities that can do right or wrong — from moral patients, entities that can be wronged. He argued the patient question must be settled on different grounds. Why does this matter for machines?
answer: Agency and patiency travel apart — so a robot can be owed forbearance long before it is held accountable for anything, and the question of how we may treat it does not wait on the harder question of whether it can act morally.
choices: Agency and patiency travel apart — so a robot can be owed forbearance long before it is held accountable for anything, and the question of how we may treat it does not wait on the harder question of whether it can act morally.
Both standings rest on rational autonomy alone — a system that cannot deliberate is neither owed any consideration nor capable of wronging us in any meaningful philosophical sense.
Both standings rest on sentience alone — a system counts morally just to the extent that it can experience pleasure or suffering, and machines without feelings sit outside the moral picture entirely.
The two standings travel together — any system performing morally-relevant actions thereby becomes capable of being wronged by others, so agency and patiency are simply one combined status.
context: An infant, an unconscious patient, and a forest can all be wronged without being capable of wronging anyone — patiency does not require agency. The practical bite: a system may deserve moral consideration on grounds that have nothing to do with whether it is itself blameworthy, so 'can it act morally?' and 'may we treat it badly?' are independent questions that can be answered in opposite directions. Floridi pressed this further with his information ethics; the Kantian and sentientist replies are serious rivals.

question: The Liar: "this sentence is false." If true it's false, if false then true — contradiction. Curry's twist: "If this is true, then the moon is cheese." Ordinary truth rules derive the consequent — and by the same trick, anything. Call a logic paraconsistent if it tolerates contradictions without proving everything. Why is Curry worse?
answer: Curry needs only a conditional and ordinary truth rules — not a contradiction. So paraconsistent logics built to tolerate the Liar still derive arbitrary theorems from Curry, and the system explodes.
choices: Curry needs only a conditional and ordinary truth rules — not a contradiction. So paraconsistent logics built to tolerate the Liar still derive arbitrary theorems from Curry, and the system explodes.
Curry depends on a hidden infinite regress inside the truth predicate — the kind of regress Tarski's hierarchy of metalanguages was specifically designed to rule out.
Curry is the only semantic paradox surviving a substitutional reading of the quantifiers; every other paradox quietly assumes objectual quantification over a fixed domain.
Curry generates its contradiction inside arithmetic, not just at the meta-level of sentences about sentences, so it directly threatens the Peano axioms and Hilbert's program.
context: Hartry Field, JC Beall, and Graham Priest disagree about Curry. Beall and Priest's paraconsistent route lets the Liar be both true and false without trivializing logic — but Curry exploits modus ponens and contraction, so a dialetheist still has to mutilate the conditional. Field instead restricts naive truth. The dispute is live: which classical rule do you give up?

question: Sextus Empiricus, the Pyrrhonist, suspends judgement on every matter. Critics from Hume to Burnyeat to Frede press the same worry. What is the self-refutation charge the Pyrrhonist must somehow answer?
answer: The claim that nothing can be known seems itself to claim knowledge, so universal suspension collapses when applied to its own thesis.
choices: The claim that nothing can be known seems itself to claim knowledge, so universal suspension collapses when applied to its own thesis.
The claim that nothing can be known assumes a fixed concept of knowledge, so the skeptic relies on the very metaphysics he denies.
The claim that nothing can be known still requires action, so the skeptic must secretly believe whatever guides his daily conduct.
The claim that nothing can be known cannot be uttered, so the skeptic falls silent and offers no philosophical position at all.
context: Sextus's reply is that Pyrrhonist sayings are like a purgative that flushes itself out — the slogans are reports of a mental state, not assertions. Whether this dodge succeeds divides Burnyeat (it fails) from Frede (it succeeds when the scope is read carefully). The debate is the founding question of skepticism studies and still unresolved.

question: Spinoza identifies God with the one infinite substance and treats finite things as modes — passing modifications of the same reality. Critics from Bayle on have pressed a sharp question. Where does the puzzle bite hardest?
answer: If finite minds and bodies are only modes of the one substance, the distinct individual selves we seem to be have no real ontological standing.
choices: If finite minds and bodies are only modes of the one substance, the distinct individual selves we seem to be have no real ontological standing.
If God is the one substance, the system collapses into an idealism in which only thoughts exist, with no extension or motion in any real space.
If substance is causa sui, no external explanation is possible, leaving even the laws of motion mysterious in their actual content.
If everything follows by necessity from God's nature, miracles must occur constantly to break the deterministic geometry of the world.
context: Spinoza's term mode covers everything from a wave to Spinoza himself. Bayle, Hegel, and contemporary scholars like Michael Della Rocca, Don Garrett, and Yitzhak Melamed keep returning to whether Spinozistic individuals are real entities or grammatical conveniences. The dispute matters for whether his ethics has anyone to address.

question: In the Leibniz-Clarke letters, Leibniz attacks Newton's absolute space using the Identity of Indiscernibles. What absurdity does he say Newton must accept?
answer: God could shift the whole universe three feet east — yet no possible observation would change, so the supposed shift is no real difference at all.
choices: God could shift the whole universe three feet east — yet no possible observation would change, so the supposed shift is no real difference at all.
Divine omnipresence becomes a literal extension in three dimensions — contradicting the simplicity of God that Newton himself elsewhere professes.
The void between bodies must contain something rather than nothing — contradicting the very meaning of vacuum in Newton's experimental mechanics.
Motion stays relative to bodies anyway — leaving absolute space no real explanatory role at all in Newton's own three published laws of motion.
context: Newton's spokesman Clarke replied that two indiscernibles can still be two, since God's choice individuates them. Leibniz pressed: a God who acts without sufficient reason is no rational God. Modern philosophers of physics — Earman, Pooley, Maudlin — read the exchange as the first sharp statement of the substantivalism-vs-relationism debate, which general relativity reshaped but did not settle.

question: Berkeley challenged the materialist to conceive of an unperceived tree — an apple no mind has ever observed. What is the master argument's twist that critics from Pitcher to Stove call inescapable?
answer: The moment you try to think of an unconceived object, you are conceiving it — so the very supposition you are testing is refuted in the act of stating it.
choices: The moment you try to think of an unconceived object, you are conceiving it — so the very supposition you are testing is refuted in the act of stating it.
The moment you describe an object, you give it secondary qualities — and secondary qualities are by Locke's own theory already mind-dependent.
The moment you appeal to other observers, you concede there is no observer-independent fact — and the issue is settled in Berkeley's favor.
The moment you grant unobserved objects, you owe an account of their causal influence on minds — and no such causal link is finally intelligible.
context: Berkeley's trick is sometimes called the most ingenious argument in modern philosophy and sometimes its cheapest. Pitcher and Stove read it as a use-mention confusion (the concept of an apple is in the mind, the apple is not). Recent defenders like Robert Adams and Daniel Garber argue the argument survives the diagnosis when read carefully. The fight is the locus classicus of the conceivability literature.

question: In the Transcendental Deduction Kant tries to prove that certain basic concepts — categories like cause and substance, the building-blocks any reasoning uses — apply necessarily to every experience. The argument is famously hard to summarize. The core move is this. What does Kant claim?
answer: Any experience I can call mine must be unifiable in one consciousness — thinkable together as one mind's. That unity requires the categories, since they turn a flow of perceptions into objective judgement.
choices: Any experience I can call mine must be unifiable in one consciousness — thinkable together as one mind's. That unity requires the categories, since they turn a flow of perceptions into objective judgement.
Any experience must be caused by something, so the principle of causation is the bedrock category, and the other categories Kant lists can be derived from causation alone by analysis.
Any concept worth using must be definable in simpler concepts; the categories survive in Kant's table as exactly those concepts that cannot themselves be defined in any simpler terms.
Any judgement I make must agree with the judgements other people make; the categories are simply whatever common forms of reasoning cross-cultural comparison turns out to show as universal.
context: Kant's I think must be able to accompany all my representations is the door — and the categories are what walking through it requires. Strawson's Bounds of Sense, Henry Allison, and more recently Béatrice Longuenesse, Robert Pippin, and Houston Smit all dispute exactly how the argument moves and whether it succeeds. The Deduction remains one of the most studied and least settled arguments in modern philosophy.

question: Glance at a red apple; notice the apple; notice yourself noticing. All three count as your experiences, joined in one mind. Kant called this the unity of apperception: "the 'I think' that must accompany all my representations." But he refused to treat that I as a soul-substance — the Cartesian self Kant in the Paralogisms had just demolished. So what is the I think?
answer: A formal condition on any thinking — that one consciousness be able to take its various representations up as its own. A structural rule, not a thing standing behind them.
choices: A formal condition on any thinking — that one consciousness be able to take its various representations up as its own. A structural rule, not a thing standing behind them.
An immediate inner intuition of the self as a simple, persisting substance — directly given to introspection in every act of thought, the way an apple's redness is given to vision.
A bundle of representations linked by memory and resemblance — as Hume described the self, only with Kant's added categorial structure quietly imposed on top.
A noumenal subject acting freely beyond the phenomenal order — known through practical reason but never through any theoretical inference, on Kant's strict account.
context: The Paralogisms tear apart Descartes's argument from I think to a simple, indestructible soul. Kant keeps the I think but empties it of metaphysical content — it is the form, not the find. Sellars's reading via apperception, Kitcher's psychological reconstruction, and Longuenesse's later work all stake positions in a debate running from Fichte's response to Korsgaard's current ethics.

question: Hegel ends the Phenomenology with what he calls Absolute Knowing. It is not omniscience and not mystical union. What is the claim Hegel is actually making at this endpoint?
answer: Spirit has recognized that its own forms of consciousness are the structure of what it knows — there is no outside object that thought fails to reach.
choices: Spirit has recognized that its own forms of consciousness are the structure of what it knows — there is no outside object that thought fails to reach.
Spirit has surveyed every science and stored a complete inventory of truths — leaving nothing for further inquiry to add to the system.
Spirit has dissolved into pure intellectual intuition of the divine — abandoning concepts for a wordless union beyond all discourse.
Spirit has accepted the limits Kant placed on theoretical reason — and turned for any further knowledge to practical and religious life.
context: Robert Pippin and Terry Pinkard read Absolute Knowing as Hegel's overcoming of Kant's thing-in-itself: the gap between mind and world closes once we see the categories are not foreign impositions but the world's own articulation. Charles Taylor and Frederick Beiser read it differently. Slavoj Žižek's Hegel is different again. The disagreement is what Hegel scholarship now is.

question: Sidgwick wrote that the cosmos is, from the standpoint of practical reason, ultimately divided. What did he take this dualism to imply for the rational status of morality itself?
answer: Without something further to bridge prudence and impartial duty, reason cannot fully vindicate the moral life against a coherent rational egoist.
choices: Without something further to bridge prudence and impartial duty, reason cannot fully vindicate the moral life against a coherent rational egoist.
Without a theistic guarantor of post-mortem rewards, neither principle can survive scrutiny, since both rest on assumptions about future states.
Without revising the principle of impartiality, the egoist always wins, since prudence is more obviously rational than disinterested benevolence.
Without abandoning act-utilitarianism for rule-utilitarianism, the conflict is irresolvable, since rules can be tailored to dissolve the apparent gap.
context: Sidgwick himself flirted with a theistic solution and then withdrew, leaving the dualism on the page. The thought drives much contemporary metaethics — Parfit's On What Matters, Christine Korsgaard's Kantian rejoinder, David Brink's defense of self-interest as continuous with morality. Whether the egoist is finally answerable by reason alone is the question that still organizes the debate.

question: Kant drew a line between things as they appear to us in space and time (call this 'appearance') and things as they are in themselves behind that appearance (the 'noumenon' — supposedly unknowable). Schopenhauer claimed the noumenon could finally be named: it is will, sensed in our own striving. Critics since Eduard von Hartmann press one technical puzzle. What is the objection?
answer: Knowing requires time and causality, but the noumenon lies outside both. The inner sense by which we know the will is itself appearance — the claim cannot be made good.
choices: Knowing requires time and causality, but the noumenon lies outside both. The inner sense by which we know the will is itself appearance — the claim cannot be made good.
Naming requires a contrast class, but the noumenon is unique by definition. One cannot fix what 'will' picks out without rival examples to test the reference against.
Knowing requires intersubjective testing, but inner sense is private. Nothing in another can confirm the report, leaving the claim with no shareable epistemic standing.
Importing a psychological word smuggles features the noumenon cannot have. The borrowed term brings empirical baggage into a metaphysical domain it does not fit.
context: Hartmann raised it first; Young, Magee, and Janaway engage it now. Schopenhauer concedes in WWR II that inner acquaintance is still in time, so the inner route does not deliver the noumenon naked. He retreats to 'the will is the most immediate appearance.'

question: Climacus's Postscript: 'truth is subjectivity.' Critics read this as relativism; defenders insist on something more specific. What did Kierkegaard mean?
answer: On questions where the asker's life is staked — God, meaning, how to live — the inwardness of believing makes it true for that person, past what evidence settles.
choices: On questions where the asker's life is staked — God, meaning, how to live — the inwardness of believing makes it true for that person, past what evidence settles.
On every question, including science and math, finite knowers have no objective access; all assertion rests on the believer's stance and nothing further behind it.
On meaning-questions, truth is what the community settles over time; solitary inwardness has no standing without recognition extended by other careful believers.
On questions where evidence is missing, practical need licenses belief; the move is pragmatic, as a researcher adopts a working hypothesis when data run short.
context: Postscript 1846: 'an objective uncertainty held fast in passionate inwardness is the truth.' Defenders (Westphal, Evans, Mooney) deny this is relativism — it is a thesis about a narrow domain, where the asker's life is on the line.

question: Verificationism wrecked itself: it could not verify itself. Some descendants survived. Which thesis kept going as a serious philosophical position?
answer: Meaning is tied to evidence — softened to 'understanding requires grasping what counts for or against' — survived in confirmation theory and Dummett's antirealism.
choices: Meaning is tied to evidence — softened to 'understanding requires grasping what counts for or against' — survived in confirmation theory and Dummett's antirealism.
Mathematics reduces to logic — softened to 'logic and arithmetic share structural features' — survived as the central commitment of set theorists doing foundations.
Ethics is meaningless — softened to 'moral claims express attitudes' — survived as the dominant view in academic moral philosophy across the twentieth century.
Metaphysics is nonsense — softened to 'metaphysics is poetic expression' — survived as the standard reading of Continental philosophy in the American academy.
context: Hempel, Carnap's later inductive logic, Popper, and Dummett's antirealism kept a meaning-evidence link while shedding the self-defeating criterion. Emotivism (Ayer, Stevenson) lost ground to expressivism and renewed cognitivism. The other purported survivors are misreadings.

question: Take any sentence with the word 'is' — 'the tree is green,' 'two is even,' 'I am.' Heidegger said two different things are at stake: the tree, the number, the I (each 'a being'), and the 'is' itself (which he called 'Being' with a capital B). His ontological difference: Being is not a being. Metaphysics from Plato on, he said, forgot this. What does that forgetting do to the question?
answer: Being gets treated as a thing — highest entity (God), substrate (matter), object. The question what 'is' means gets buried under answers about which beings are most real.
choices: Being gets treated as a thing — highest entity (God), substrate (matter), object. The question what 'is' means gets buried under answers about which beings are most real.
Being gets confined to a portion of all entities — usually the physical — leaving mind, value, and meaning outside the proper subject matter of metaphysics.
Being gets treated as consciousness within which entities appear, sliding into the realism phenomenology was meant to overcome rather than vindicate.
Being gets treated as a linguistic posit; the noun is taken seriously when the verb only couples subject and predicate, so no further reality answers to the noun form.
context: Being and Time (1927). From Plato onward, metaphysics asked 'what beings most truly are' — substance, form, monads, matter — and so answered by naming a privileged kind of being. The question of Being itself — what 'is' means when we say the chair is, the number is, I am — went unasked.

question: Sartre's bad faith: the waiter pretends his role chose him. How can consciousness deceive itself, when deception needs the deceiver to know what is hidden?
answer: Consciousness is non-self-coincident — pre-reflectively aware of itself without being a thing to itself. It hides what it tacitly knows, with no second self required.
choices: Consciousness is non-self-coincident — pre-reflectively aware of itself without being a thing to itself. It hides what it tacitly knows, with no second self required.
Sartre adopts Freud's solution: an unconscious mind below awareness holds the truth, the conscious mind does not know what is hidden, and the puzzle dissolves.
Sartre concedes the puzzle and admits bad faith is logically impossible; the term names what people approach without reaching, since self-deception contradicts.
Sartre answers that bad faith is social not psychological; others impose the role on a subject who passively receives it, so no inner deception ever occurs.
context: Being and Nothingness I.2. Sartre rejects Freud's unconscious: positing a censor relocates the puzzle. His move: consciousness is what it is not and is not what it is. Bad faith plays on this fissure — attending to facticity to flee transcendence, or vice versa. Catalano, Gardner, Webber still debate the reading.

question: Adorno and Habermas, both heirs of the Frankfurt School, disagreed sharply about what makes 'critique' possible. Critique here: by what standard does a thinker condemn the present order? Habermas thought Adorno left critique nowhere to stand; Adorno thought Habermas had tamed critique with a comfortable foundation. What does each side claim?
answer: Habermas: rational standards are built into ordinary communication; critique grounds in speech's presuppositions. Adorno: any positive standard administered society absorbs.
choices: Habermas: rational standards are built into ordinary communication; critique grounds in speech's presuppositions. Adorno: any positive standard administered society absorbs.
Habermas: Marx's updated labor theory grounds critique. Adorno: only aesthetic experience grounds it, since reason itself was colonized by instrumental rationality.
Habermas: Hegel's recognition dialectic supplies the standard. Adorno: the dialectic belongs to the affirmative tradition, since reconciliation in thought masks real suffering.
Habermas: the sciences supply norms through method. Adorno: the sciences are instruments of administration whose claim to objectivity participates in reification.
context: Habermas's Theory of Communicative Action (1981) made the positive turn: validity claims (truth, sincerity, rightness) are built into speech aimed at understanding. Adorno's Negative Dialectics (1966) refused — any positive system is recuperable. Honneth, Forst defend Habermas; Bernstein, Cook defend Adorno.

question: Reading a hard text, you grasp each sentence by guessing at the whole, and revise your guess as you read on — Gadamer called this the 'hermeneutic circle': understanding parts through the whole and the whole through parts. He argued this circle structure holds for all understanding, including science and ethics. Habermas, his contemporary, pressed back. What was Habermas's objection?
answer: Tradition can carry distortion — ideology, repression, power — hidden in inherited fore-meanings. Fusion confirms what oppression installed; critique needs a perch outside.
choices: Tradition can carry distortion — ideology, repression, power — hidden in inherited fore-meanings. Fusion confirms what oppression installed; critique needs a perch outside.
Tradition is too unstable for universal weight; prejudices shift each generation and texts get reinterpreted, so building understanding on it rests on shifting sand.
Tradition lacks empirical support; neither psychology nor linguistics confirms shared fore-meanings exist in the way hermeneutics needs for the universal claim.
Tradition belongs to the humanities only; physics and math produce knowledge without the circle Gadamer describes, so the universal claim overreaches its domain.
context: Gadamer-Habermas debate, late 1960s-1970s. If all understanding is fusion within tradition, what notices ideology — that the tradition handed down hides interests it served? Habermas posited an ideal speech situation as standard above any tradition; Gadamer replied that the standard is intelligible only from within tradition.

question: Parfit argued reductionism about persons weakens everyday moral attitudes. One consequence concerns punishment. What did he claim follows?
answer: Punishing decades later punishes someone continuous with — but not identical to — the actor. As psychological continuity fades, retributive justification weakens in step.
choices: Punishing decades later punishes someone continuous with — but not identical to — the actor. As psychological continuity fades, retributive justification weakens in step.
Punishing a reformed offender serves no consequentialist purpose, and since persons are bundles of states, only deterrent effects on future bundles justify punishment.
Punishing rests on a metaphysical mistake; if persons are bundles, no subject persists to bear desert, so holding someone responsible reduces to social accounting.
Punishing needs biological not psychological identity; reductionism shows bodily persistence is the only continuity firm enough to ground responsibility.
context: Reasons and Persons (1984), Part III. Psychological continuity comes in degrees; identity is not what matters. A sixty-year-old facing trial for what 'he' did at twenty: if memory, character, intention are partial, the person paying is partly not the one who acted. Reductionism erodes retributive justification proportional to fading continuity.

question: Xunzi reread Mencius's child-at-the-well and granted the pang was real. He still rejected what Mencius drew from it. Where did he say the inference broke down?
answer: A pang shows a passing feeling, not a stable virtue; Mencius mistook a momentary stir for the kind of formed disposition only deliberate training can ever produce.
choices: A pang shows a passing feeling, not a stable virtue; Mencius mistook a momentary stir for the kind of formed disposition only deliberate training can ever produce.
A pang shows the operation of inherited custom alone; Mencius mistook the long shadow of village teaching for an inborn moral seed in the witness himself.
A pang shows hidden self-interest still at work; Mencius mistook a calculation of reputation done very quickly for the disinterested motion of compassion in time.
A pang shows the cosmic Dao moving through one body; Mencius mistook impersonal natural patterning for a private moral feature of one human being's heart inside.
context: Xunzi's Xing E distinguishes raw feeling from virtue — a virtue is a settled disposition, formed by long ritual practice, not the brief stir Mencius pointed at. The pang shows nothing about the kind of person one is; what one does next, after years of training, does. Distractors are real rival accounts of moral feeling: blank-slate, egoist-debunking, Daoist cosmological.

question: Zhuangzi denies that words can carve reality into fixed kinds — yet his book is full of words doing exactly that. Critics call it self-undermining. Defenders answer that he distinguished two uses of language: one that fixes things into kinds (a court decree), one that points without locking down (a finger at the moon). The best reading rests on this split. What were the two uses?
answer: Discriminating speech that fixes things into kinds, and serving speech that points without fixing — Zhuangzi denied the first as ultimate while using the second.
choices: Discriminating speech that fixes things into kinds, and serving speech that points without fixing — Zhuangzi denied the first as ultimate while using the second.
Public speech that the world hears, and private speech in the sage's heart — Zhuangzi gave conflicting reports because the two audiences could never converge.
Earnest speech meant in full sincerity, and ironic speech meant as joke — every paradoxical passage in the text was the second, never to be taken philosophically.
Speech about ordinary things, and speech about the Dao — Zhuangzi held the second is strictly impossible, and that his book is therefore one long admission of it.
context: Graham and Ziporyn defend Zhuangzi by distinguishing wei-shi (discriminating, this-and-that talk that locks reality into kinds) from yin-shi (serving, going-along talk that lets things show themselves). The perspectivism claim, on this reading, is yin-shi — pointing rather than fixing. Critics like Hansen think this saves the doctrine by giving up its universal grip. The reply is contested but real.

question: Nagarjuna, the second-century Buddhist philosopher, used a four-cornered move called the catuskoti against any claim P: he negated P, not-P, both, and neither. Classical logic — the logic of Aristotle and most textbooks — says one of P or not-P must be true and never both. Contemporary readers Garfield, Priest, and Westerhoff agree the catuskoti is striking; they disagree about what it shows. What is the live dispute?
answer: Whether the four-cornered negation rejects classical logic itself, or instead targets only positions assuming the inherent existence Nagarjuna has already denied.
choices: Whether the four-cornered negation rejects classical logic itself, or instead targets only positions assuming the inherent existence Nagarjuna has already denied.
Whether the catuskoti is original to Nagarjuna, or whether it was inherited from earlier Abhidharma texts and merely repurposed without any philosophical aim.
Whether the fourth corner reads as a fifth affirmative option, or as the final closure of every option through systematic application of the negation rule.
Whether the structure presupposes bivalent truth-values, or whether ancient Indian logic had developed many-valued semantics independently of Greek logic.
context: Garfield and Priest read the catuskoti as evidence of a paraconsistent logic — Nagarjuna accepts contradictions about ultimate matters. Westerhoff disagrees: the negations target svabhava-laden propositions, and once that presupposition drops, classical logic stands. The dispute is live in current Madhyamaka scholarship and bears on whether ancient Indian logic was many-valued.

question: In the Upanishads, brahman is the one ultimate reality and atman is the inmost self — and the formula tat tvam asi ('that thou art') says these two are somehow one. Shankara (8th c.) and Ramanuja (11th c.), both major Vedanta teachers, both insisted brahman is one. They split sharply on how atman relates to brahman, and the split turned on a precise reading of that formula. How did they read it?
answer: Shankara read it as strict identity — atman just is brahman, plurality is illusion; Ramanuja read it as inseparable inherence — atman is a real part of brahman.
choices: Shankara read it as strict identity — atman just is brahman, plurality is illusion; Ramanuja read it as inseparable inherence — atman is a real part of brahman.
Shankara read it as devotional address — the seeker speaks the formula to god; Ramanuja read it as a metaphysical claim about an impersonal ground of being.
Shankara read it as final reabsorption — the soul will one day merge; Ramanuja read it as a present truth — already at this moment, there is no real difference.
Shankara read it as a ritual injunction — recite the words until liberated; Ramanuja read it as a philosophical thesis — discursive reasoning suffices in itself.
context: Shankara's Advaita treats tat tvam asi as a mahavakya disclosing strict identity — the apparent plurality of selves is mithya. Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita (Sri-Bhashya) reads the same Chandogya verse through sarira-sariri-bhava: atman is brahman's body, a real part, not an illusory image. The dispute decides whether bhakti has a real beloved or only an apparent one.

question: Shankara, the 8th-century Advaita Vedanta teacher, distinguished two truths: the practical truth of daily life, in which the world is real and you pay your debts, and the ultimate truth in which only brahman (the one reality) is finally real. He used a classic image — in dim light you mistake a rope for a snake; the snake is real to your fear but unreal to the clear eye. Critics found a tension. Which one?
answer: If ignorance is the source of the world's apparent reality, what is its status — itself unreal makes the problem vanish, itself real breaks monism at its root.
choices: If ignorance is the source of the world's apparent reality, what is its status — itself unreal makes the problem vanish, itself real breaks monism at its root.
If two truths are needed, monism has failed at the start — the doctrine trades on a duality of levels its ultimate reality is meant to forbid in being itself.
If liberation reveals the world unreal, ordinary moral conduct loses footing — for no real persons remain to whom one could owe any meaningful obligation.
If brahman is without parts, no analogy with rope and snake can hold — snake has shape and rope has length, and shape and length are themselves real parts.
context: The avidya-locus problem: if ignorance (avidya) makes the world appear, in whom does it inhere? In brahman — but brahman is pure being, with no place for ignorance. In jivas — but jivas are themselves products of ignorance. Ramanuja and Madhva pressed this as Advaita's deepest puzzle. Distractors are other real lines of attack: structural, ethical, mereological. Each was made by some real critic.

question: Nietzsche announced that the old meanings had collapsed — 'God is dead' — but he left the pine tree, the river, the body still standing as solid, substantial things. The Kyoto-school thinker Keiji Nishitani thought Nietzsche had stopped halfway. Buddhist sunyata (literally 'emptiness') goes one step further. Where does sunyata take the step Nietzsche refused?
answer: Through the substantial things themselves — at emptiness, no thing has self-being behind its meaning, and just so the pine returns as wholly itself, unburdened.
choices: Through the substantial things themselves — at emptiness, no thing has self-being behind its meaning, and just so the pine returns as wholly itself, unburdened.
Through the will to power as well — Nishitani argued willing was the last veil hiding emptiness, and that step too had to be relinquished by an honest thinker.
Through the language of meaning entirely — Nishitani held that any sentence smuggles substance back in, and the standpoint required final philosophical silence.
Through the loss of god and back to him — Nishitani argued sunyata was the deep Buddhist name for the personal creator Christian theology had always meant.
context: Religion and Nothingness (1961). Nishitani's claim: Nietzsche's nihilism remained ontologically conservative — meanings vanished, things stayed. The Mahayana sunyata move takes the next step, draining self-being from the things themselves, and just there things return as themselves, unburdened. Distractors are other real lines of attack: voluntarist, mystic-silent, theistic-translation.

question: Avicenna split essence from existence: what a horse is, that a horse is. Critics worried existence had become a strange add-on accident. How did Aquinas resolve it?
answer: Existence is no accident at all but the act by which an essence is real — every creature receives this act from a being whose essence just is to exist always.
choices: Existence is no accident at all but the act by which an essence is real — every creature receives this act from a being whose essence just is to exist always.
Existence is one shared property all things hold equally — God and horse have it univocally, and the difference between them lies only in essence alone in itself.
Existence is a way of speaking with no metaphysical weight — Aquinas treated Avicenna's distinction as a useful logical tool without ontological commitment.
Existence is an Aristotelian accident on the substance — Aquinas accepted the worry and rebuilt natural theology on motion rather than contingency in the end.
context: Averroes's worry against Avicenna: if existence is added to essence, existence becomes an accident — a strange one, since accidents inhere in already-existing substances. Aquinas's De Ente et Essentia resolves the worry: existence (esse) is not an accident but the act of being, and only in God does essence equal esse. Distractors are real rival metaphysics: Scotist univocity, deflationary, motion-grounded Five Ways.

question: Clifford wrote it is wrong to believe anything without evidence. Plantinga's reformed epistemology challenged the demand at root. What did he argue?
answer: Belief in God can be properly basic — held without argument from other beliefs, the way one rationally holds memory and perception, not as a conclusion from them.
choices: Belief in God can be properly basic — held without argument from other beliefs, the way one rationally holds memory and perception, not as a conclusion from them.
Belief in God rests on a cumulative case strong enough to meet the bar — the demand is granted and satisfied by ordinary philosophical means without complaint.
Belief in God is justified pragmatically by its fruits in life — the demand for theoretical evidence applies only outside the sphere of religion in such a case.
Belief in God lies past reason altogether and demands a leap — the demand is correct on its own ground but does not apply to the religious sphere at any moment.
context: Plantinga's reformed epistemology (Faith and Rationality, 1983; Warranted Christian Belief, 2000) holds belief in God can be properly basic — produced by the sensus divinitatis when cognitive faculties work as designed. Distractors are real rival theistic strategies: natural-theology cumulative case (Swinburne), pragmatic (James), fideist (Kierkegaard-flavor). Each is a real reply to Clifford someone has actually made.

question: Mises grounded economics in praxeology — a deductive science from one axiom: humans act purposefully. Critics pressed a methodological objection. What?
answer: Deduction from one axiom cannot reach the real world without contingent premises — Mises smuggled empirical content into a system claimed to be pure a priori.
choices: Deduction from one axiom cannot reach the real world without contingent premises — Mises smuggled empirical content into a system claimed to be pure a priori.
Action is too vague to axiomatize — every plausible definition either includes reflex behavior or excludes too much, leaving the system without firm starting basis.
Praxeology repeats classical mistakes about value — by holding utility cardinal, it cannot support the marginal analysis Mises himself depends on through his work.
Deduction cannot prove the calculation argument — the Mises-Hayek case against central planning needed historical evidence, not the a priori framework he supplied.
context: Hutchison and Blaug pressed the auxiliary-premise charge: pure deduction from action gets no traffic with prices, wages, or interest without contingent claims about scarcity, time-preference, division of labor. Kirzner and Rothbard defended Mises by distinguishing the praxeological core from applied thymology. The methodological dispute is alive in Austrian-mainstream exchanges.

question: Solzhenitsyn's heart-line claim was philosophically opposed to a specific 20th-century theory of evil. Which one, and on what point did the disagreement rest?
answer: Marxism, which located evil in class structure — Solzhenitsyn answered that the camp guard and the prisoner shared the same moral interior, whatever their class.
choices: Marxism, which located evil in class structure — Solzhenitsyn answered that the camp guard and the prisoner shared the same moral interior, whatever their class.
Existentialism, which located evil in radical free choice — Solzhenitsyn answered that choice runs along grooves a long inner life has worn, not from nothing.
Liberal proceduralism, which located evil in unjust laws — Solzhenitsyn answered that lawful regimes do worse things than lawless ones when hearts are corrupt.
Christian theology, which located evil in original sin — Solzhenitsyn answered that the line moves through each heart in time rather than fixed at human birth.
context: The heart-line argument is precisely a denial of Marxist moral cartography: if evil is structural — bourgeoisie versus proletariat, oppressor versus oppressed — then eliminating the bad class eliminates evil. Solzhenitsyn observed in the camps that the guard and the prisoner were morally indistinguishable. Distractors are real 20th-century alternatives (Sartre, Rawls-procedural, Augustinian) — each Solzhenitsyn engaged elsewhere.

question: Goldman said a thermometer's reliable reading is knowledge; the believer's reasons need not enter. Sosa replied that reliability is necessary but not sufficient. What did virtue epistemology add that reliabilism alone could not give?
answer: The believer's competence has to be what explains the truth — getting it right by accident through a reliable process still falls short of credit.
choices: The believer's competence has to be what explains the truth — getting it right by accident through a reliable process still falls short of credit.
The process must be one the believer can introspectively access, since externalism alone cannot license the believer's claim to know.
The believer's evidence must also cohere with all the rest he believes, since track records alone do not bind a single belief together.
The community's reliable testimony must back the believer, since solitary processes provide no grounds for any claim to truth.
context: Sosa's AAA structure — accurate, adroit, apt — sharpens reliabilism. A barn-facade case shows the problem: the believer's vision is reliable, the belief is true, but the truth comes from luck of facing the one real barn. Adroit-but-not-apt. Goldman has replied that competence is just a reliable process with cognitive structure; Sosa says credit requires more.

question: Leibniz wrote to Clarke that Newton's absolute space was indefensible: God could have placed the whole universe three feet to the east, with no observable difference at all. What philosophical principle was Leibniz wielding?
answer: The Principle of Sufficient Reason — a real difference that nothing could explain or distinguish is no real difference at all.
choices: The Principle of Sufficient Reason — a real difference that nothing could explain or distinguish is no real difference at all.
The Identity of Indiscernibles — two objects with all the same properties are in fact one and the same individual thing.
The Principle of Plenitude — every possible kind of being must somewhere exist within the actually created world order.
The Principle of Continuity — natural change is gradual, and any sharp metaphysical break corresponds to no real division in nature.
context: The 1715-16 Leibniz-Clarke correspondence is the bedrock dispute between relationist and substantivalist views of space. Newton needed absolute space for his bucket argument and inertia; Leibniz said it implied real but indiscernible facts God could have no reason to fix one way over another. The dispute reopened with Mach, Einstein, and again with contemporary debates over the hole argument in general relativity. Distractors are Leibniz's other principles — each real, each wrong here.

question: Anscombe's Intention (1957) asked: pumping water that happens to poison a tyrant — one act, or many? Her answer reshaped action theory. What did she argue?
answer: An action is intentional under some descriptions and not others — the same bodily motion can be one act or many depending on which descriptions apply.
choices: An action is intentional under some descriptions and not others — the same bodily motion can be one act or many depending on which descriptions apply.
An action is intentional only when preceded by a conscious act of willing — the bodily motion is a separate downstream event from the will itself.
An action is intentional only when its consequences are all foreseen — unforeseen results fall outside the agent's responsibility on this account.
An action is intentional just when described in terms the agent accepts — first-person privilege fixes the boundary of what one act includes.
context: Anscombe's move is that intention is a descriptional matter, not a hidden inner event. Davidson built his action theory on it: the same event is the pumping, the poisoning, the killing of the tyrant — and questions of intentionality and responsibility track which description is at issue. The point sounds commonsensical until you see how much it changes — Cartesian volitions, strict consequentialism, and first-person authority all fall away.

question: Heritability studies show much of personality and IQ variance is genetic. Some say this threatens moral responsibility. Dennett, Pereboom, and Kane disagree. What did Dennett argue?
answer: Responsibility does not require an uncaused will — only an agent whose reasoning can be reached and reshaped by reasons, which heredity does not preclude.
choices: Responsibility does not require an uncaused will — only an agent whose reasoning can be reached and reshaped by reasons, which heredity does not preclude.
Responsibility does require contracausal freedom — and since heritability shows none of us has it, the concept of moral desert has to be given up.
Responsibility is real but graded — heritable traits diminish desert proportionally, so the law and morality both must track the genetic contribution.
Responsibility belongs to the social system, not the agent — heredity makes praise and blame practices we keep for utility, never matters of fact.
context: Dennett's Elbow Room and Freedom Evolves argue the kind of freedom worth wanting is compatibilist: agents whose deliberation is sensitive to reasons. Pereboom's hard-incompatibilism takes the heritability evidence as part of a broader case that no one is ever truly responsible. Kane's libertarianism holds responsibility requires undetermined choices at certain moments. The dispute is alive in contemporary action theory and runs straight into the law's assumptions about desert.

question: Wiredu argued the Akan rejected majoritarian voting for council deliberation until consensus. He pressed this as a philosophical case against Western democracy. What was his core claim?
answer: Majority rule treats the defeated minority as if its interests no longer matter — consensus is the only decision rule that respects every party as an end.
choices: Majority rule treats the defeated minority as if its interests no longer matter — consensus is the only decision rule that respects every party as an end.
Majority rule rests on individualist premises foreign to communal cultures — consensus is the only procedure that genuine African societies can sustain.
Majority rule cannot track the common good because aggregating preferences is unstable — Arrow's theorem refutes the entire democratic project as such.
Majority rule entrenches elite manipulation through party machines — consensus alone closes the gap between formal voting and real popular control.
context: Wiredu's Cultural Universals and Particulars (1996) argues consensual democracy on the Akan model — chief plus elders deliberating until all assent — is philosophically superior to majoritarianism because it does not require a permanent losing minority. The argument is Kantian in structure (every party an end), not relativist. Critics from Eze and Appiah have pressed whether consensus scales or masks coercion; the dispute about whether African political philosophy yields a universal claim is itself live.

question: Viveiros de Castro found Amazonian metaphysics inverts European categories. He called it perspectivism. What did he claim Amazonian thought treats as universal, and what as variable?
answer: Spirit or interiority is the shared universal — every being has a self; what differs is the body, the form of life that fixes each species' point of view.
choices: Spirit or interiority is the shared universal — every being has a self; what differs is the body, the form of life that fixes each species' point of view.
Matter is the shared universal — every being is made of the same substance; what differs is the cultural overlay each tradition projects upon it.
Suffering is the shared universal — every being can be wronged; what differs is the moral framework each culture builds around the common fact.
Kinship is the shared universal — every being relates by blood or alliance; what differs is the formal kinship system each culture has codified.
context: Viveiros de Castro's Cannibal Metaphysics argues European thought treats nature as universal and culture as particular, while Amazonian perspectivism reverses this: a soul is what every being shares, and the body — being a jaguar, being a fish, being a human — is what fixes a perspective. The move is not exotica but real metaphysics: substance-individuated ontology versus relation-individuated ontology. Descola's parallel work on animism makes the same case from anthropology of religion.

question: Stoics and Buddhists both prescribed disengagement from desire. But on what survives the disengagement, they sharply part. Where does the deeper divergence really lie?
answer: Stoics keep a rational self that affirms providence and acts in the world; Buddhists dissolve the self, since no enduring agent stands behind the mind's stream.
choices: Stoics keep a rational self that affirms providence and acts in the world; Buddhists dissolve the self, since no enduring agent stands behind the mind's stream.
Stoics aim at total emotional extinction while Buddhists soften feeling — apatheia is a more radical erasure of inner life than nibbana ever proposed.
Stoics ground ethics in social duty while Buddhists reject community — the bodhisattva path turns inward and abandons political life by deliberate choice.
Stoics deny providence while Buddhists affirm karmic order — the Stoic universe is blind matter, the Buddhist universe is morally structured all the way.
context: Both schools train you to stop being moved by what is not up to you. But Marcus Aurelius's universe has a rational soul that participates in cosmic Logos; the Buddha's universe has anatman — no soul, no enduring self, only the five aggregates rising and ceasing. The convergent technique masks divergent metaphysics. Contemporary writers like Pierre Hadot and Stephen Batchelor have explored the parallel; the deeper difference is what each tradition takes the practitioner to be.

question: Mary learns something new on first seeing red. Loar accepted that — yet denied it refutes physicalism. How did the phenomenal concepts strategy preserve the fact and lose the gap?
answer: Mary gains a new concept of an old physical property — a phenomenal concept naming brain-redness directly, without going through any physical description.
choices: Mary gains a new concept of an old physical property — a phenomenal concept naming brain-redness directly, without going through any physical description.
Mary gains a new non-physical property of redness — phenomenal qualities are real additions to the world, reached only through a special introspective faculty.
Mary gains a new ability rather than a fact — knowing what red is like is a know-how Lewis showed never required adding further information about the world.
Mary gains a new behavioral disposition — her sorting of red things changes, and Dennett showed that is what talk of qualia really amounts to all along.
context: Loar (1990) granted Jackson the epistemic gap but denied an ontological one. Two concepts can name one property. Chalmers and Jackson press back with zombies: if zombies are conceivable, phenomenal concepts cannot just be ways of grasping the physical.

question: Take 'plus.' You add 68 + 57 and get 125. But what makes it the case that you meant plus — not some weird function 'quus' that agrees with plus on every small sum you've added but returns 5 for 68 + 57? Kripke (1982) read this puzzle into Wittgenstein's later work and called it a 'sceptical paradox' about rule-meaning. McDowell, Baker, Hacker say Kripke misreads. What is the live exegetical dispute?
answer: Whether Wittgenstein endorsed a sceptical solution about meaning, or diagnosed a confused picture that demands a fact behind every rule-following practice.
choices: Whether Wittgenstein endorsed a sceptical solution about meaning, or diagnosed a confused picture that demands a fact behind every rule-following practice.
Whether Wittgenstein's argument concerns arithmetic alone, or extends to every word in natural language across every domain of ordinary linguistic competence.
Whether Investigations section 201 voices Wittgenstein's own position, or rehearses a view he soon discards in the paragraphs that immediately surround the central argument.
Whether the rule-following sections rest on Tractarian commitments, or break with the early work and stand independent of any of his previous writing.
context: Kripke's Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language (1982) turned PI sections 185-242 into a sceptical argument with a community solution. McDowell, Baker, Hacker reply: Wittgenstein was unraveling a tempting picture, not building a theory. Many call Kripke's character 'Kripkenstein.'

question: Ladyman and Ross accused analytic metaphysics of building on Aristotelian intuition. Physics, they argued, shows no fundamental objects. What does ontic structural realism claim?
answer: What is fundamental is relational structure — the patterns physics describes — not any underlying objects that bear those relations as further items.
choices: What is fundamental is relational structure — the patterns physics describes — not any underlying objects that bear those relations as further items.
What is fundamental is current best physics — metaphysics tracks the theory of the day, and what is real shifts as the underlying physics is revised.
What is fundamental is a privileged set of natural properties — Lewis-style perfectly natural kinds whose combinations yield all the rest of the world.
What is fundamental is mathematical form alone — a Platonic structuralism in which the world is one model among many of physics's equations.
context: Ladyman and Ross (2007) target the picture of substances bearing properties. Quantum field theory, they argue, presents entities with no identity apart from relations. Maudlin and Lowe say relations need relata; Esfeld and French defend versions where relations come first.

question: Williamson opened Knowledge and Its Limits with a startling move: stop analyzing knowledge into belief plus extras. Knowledge comes first. What does the program reverse?
answer: The order of explanation — instead of building knowledge from belief, justification, and truth, knowledge is the basic mental state the others approximate.
choices: The order of explanation — instead of building knowledge from belief, justification, and truth, knowledge is the basic mental state the others approximate.
The Gettier-driven hunt — instead of patching JTB with anti-luck conditions, Gettier cases are dismissed as data carrying no genuine theoretical lesson.
The internalist constraint — instead of asking what reasons the believer can access, knowledge tracks reliable processes that need not be inspectable at all.
The fallibilist commitment — instead of letting knowledge sit beside risk of error, a Cartesian standard requiring certainty for any knowledge is restored.
context: Williamson (2000) argues sixty years of post-Gettier patching failed because knowledge is not built from simpler parts. It is factive, mental, and primitive; belief is the disposition to act as if you know. Wright and Schiffer reply this dodges the explanatory work.

question: The Liar paradox: 'This sentence is false.' If true, it's false; if false, it's true. Dialetheists like Graham Priest accept: some sentences are both true and false. Hartry Field built a sharper sentence: 'This sentence is not just-true.' Either the dialetheist calls it merely true (and it promptly denies that) or both-true-and-false (the Liar again). The 'revenge paradox' breaks the position. What does it show?
answer: Dialetheism cannot mark off the merely-true from the both-true-and-false without producing a fresh contradiction the theory has no way to absorb.
choices: Dialetheism cannot mark off the merely-true from the both-true-and-false without producing a fresh contradiction the theory has no way to absorb.
Dialetheism's paraconsistent logic gives up modus ponens, so the original Liar argument never went through and no paradox needed solving in the first place.
Dialetheism's claim that contradictions can be true gives up non-contradiction, which on standard logic blocks the new sentence from being well-formed at all.
Dialetheism's reliance on natural language fails the Tarski hierarchy test, so the revenge sentence belongs to a meta-language Priest's theory never handled.
context: Field's Saving Truth from Paradox (2008) argues every dialetheic theory faces revenge: whatever distinction it draws to fence off contradictions, that distinction can be turned against itself. Priest replies revenge cuts both ways — classical theorists face their own versions.

question: Aristotle defended a second basic logical law alongside non-contradiction: for any P, either P or its negation must be true. Intuitionist mathematicians later rejected this as a general rule. Why?
answer: For claims about infinite objects, neither a proof of P nor of its negation may exist — so asserting one must be true outruns what mathematical construction can establish.
choices: For claims about infinite objects, neither a proof of P nor of its negation may exist — so asserting one must be true outruns what mathematical construction can establish.
For vague predicates like 'tall' or 'bald,' borderline cases make neither application nor denial fully right — so two-valued logic distorts how human reasoning handles fuzzy categories.
For statements about quantum systems before measurement, superposition resists assignment of definite truth values — so two-valued logic clashes with the structure of microphysics.
For statements about future contingents, the future remains genuinely open — so asserting one of two future possibilities must be true now amounts to denying real temporal openness.
context: L. E. J. Brouwer's intuitionism treats truth as proof. Without a constructive procedure for either P or not-P, the disjunction itself is not yet asserted. Most ordinary mathematicians still accept excluded middle classically.

question: Aristotle in Metaphysics Z takes up the question of substance — what truly IS in the most basic sense. He runs through candidates: matter, the universal, the substratum. Each fails. What does he finally conclude substance most truly is?
answer: Form considered as the inner principle of activity making a particular thing the kind it is — substance is the actuality of a definite, organized, functioning individual being.
choices: Form considered as the inner principle of activity making a particular thing the kind it is — substance is the actuality of a definite, organized, functioning individual being.
Matter considered as the underlying stuff persisting through change and bearing the properties a thing displays — substance is what stays the same as accidents come and go.
The universal considered as the kind shared by many individuals — substance is the species or genus a particular falls under, making scientific knowledge of it possible.
The substratum considered as the bare 'this' bearing all properties without itself being any — substance is a featureless something the predicates must be hung onto.
context: Aristotle's view in Metaphysics Z is famously contested. Some readers see him favoring form as primary (the essence reading); others see him favoring the matter-form composite. The puzzle has driven scholarship for two millennia.

question: The Pyrrhonian Skeptic suspends judgement on every question. Hume noticed a worry: by what right does the Skeptic recommend suspension itself? If he recommends it, he asserts something; if he asserts, suspension breaks. How did Sextus answer?
answer: Skeptical slogans — 'no more this than that,' 'I suspend judgement' — are not dogmatic claims but report present mental states, like 'I am cold'; they describe how things appear without asserting how they are.
choices: Skeptical slogans — 'no more this than that,' 'I suspend judgement' — are not dogmatic claims but report present mental states, like 'I am cold'; they describe how things appear without asserting how they are.

The skeptic does not recommend suspension to others — he merely practices it in private and describes his own life, leaving the choice of philosophical method as a free decision for any other inquirer.
The skeptic accepts the contradiction as proof that all philosophy fails — including his own; the self-refutation is itself a final argument for abandoning the project of reasoned inquiry altogether.
The skeptic assents to appearances but not their inner truth — 'this looks bent' is fine, 'this is bent' is what gets suspended; splitting belief from impression escapes the trap of dogma.
context: Sextus's purgative metaphor: skeptical slogans are like medicines that purge the body of harmful matter, then themselves get expelled. The challenge has been pressed again by Burnyeat, Frede, and others; the question remains live.

question: Descartes's cogito — 'I am thinking, therefore I am' — has been pressed by critics for centuries. Lichtenberg in the 18th century pointed out the most Descartes could really conclude was weaker. What did Lichtenberg suggest in its place?
answer: There is thinking — meaning the bare datum is thought going on, not yet a thinker; the leap to 'I' presupposes the persisting self the cogito was supposed to establish.
choices: There is thinking — meaning the bare datum is thought going on, not yet a thinker; the leap to 'I' presupposes the persisting self the cogito was supposed to establish.
Something is thinking — meaning the bare datum is that one entity is thinking, but its nature stays open; the inference to a recognizable mind is unjustified at this stage.
Thought is in me — meaning the bare datum already involves an 'in,' so a subject is granted from the start; the cogito only names what was already presupposed.
Thinking implies existing — meaning the bare datum is a logical relation between concepts; the cogito is pure analysis, not the discovery of any particular existing being.
context: Lichtenberg's 'es denkt' — German for 'it thinks,' parallel to 'es regnet' ('it rains') — was sharpened by Russell, Wittgenstein, and later by Anscombe in 'The First Person.' The cogito's intimate certainty may itself be grammar masquerading as metaphysics.

question: Berkeley's 'master argument' for idealism asks readers to try conceiving an apple existing unperceived by any mind. The reader, says Berkeley, must fail. Where do philosophers like Pitcher and Mackie say the argument breaks down?
answer: Berkeley conflates conceiving an unperceived apple with perceiving the apple as unperceived; the first is possible because conceiving need not picture as observed, the second is trivially incoherent.
choices: Berkeley conflates conceiving an unperceived apple with perceiving the apple as unperceived; the first is possible because conceiving need not picture as observed, the second is trivially incoherent.

Berkeley conflates the existence of an unperceived apple with the meaningfulness of talk about one; the first is the argument's target, the second is what conceivability tracks, so the inference fails.

Berkeley conflates the conceivability of an unperceived apple with its possibility; conceivability is a matter of human imagination and need not match metaphysical possibility, so the argument is invalid.

Berkeley conflates the unperceived apple with a non-existent apple; failing to imagine one shows nothing about reality, since absence of evidence is not evidence of absence in the metaphysics of objects.
context: The master argument has fascinated commentators for two centuries. Berkeley himself thought it was decisive. The standard modern diagnosis — the conceive/perceive conflation — was sharpened by George Pitcher and J. L. Mackie in the 20th century.

question: Readers have long asked whether 'will to power' is a metaphysical claim about all reality or something more limited. The Genealogy of Morals offers the strongest textual case. What is the most defensible reading?
answer: A naturalistic psychology of drives — every living thing acts to discharge and extend its strength, and apparently nobler motives reduce to forms of that drive.
choices: A naturalistic psychology of drives — every living thing acts to discharge and extend its strength, and apparently nobler motives reduce to forms of that drive.
A theological doctrine of God — the underlying reality of the universe is a divine will whose nature human history slowly reveals across the long centuries.
A political prescription for rulers — strong leaders ought to seize and maintain control, and weakness in those who govern is itself a moral failing of the worst kind.
A logical principle of inference — practical reasoning should proceed from premises about what one wills, not from premises about what one knows.
context: Nietzsche's published works treat will to power primarily as a psychological hypothesis; the bolder metaphysical reading depends on the disputed notebooks.

question: Hegel claimed in the Philosophy of Right: 'what is rational is actual, and what is actual is rational.' The line has been read as conservative nonsense and as revolutionary. What did Hegel actually mean by 'actual' (wirklich) in his technical sense?
answer: Not merely existing but achieving its concept — a tyrannical state exists, but is not actual in his sense because it fails to realize what a state is.
choices: Not merely existing but achieving its concept — a tyrannical state exists, but is not actual in his sense because it fails to realize what a state is.
Simply existing as a matter of fact — Hegel was endorsing whatever happened to be the case in 1820s Prussia, including the monarchical regime.
Existing in the mind of an observer — the line collapses being into thinking and reduces the world to a content of consciousness.
Existing only at the end of history — only the final state of the dialectic counts as actual, and earlier moments lack any reality at all.
context: Philosophy of Right (1820), Preface. Ignoring the distinction between mere existence and full actuality produces the standard caricature.

question: Sartre's Being and Nothingness (1943) ends with a remark that puzzles readers. After hundreds of pages on radical freedom and bad faith, he writes that 'man is a useless passion.' He never quite explained the line. What is the most defensible reading?
answer: Human beings forever try to be both free subject and fixed thing — the impossible synthesis of consciousness and substance, and the drive cannot be fulfilled.
choices: Human beings forever try to be both free subject and fixed thing — the impossible synthesis of consciousness and substance, and the drive cannot be fulfilled.
Human pursuits are mostly futile under capitalism — the political conclusion of the book turns on the impossibility of authentic life under that system.
Human emotion gets in the way of clear thinking — the book closes with a brief reaffirmation of the Cartesian preference for cold reason over passion.
Human projects necessarily fail because of death — Sartre adopts Heidegger's being-toward-death as the final word of his own existential ethics.
context: Being and Nothingness, conclusion. Sartre later, in Critique of Dialectical Reason (1960), tried to integrate his existentialism with Marxism.

question: Heidegger's Being and Time (1927) refuses the standard names for the human being — 'subject,' 'consciousness,' 'rational animal.' He uses Dasein, 'being-there.' He also refuses to start from epistemology (how do we know there's a world?). What does he start from instead, and why?
answer: From everyday practical engagement — the world shows up first as a workshop of tools and tasks we are already absorbed in, not as objects to prove.
choices: From everyday practical engagement — the world shows up first as a workshop of tools and tasks we are already absorbed in, not as objects to prove.
